7.4     The supermoduli space

7.4.1   Odd moduli

An infinitesimal moduli deformation of an ordinary Riemann surface Σ is in 1-1 correspon-
dence with a zero mode of the b ghost, i.e. a holomorphic quadratic differential. Similarly,
an infinitesimal odd moduli deformation of a split SRS C0 is in 1-1 correspondence with a
zero mode of the β ghost subject to the spins structure. In the absence of punctures, the
difference between the number of β zero modes (or odd moduli) and the number of γ zero
modes (or superconformal Killing spinors) can be determined from the anomaly of the βγ
ghost number (6.26) to be equal to 2h − 2, where h is the genus of the surface, regardless of
the spin structure. As we have seen in the previous section, each NS puncture introduces one
additional odd modulus, and each pair of R punctures introduce one additional odd modu-
lus. In the case of genus h = 0 with at least 3 punctures, h = 1 with at least 1 puncture, or
h ≥ 2 with any number of punctures, there are no superconformal Killing spinors (as they

                                              147
would square to conformal Killing vectors), and therefore the number of odd moduli do is
equal to the βγ ghost number anomaly
                                                                  nR
                                       do = 2h − 2 + nNS +           ,                              (7.38)
                                                                   2
where nNS and nR are the number of NS and R punctures respectively. This conclusion holds
for non-split punctured SRS as well.

7.5    Unitarity of superstring amplitudes

Similarly to the bosonic string consideration of section 4.6, the superstring amplitude (7.18) is
subject to highly nontrivial consistency conditions imposed by the unitarity of the S-matrix in
10-dimensional Minkowskian spacetime. In particular, integration near the boundary of the
moduli space gives rise to singularities of the (analytically continued) scattering amplitude
that correspond to the propagation of intermediate on-shell particles.
    Near the degeneration limit where the worldsheet surfaces Σ pinches into surfaces Σ1 and
Σ2 joined at a puncture, the geometry of the SRS C can be constructed via the plumbing
fixture. We begin with the case of a pair of NS punctures, located at super coordinate
(z, θ) = (0, 0) on a disc D1 in the SRS C1 , and at (z ′ , θ′ ) = (0, 0) on a disc D2 in the SRS
C2 . The plumbing fixture reduces the total number of NS punctures by 2, and according to
(7.38) leaves the total number of odd moduli unchanged. It suffices to consider the plumbing

7.8       The full PCO contour with vertical integration

In the PCO formalism, spurious singularities occur along the complex codimension 1 locus86
det(fa (zb )) = 0 in the fiber bundle Yh,n → Mh,n . It is generally not possible to avoid the
spurious singularities by any choice of the sections Sh,n,ϵ in (7.72). From the SRS perspective,
this amounts to the statement that the fermionic coordinates defined by (7.40) cannot be
extended to the entire supermoduli space. Nonetheless, it is possible to perform the super-
moduli integration of (7.18) by breaking up the integration contour Gh,n,ϵ into patches, each
of which admits a non-singular fermionic coordinate system, as follows.

8.3      One-loop amplitudes involving Ramond states

To calculate one-loop amplitudes that involve Ramond states requires some care in treating
spin structures and the correlation function of spin fields on the torus. Consider for instance a
torus of modulus τ with m Ramond punctures at z = z1 , · · · , zm , and periodicity assignment
ϵ1 , ϵ2 = ± for the worldsheet spinor fields along the spatial circle α at Im(z) = 0 and along
the Euclidean time circle β at Im(z/τ ) = 0 respectively. Note that if we move the position zi
of a Ramond puncture continuously across α (or β), ϵ1 (or ϵ2 ) changes sign. We also need to
insert do = m2 holomorphic PCOs, whose locations are denoted x1 , · · · , x m2 . The βγ system

                                  √

where · · · stands for higher derivative terms that come with additional powers of α′ . Up
to a field redefinition, (9.8) is equivalent to the string tree-level massless effective action
(8.9), truncated to the (NS,NS) sector. In particular, the two-derivative terms shown in
(9.8) are determined by the vanishing of Weyl anomaly at 1-loop order with respect to α′ .
The absence of order α′ and α′2 corrections to (8.9), and the presence of order α′3 correction
(8.18), indicate that there are no nontrivial 2-loop and 3-loop corrections to the condition of
vanishing Weyl anomaly, but there is a nontrivial correction at 4-loop order! Remarkably,
this has been shown via direct perturbative computations in the supersymmetric NLSM.109
    Depending on whether the type IIA or IIB GSO projection is imposed, the full spacetime
massless effective action including (R,R), (NS,R), and (R,NS) fields should admit N = (1, 1)
or N = (2, 0) local super-Poincaré symmetry. The leading low-energy effective theory at
two-derivative order is uniquely determined by supersymmetry to be the type IIA or IIB
supergravity, described in Appendix N. It would be desirable to have a worldsheet the-
ory of superstrings propagating in general spacetime backgrounds with, for instance, (R,R)
fields turned on. However, a background deformation of (R,R) type necessarily couples the
matter system to the superconformal ghosts nontrivially, and there is no obvious prescrip-
tion analogous to (9.3) due to the necessity of half-integer picture number. To characterize
(R,R) backgrounds beyond the low-energy effective theory requires either a formulation of
the worldsheet theory in which the (R,R) fields can be represented by a local CFT deforma-
tion,110 or through the closed superstring field theory introduced in Chapter 10.


9.2     Superstrings in Calabi-Yau spaces

An important class of superconformal NLSM are those with Calabi-Yau target spaces, which
admit (2, 2) superconformal symmetry (see Appendix J.4), as well as holomorphic/anti-
holomorphic spin fields that give rise to spacetime supersymmetries.

                                                          187
    Now we turn to the quantum NLSM. At 1-loop order in the α′ -expansion, in the absence
of B-field and the dilaton, the vanishing of beta function demands that the target space M is
Ricci flat. For a Kähler metric (9.10), the only non-vanishing component of the Ricci tensor
can be expressed as
                                   RI J¯ = ∂I ∂J log det(GKL ).                        (9.17)
The vanishing of (9.17) implies that on a local coordinate chart of M we can write
                                            det(GKL ) = |Ω(Z)|2 ,                                         (9.18)
where Ω(Z) is a non-vanishing holomorphic function on the chart. Moreover, the holomorphic
(n, 0)-form
                             Ω ≡ Ω(Z) dZ 1 ∧ dZ 2 ∧ · · · ∧ dZ n                    (9.19)
is well-defined and nowhere vanishing on the entire manifold M .112
    Up to a constant rescaling, the nowhere vanishing holomorphic top form Ω is determined
by the structure of M as a complex manifold, and independent of the choice of the Kähler
metric. In fact, the existence of Ω relies only on the triviality of the canonical bundle of M ,
or equivalently the vanishing of the first Chern class113 c1 (T M ) (where T M is the complex
tangent bundle of M ). Yau’s theorem114 asserts that any Kähler manifold M with vanishing
first Chern class admits a holomorphic top form Ω that satisfies (9.18) for some Kähler
metric GIJ . Moreover, for a complex structure on M , there is a unique solution to (9.18)
within a given cohomology class of the Kähler form ω = iGIJ dZ I ∧ dZ J . Said equivalently, a
Ricci-flat Kähler metric on M , known as a Calabi-Yau manifold, is specified by the complex
structure of M together a choice of the Kähler class [ω] ∈ H 1,1 (M ) ∩ H 2 (M ; R).
    The holomorphic top form Ω is preserved by parallel transport with respect to the Levi-
Civita connection on T M ,115 which implies that the holonomy group of M is restricted
to an SU (n) subgroup of the structure group SO(2n) of T M , or Spin(2n) of the spin
bundle. The 2n dimensional spinor representation of the corresponding Clifford algebra
can be decomposed into irreducible representations with respect to the SU (n) holonomy
subgroup of Spin(2n), including singlet representations corresponding to a pair of spinors
that are invariant under the holonomy. The latter, via parallel transport, give rise to a pair
of covariantly constant spinor fields ζ±,α on M (i.e. ∇spin
                                                       µ ζ± = 0) that obey

                                   ΓI ζ− = ΓI ζ+ = 0,        I = 1, · · · , n,                            (9.20)
 112
     Under a holomorphic coordinate change Z ′I = f I (Z), dZ ′1 ∧ · · · ∧ dZ ′n = det(∂J f I )dZ 1 ∧ · · · ∧ dZ n
whereas Ω′ (Z ′ ) = (det(∂J f I ))−1 Ω(Z) by (9.18), and hence the form Ω′ defined in the Z ′ -coordinates agrees
with Ω.

   One might worry that the scale invariance of the NLSM is spoiled by higher order α′ -
corrections to the beta function. Assuming that we can adopt a renormalization scheme
that preserves (2, 2) supersymmetry, it suffices to consider the beta function for the Kähler
potential K,
                               βK = α′ ln det(∂I ∂J K) + δβK ,                         (9.22)
where the first term on the RHS is the 1-loop contribution, and δβK represents higher loop
order corrections in α′ . Up to an adjustment of the Kähler class which can be absorbed into
the renormalization scheme, δβK can be taken to be a globally defined scalar function on
                                                (0)
M . Starting from a Ricci flat Kähler metric GIJ = ∂I ∂J K (0) , we seek an adjustment of the
Kähler potential by δK such that
                                         βK+δK = 0.                                     (9.23)
To leading order in δK, this condition can be expressed as
                                            ¯                 ¯
                         −δβK = α′ (G(0) )I J ∂I ∂J¯δK + O((∂ ∂δK)2
                                                                    ),                 (9.24)

which amounts to a Laplace equation for δK that can be solved on any local coordinate patch.
As δβK is a globally defined function, the solutions to δK on different coordinate patches
can differ at most by a harmonic function on the overlap, and therefore the adjustment of
the metric δGIJ = ∂I ∂J δK is well-defined. This procedure can be iterated
                                                                        √ to solve (9.23),
at least in the regime where the curvature radius is large compared to α′ , resulting in a
superconformal NLSM.
    The above construction can be generalized by including a “flat” background B-field with
vanishing field strength, i.e. Hµνρ = 0. This leads to a modification of the NLSM action
(9.12) by                       Z                               Z
                             1                              i

                                  d zBµν (X)∂z X ∂z̄ X =           X ∗ B2 ,          (9.25)
                          2πα′                            2πα′ Σ
where X ∗ B2 is the pullback of the 2-form B2 ≡ 21 Bµν (X)dX µ ∧ dX ν on the target manifold
M to the worldsheet Σ. It follows from the closure of B2 that (9.25) is a topological term
that vanishes for any homologically trivial worldsheet configuration X(Σ), and has no effect
on the dynamics to any perturbative order in α′ . However, when M admits nontrivial
homology 2-cycles, the NLSM path integral receives non-perturbative contributions in α′
from worldsheet configurations X(Σ) that are homologically nontrivial, known as worldsheet
instantons, whose phases are modified by the coupling (9.25).

       Deformations of the complex structure, the Kähler class, as well as the flat B-field on

deformation connects the NLSM to a free field theory in the infinite radius limit, which by
the c-theorem116 implies that the central charge is equal to that of the free field theory limit,
namely c = ce = 3n. The holomorphic top form (9.19) gives rise to the holomorphic weight
( n2 , 0) operators with U (1) R-charge ±n,

   In the large radius limit, the covariantly constant spinor fields ζ± on M gives rise to

                                              Θ± = (ζ±T C)α Sα ,                                  (9.27)

    We can now describe type II string theory in the spacetime R1,9−2n × M , i.e. “Calabi-Yau
compactification”, in terms of the matter SCFT on the worldsheet realized by the supercon-
formal NLSM with R1,9−2n × M target space. For 1 ≤ n ≤ 4, the holomorphic spin fields
built out of the product (9.27) with the 25−n spin fields in the theory of 10−2n free fermions,
and their anti-holomorphic counterparts, upon chiral GSO projection give rise to the world-
sheet currents associated with 26−n spacetime supersymmetries. Of particular interest is the
n = 3 case, which serves as a plausible starting point for constructing superstring vacua that
resemble the observed Universe.

action is indeed invariant under the κ-symmetry.
    Remarkably, the geometry of the target superspace characterized by the super-metric
GM N and super-B-field BM N can be generalized to describe any solution of type IIA or IIB
supergravity, and the action (9.44) remains κ-symmetric and describes the effective action of
a superstring in a general massless background.123 For a general (on-shell) target superspace,

    Despite the elegance of the action (9.44), it can be exceedingly difficult to write down
the explicit functional in a nontrivial supergravity background, due to the complexity in
solving the superspace background fields. In practice, apart from flat spacetime, the Green-
Schwarz superstring action is known explicitly only in a handful of highly (super-)symmetric
backgrounds, such as pp-wave and AdS5 × S 5 (see section 23.2).




                                              197
10      Closed superstring field theory
The on-shell formulation of superstring amplitudes introduced in Chapter 7, similarly to the
case of bosonic string theory, is subject to divergences near the boundary of the moduli space
and ambiguities in the regularization of such divergences. A fully consistent treatment of
superstring perturbation theory, including accounting for mass and field renormalization, as
well as possible quantum corrections to the spacetime background, is made possible through
the off-shell framework of (closed) superstring field theory. Moreover, the SFT formulation of
type II superstrings allows for describing general deformations of the spacetime background,
including those with nonzero Ramond-Ramond field strengths that cannot be represented as
deformations of the worldsheet matter SCFT.


10.1     The space of NS and R string fields and off-shell superstring
         amplitudes

We begin with the worldsheet theory in the superconformal gauge, consisting of a mat-
ter SCFT (such as the (X µ , ψ µ , ψeµ ) system for the Minkowskian spacetime background),
together with the superconformal ghost system of bcβγ and their anti-holomorphic coun-
terparts, with total central charge zero and a BRST charge QB that satisfies (6.64). The
space of states of the full worldsheet SCFT a priori contains Hϵ,eϵ defined as in (9.2), where
(ϵ, ϵe) = (−, −), (−, +), (+, −), (+, +) correspond to (NS,NS), (NS,R), (R,NS), (R,R) sectors
respectively, with the assignment of picture number −1 in the NS sector and − 21 in the R
sector.

picture number − 23 , there is an infinite degeneracy of the βγ system ground states, of the
form126
                                       β0n | − 32 ⟩, n ≥ 0.                          (10.19)
Likewise, any picture number − 32 state |χ⟩ of the matter+ghost system of weight h and ghost
number Nβγ = nχ comes with an infinite tower of degenerate states of the form
                                                    β0n |χ⟩,     n ≥ 0,                                          (10.20)
whose βγ ghost number is Nβγ = nχ − n. Acting on (10.20) with X0 produces a picture
number − 21 state of weight h and ghost number Nβγ ≤ nχ − n + 1. At picture number − 12 ,
the βγ system ground states are of the form γ0m | − 12 ⟩, m ≥ 0, which carry ghost number
Nβγ = m − 12 , and the ghost number is bounded from below at any given oscillator level.
Therefore, X0 β0n |χ⟩ vanishes for all but finitely many values of n. This evades a potential
divergence of (10.12) due to the infinite degeneracy in Ramond sector string fields (which
would have been equivalent to a spurious singularity), as all but finitely many string fields
in a given degenerate family propagate.

11.1     The worldsheet theory and string spectrum

The heterotic string is defined by a worldsheet theory with local chiral supersymmetry, whose
field content includes the metric gab , a chiral gravitino field χa− , the embedding coordinate
                                                                µ
fields X µ and their right-handed fermionic super-partner ψ+      , µ = 0, 1, · · · , 9, together with
                                   A
a set of 32 left-handed fermions λ− (A = 1, · · · , 32) that are needed to cancel the worldsheet
gravitational and Weyl anomalies. The worldsheet action (in Euclidean convention) reads

S[g, χ, X, ψ, λ]

subject to the chirality constraint Γ̂− ε = 0, and under the chiral super-Weyl transformation
of the same form as (6.3) except that the generating spinor ζ is subject to the chirality
constraint Γ̂+ ζ = 0.
    Quantization of the heterotic string in the superconformal gauge, where the chiral grav-
itino field is (locally) set to zero, proceeds similarly to that of the superstring introduced in
Chapter 6 and 7. The gauge-fixed worldsheet theory is a (0, 1) superconformal field theory,
whose ghost sector consists of bcebe c and the right-handed β,eγ
                                                               e system. The matter sector con-
                            µ                               µ
sists of the free bosons X , the right-handed fermions ψ , and additionally the 32 left-handed
                                                          e
fermions λA , such that the total central charge vanishes. Modular invariance requires chiral
GSO projection on the anti-holomorphic (ψeµ , β,   eγe) system as described in section 6.4.2, and
separately a chiral GSO projection on the holomorphic free fermions λA , the latter producing
a (c, ce) = (16, 0) chiral CFT.
   There are in fact two distinct GSO projections that can be consistently imposed on the λ
system, yielding two possible c = 16 chiral CFTs. The first kind of GSO projection is defined
with respect to the fermion number (−)F that anti-commutes with all λA . This results in a
CFT that admits holomorphic weight (1, 0) currents

                                j AB = λA λB ,    A, B = 1, · · · , 32,                        (11.2)

that generate so(32) global symmetry. The second kind of GSO projection is defined with
respect to fermion numbers (−)F1 and (−)F2 , associated with two groups of 16 chiral fermions

    The GSO-projected λ system may be equivalently described as free boson theories via the
Narain lattice construction (Appendix H.4). There are precisely two distinct even, positive
definite unimodular lattices of rank 16, Γ16 (H.47) and Γ8 ⊕ Γ8 (H.46), that give rise to
the chiral CFTs that result from the aforementioned two distinct GSO projections on the λ
system.

    In the E8 × E8 heterotic string theory, the λ system is equivalently described by the
chiral boson CFT associated with the Narain lattice Γ8 ⊕ Γ8 , where Γ8 is the root lattice of
E8 . The massive heterotic string states, built out of states in Hλ , may transform in general
representations of E8 ×E8 (all of which arise in the tensor product of adjoint representations).
    In the so(32) heterotic string theory, on the other hand, the λ system corresponds to
the Narain lattice Γ16 , which is the sum of the root lattice together with the chiral spinor
weight lattice of so(32) as seen in (H.47). In particular, Γ16 does not contain the weights
of the vector nor the anti-chiral spinor representation of so(32). Consequently, the massive
heterotic string states may transform in representations of so(32) that appear in the tensor
products of the adjoint and chiral spinor, but not of the vector nor the anti-chiral spinor.
This suggests that the global form of the gauge group is Spin(32)/Ze 2 , where the Z
                                                                                   e 2 subgroup
is generated by a central element of Spin(32) that acts as the identity in the chiral spinor
representation, and −1 in the vector or anti-chiral spinor representations.

    The low energy effective theory that governs the massless states of the heterotic string,
completing the action (11.20) in a locally supersymmetric manner, is known as type I or
N = 1 supergravity in 10 dimensions (Appendix N.4). Note that even at the two-derivative
level, the type I supergravity involves two distinct length scales, one set by the gravitational
coupling κ and the other set by the gauge coupling gYM . Another unusual feature of this
effective theory is that certain higher-derivative corrections, such as “Green-Schwarz term”

11.3         Mass renormalization

In the so(32) heterotic string theory, there is a special set of massive string states that
transform in the chiral spinor representation of the so(32) gauge algebra, built out of weight
(2, 0) holomorphic spin fields Sα (α = 1, · · · , 215 ) of the λ system and anti-holomorphic
oscillator level 23 states in the NS sector or oscillator level 1 in the R sector. Explicitly, the
NS states which correspond to spacetime bosons are represented by the vertex operators
                              e 1
                                                                       
                            −ϕ                         µ¯ ν        ¯
                      ce

where the polarization tensors d[µνρ] , eµν , fµ are subject to the OCQ constraints dµνρ k ρ −
2e[µν] = 0, α′ eµν k µ + 2fν = 0, eµ µ + f · k = 0. Together the NS and R sector states form a
non-BPS multiplet of the 10-dimensional N = 1 supersymmetry that contains 128 bosons
and 128 fermions. These states represent stable massive particles in heterotic string theory,
as they cannot decay into the massless particles which are either singlets or transform in the
adjoint representation of the gauge group. On the other hand, their mass-shell condition
                                                                    4

is expected to be corrected by string interactions.

11.6         A quantum-corrected heterotic vacuum

A general (perturbative) spacetime background of heterotic string theory, as defined through
a worldsheet (0, 1) SCFT, may receive nontrivial string loop corrections that are determined
by tadpole terms (i.e. linear terms in the string field) in the quantum effective action of the
string field theory. A particularly instructive example, which we will examine in some detail
in this section, is the compactification of the heterotic so(32) string theory on a Calabi-Yau
threefold M with the standard embedding. As discussed in the previous section, the 4D
massless effective theory is N = 1 supergravity with SO(26) × U (1) gauge group, whereas
the worldsheet matter SCFT is equivalent to the (2, 2) superconformal NLSM with target
                                                     ′
space M combined with 26 free chiral fermions λA through the chiral GSO projection.
    In particular, the U (1) gauge symmetry of the 4D effective theory is associated with the
U (1)R current of the holomorphic N = 2 superconformal algebra on the worldsheet. The
charged massless fields organized into 4D N = 1 chiral multiplets, consisting of complex
scalars and chiral fermions represented by NS and R sector vertex operators of the form

by holomorphic spectral flow give rise to h2,1 chiral multiplets in the singlet of SO(26) with
U (1) charge −2, and h1,1 chiral multiplets in the singlet of SO(26) with U (1) charge +2.


11.6.1    The 4D effective theory

The 4D low energy effective theory takes the form of the N = 1 supergravity, consisting of a
supergraviton multiplet, vector multiplets associated with the SO(26) × U (1) gauge group,
and neutral as well as charged chiral multiplets. We will denote the vector potentials as
AA                                                      I
  µ , and the complex scalars of chiral multiplets as ϕ . As described in Appendix N.6, the
2-derivative effective action is determined by the Kähler potential K(ϕ, ϕ∗ ), the holomorphic
superpotential W (ϕ), the holomorphic functions τAB (ϕ) that amount to the complexified
gauge coupling, and momentum maps PA (ϕ, ϕ∗ ) that govern the gauge transformation of
the chiral multiplets. The kinetic term of chiral multiplets takes the form of a NLSM whose

                                                228
target space M is equipped with the Kähler metric GIJ = ∂I ∂J K. The gauge transformation

11.6.4        Shifted vacuum and restoration of supersymmetry

To identify the quantum vacuum configuration of the compactified heterotic so(32) string
theory with standard embedding, in addition to the D-term potential (11.114) we must also
account for the contribution from the superpotential as in (11.98). A priori a holomorphic
function of the complex scalars of the chiral multiplets, the superpotential W of the 4D
N = 1 effective supergravity theory originates, in the large volume regime, from the Kaluza-
Klein reduction of the 10D effective coupling of the gauge field Aµ and gaugino χα , as the
latter gives rise to Yukawa couplings of the 4D charged chiral multiplets.
    We will not elaborate on the explicit expression of W , except for noting that it does
not contain quadratic terms in the charged scalars ϕI appearing in (11.110) as the latter
are massless. Due to the gauge invariance of W , there can be no contribution to the scalar
potential that depends only on a single charged scalar field ϕI . Provided that h1,1 and h2,1
are both nonzero, it is then possible to turn on a nonzero expectation value for one of the
U (1)-charged scalars ϕI to set the effective scalar potential (11.114) to zero, thereby restoring
spacetime supersymmetry at the quantum level.

12.1         D-branes in critical bosonic string theory

A D-brane is an object on which a string can end. The critical bosonic string theory in the
presence of D-branes can be described by the path integral (4.1) over worldsheet Σ with
boundary ∂Σ. The worldsheet fields are subject to suitable boundary conditions along ∂Σ
that preserve the gauge invariance with respect to Weyl transformations as well as diffeo-
morphism generated by vector fields v a (σ)∂a that are tangent to the boundary. The latter
requires
                                     Tab na v b |∂Σ = 0,                             (12.1)
where na ∂a is any vector field normal to the boundary. In the conformal gauge, the Faddeev-
Popov ghosts bab , ca and the BRST current (jB )a are subject to the boundary conditions

                           bab na v b |∂Σ = 0,    ca na |∂Σ = 0,   (jB )a na |∂Σ = 0.                  (12.2)

To analyze the local properties of the boundary conditions, it suffices to take Σ to be the
upper half Euclidean plane parameterized by the complex coordinate z with Im(z) ≥ 0, in
which case (12.1) and (12.2) can be written as
                                                    
                                   lim T (z) − Te(z̄) = 0                            (12.3)
                                 Im(z)→0

and
                                                                                                
       lim       b(z) − eb(z̄) = 0,        lim     c(z) − ce(z̄) = 0,      lim      jB (z) − jeB (z̄) = 0.
      Im(z)→0                           Im(z)→0                          Im(z)→0
                                                                                                (12.4)
A simple class of conformal boundary conditions for the matter CFT, in the case of 26-
dimensional Minkowskian target spacetime, is defined by assigning Neumann boundary con-
dition to X 0 , · · · , X p , and Dirichlet boundary condition to X p+1 , · · · , X 25 , namely

                               lim ∂X µ (z) − ∂X ¯ µ (z̄) = 0, µ = 0, · · · , p,
                                                        
                             Im(z)→0
                                                                                                (12.5)
                               lim X i (z, z̄) = xi0 , i = p + 1, · · · , 25.
                            Im(z)→0

The boundary of the worldsheet therefore describes the endpoint of a string that is confined
to a (p + 1)-dimensional hypersurface located at X i = xi0 (i = p + 1, · · · , 25). It will become
apparent that such a hypersurface should be thought of as the world volume of a dynamical
object that extends in p spatial dimensions, known as a “Dp-brane”, that supports open
string excitations. Moreover, we will see in Chapter 13 that the Dp-brane sources closed
string fields and has a finite tension at nonzero string coupling.

to the Dp-brane, giving 25−p massless scalar particles propagating in the world volume. The
latter can be viewed as Nambu-Goldstone bosons associated with the translation symmetries
in the X i directions (i = p + 1, · · · , 25) that are spontaneously broken by the Dp-brane
configuration.


12.1.2   Deformations of a Dp-brane

Analogously to how a marginal deformation of the worldsheet matter CFT gives rise to a
deformation of the spacetime background, as seen in section 3.7.2, a marginal deformation
of the boundary condition of the matter CFT gives rise to a deformation of the D-brane
configuration (in a given spacetime background), which may also be equivalently viewed as
turning on a background open string field.

                                               246
12.1.3    Multiple Dp-branes

Given a pair of D-branes described by the boundary conditions B and B ′ on the worldsheet,
we can consider an open string stretched between the two D-branes, with the left endpoint
of the open string subject to the boundary condition B, and the right endpoint subject to
the boundary condition B ′ . The space of states of the worldsheet CFT on the strip with
left boundary condition B and right boundary condition B ′ will be denoted HBB ′ . The
physical open string states are identified with the cohomology of QoB on HBB ′ , subject to
Siegel constraint. Similarly, the open strings with the opposite orientation, stretched from
B ′ to B, are characterized by the BRST cohomology in HB ′ B .
   Under the conformal map (12.6), a state |ψ⟩ ∈ HBB ′ corresponds to a boundary operator
ψ(0) inserted at the interface between B along R− and B ′ along R+ . Suppose B represents a
Dp-brane extended along X 0 , · · · , X p , with X i = xi0 , i = p+1, · · · , 25, and B ′ be the parallel
Dp-brane at X i = xi0 + ∆xi . Applying the doubling trick (12.7), XLµ (z) (µ = 0, · · · , p) is
analytic across both R− and R+ , whereas XLi (z) is analytic across R− and jumps by ∆xi
across R+ , namely
                          XLi (y + iϵ) = XLi (y − iϵ), y < 0,
                                                                                                 (12.28)
                          XLi (y + iϵ) = XLi (y − iϵ) + ∆xi , y > 0.
Such a discontinuity can be implemented by inserting at the origin the operator
                                                 ∆xi 
                              exp 2i(k∥ )µ XLµ + i ′ XLi ,                                      (12.29)

massless and enhance the gauge group to U (2). This is an essential feature of D-brane

   More generally, a stack of n coinciding Dp-branes is described by the direct sum boundary

                                    HB ⊕n B ⊕n ≃ HBB ⊗ M at(n),                                 (12.31)

                                                  247
string states is of the form ψ ⊗ Eij , where ψ ∈ HBB and Eij is the n × n matrix whose entries
are (Eij )ab = δia δjb , representing an open string whose left and right endpoints are attached
to the i-th and the j-th Dp-brane respectively. We will see in section 14.7 that the massless
open string states include the vector bosons of a U (n) gauge theory on the (p+1)-dimensional
world volume, whereas all other open string states transform in the adjoint representation
of the gauge group.


12.2        BPS D-branes in type II superstring theory

super-diffeomorphism. In the superconformal gauge, this amounts to boundary conditions

12.2.1       Open superstring states

An open superstring state |ψ⟩ ∈ Ho is physical provided that it is annihilated by QoB (12.15)
and obeys the Siegel constraint b0 |ψ⟩ = 0, and also β0 |ψ⟩ = 0 if |ψ⟩ is in the Ramond
sector. Moreover, two open superstring states that differ by a QoB -exact state are viewed as
physically equivalent. The mass-shell condition for the open string states is of the form

                                                   α′ k 2 + N = 0,                             (12.37)

where N is the total oscillator weight, constrained to be a non-negative integer due to the
GSO projection.
   Let us inspect the massless open string states that arise at oscillator weight N = 0. In
the NS sector, the massless states are represented by the boundary vertex operator (in the
doubling trick notation)

Similar to the bosonic string case, (12.38) describes the vector bosons of a U (1) gauge field
on the Dp-brane, whereas (12.39) describes 9 − p massless scalars that are the Nambu-

transverse collective coordinates of the Dp-brane.

16 supercharges in (p + 1)-dimensions.

can simply be viewed as the Dp-brane with the opposite orientation, thereby carrying the
opposite charge with respect to the RR fields.

12.4      More general configurations of D-branes

12.4.1    Intersecting D-branes

The analysis of open superstring spectrum in section 12.2.1 can be generalized to open strings
stretched between a Dp-brane and a Dp′ -brane which need not be parallel to one another,
and p′ need not be equal to p.
     To begin with, consider a BPS Dp-brane that extends in the X 0 , · · · , X p directions,
whose transverse coordinates are fixed to X p+1 = · · · = X 9 = 0, and a BPS Dp′ -brane
                                                         ′
that extends in X 0 , · · · , X q , X p+1 , · · · , X p+p −q , whose transverse coordinates are fixed to
                                  ′
X q+1 = · · · = X p = X p+p −q = · · · X 9 = 0. The worldsheet of an open string stretched
between the Dp and the Dp′ -branes is subject to Neumann (N) boundary condition in the
                                                                                  ′
X 0 , · · · , X q directions, Dirichlet (D) boundary condition in the X p+p −q , · · · , X 9 directions,
                                                                                                     ′
and mixed (N,D) or (D,N) conditions on the (left,right) boundaries in the X q+1 , · · · , X p+p −q
directions.
   The space of states HND of a free boson X subject to (N,D) condition on the (left,right)
boundary of strip can be constructed using a generalization of the doubling trick. Mapping
the strip to the UHP, and extending XL (z) to the complex plane by the identification (12.7),
XL (z) is analytic across R− and changes sign across R+ , namely
                               XL (y + iϵ) = XL (y − iϵ),       y < 0,
                                                                                                (12.63)
                               XL (y + iϵ) = −XL (y − iϵ),        y > 0.

                                                  255

ground state of HND can be identified with the holomorphic twist field σ, whose conformal
               1

to a classical instability.


12.4.2     D-branes at angles

We now consider more general D-branes configurations, starting with the example of a pair
of D1-branes intersecting at an angle. We may assume that the first D1-brane is extended
along the X 1 direction, with X 2 = · · · = X 9 = 0, and the second D1-brane, which we refer
to as D1′ , is at angle θ in the (X 1 , X 2 )-plane, i.e. extended along X 2 = X 1 tan θ, with
X 3 = · · · = X 9 = 0.

and applying the doubling trick, Z on the UHP is replaced by the holomorphic field ZL =

13.1        Open+closed bosonic string perturbation theory

be formulated through the path integral over worldsheet with boundaries. In the conformal

represented by boundary vertex operators Vjo inserted at boundary punctures on ∂Σ. The

are unrelated by the conformal Killing group P SL(2, R) of the UHP. This gives rise to the
two terms in the second line of (13.22).

13.3      Cylinder amplitudes

(13.2) requires at least one bulk or boundary puncture on the cylinder, and a suitable
generalization is required to formulate the cylinder amplitude with no punctures, which
contributes to the ground state energy of D-branes.

13.4      D-brane effective action

The spacetime effective action (3.84) that captures the low energy dynamics of massless
closed string fields can be generalized to include the massless open string degrees of freedom
on a Dp-brane. Note that a strictly open string tree-level effective action would only account
for the disc amplitudes, which can account for the coupling of the D-brane to a closed string
background but not to the closed strings excitations. To capture the tree-level closed string
exchange involving D-branes necessitates the consideration of the cylinder diagram i.e. open
string loops. Consequently, the D-brane effective action that includes the coupling to closed
string excitations should in principle be viewed as a quantum effective action in the Wilsonian
sense.159
    To manifest spacetime general coordinate invariance, it will be useful to parameterize
the world volume of a Dp-brane with an arbitrary non-degenerate coordinate system ξ a ,
a = 0, · · · , p, and represent the D-brane configuration by the embedding coordinate fields
X µ (ξ), µ = 0, · · · , 25. The reparameterization of the world volume coordinates will be
viewed as a gauge redundancy. The simplest invariant action that captures the dynamics of
the Dp-brane is of the Nambu-Goto form,
                                                Z      p
                          SDp [X , · · · ] = −Tp dp+1 ξ − det Gab + · · · ,
                                µ
                                                                                    (13.46)

where Tp is the tension of the Dp-brane, and

                                Gab (ξ) ≡ Gµν (X(ξ))∂a X µ (ξ)∂b X ν (ξ)                            (13.47)

is the induced metric on the (p + 1)-dimensional world volume. Here the spacetime metric
Gµν (X) can be viewed either as a background field configuration, or as a dynamical field
in which case the brane action (13.46) should be combined with the bulk action (3.84). So
far in writing (13.46) we have not accounted for the gauge fields Aµ on the Dp-brane, nor
the coupling to the other massless bulk fields, namely Bµν and the dilaton Φ, which will be
analyzed in sections 13.4.1 and 13.4.2.
   We can compare (13.46) to the open string perturbation theory by working in the static
gauge ξ a = X a and expanding the action perturbatively with respect to the transverse

13.4.1   Dilaton dependence

As seen in (4.11), shifting the background dilaton field Φ(X) by a constant ϕ0 is equivalent
to rescaling the string coupling gs by eϕ0 . As Tp is proportional to gs−1 , this determines the
Dp-brane effective action in a slowly varying dilaton background Φ(X) to be
                                          Z             p
                    SDp [X , · · · ] = −Tp dp+1 ξ e−Φ(X) − det Gab + · · · .
                           µ
                                                                                         (13.50)

It is illuminating to consider the Dp-brane with a compactified world volume direction, say
X 1 ∼ X 1 + 2πR. T-duality relates the X 1 CFT to an equivalent CFT described by the
compact boson X ′1 ∼ X ′1 + 2πR′ , with the identification
                                                                         α′
                            XL′1 = XL1 ,    XR′1 = −XR1 ,         R′ =      .           (13.51)

                                             √

                                              R

as follows from matching the normalization factor appearing in sphere amplitudes, VX ′1 gs′−2 =

a D(p − 1)-brane transverse to X ′1 , whose tension is

                                  ′           R
                                 Tp−1 = Tp−1 √ = Tp 2πR.                               (13.53)
                                              α′
The first equality follows from the rescaling of the string coupling under T-duality,
                                                                              √       and the
                                                                                ′
second equality follows from (13.49) and (13.21) which implies Tp−1 = Tp 2π α . Thus, the
effective action of the compactified Dp-brane and the effective action of the D(p − 1)-brane
in the T-dual frame produce the same result for the energy per unit (p − 1)-dimensional
noncompact spatial volume, as expected.
   Let us note that the low energy effective action is a priori √ an approximation that is
applicable at distance scales much larger than the string length α′ , and the latter condition
cannot be satisfied on both sides of the T-duality transformation. Nonetheless, the tree-level
processes that exchange closed strings that do not carry momentum or winding quantum
numbers in the compact direction are insensitive to the compactification, which justifies the
above naive application of the D-brane effective action.

13.6     D-branes in c = 1 string theory

In the c = 1 string theory, the target space is described by the c = 25 Liouville theory, which
admits two basic types of unitary conformal boundary conditions, known as Zamolodchikov-
Zamolodchikov (ZZ) type and Fateev-Zamolodchikov-Zamolodchikov-Teschner (FZZT) type.

                                                274

A defining property of the ZZ boundary condition BZZ is that the Hilbert space of Liouville

    The ZZ-brane is defined by combining the ZZ boundary condition in the Liouville CFT
with the Neumann boundary condition in the free boson X 0 CFT, together with the standard
boundary condition (12.4) of the bc ghost system. Intuitively, the ZZ-brane can be viewed
as a sort of D0-brane localized in the strong coupling region of the target space, i.e. X 1 ≫ 0
in terms of the field X 1 appearing in the Liouville action (3.106).

    The full description of the open string tachyon on the ZZ-brane, at least at the classical
level, will be given by the open string field theory (OSFT) introduced in section 15.1.3.
Let us emphasize that the OSFT is not equivalent to a single free fermion by itself, but is
rather expected to capture the dynamics of a fermion in the presence of the fermi sea (Q.13).
Indeed, a classical vacuum configuration of the open string tachyon amounts to the complete
decay of the ZZ-brane (section 15.2), and corresponds to the fermion disappearing into the
fermi surface.

of a pair of long strings, have been shown to numerically agree with the dual MQM description
of the scattering amplitudes in the adjoint or bi-adjoint sectors in Balthazar, Rodriguez and

14      D-brane dynamics in type II superstring theory

14.1     Open+closed superstring perturbation theory

We now combine the recipes of Chapter 7 and section 13.1 to formulate the open+closed type
II superstring perturbation theory. In the superconformal gauge, the superstring worldsheet
is covered by holomorphic charts Ui that are parameterized by the super coordinates (zi , θi )
with superconformal transition maps on the overlap between charts as in (7.10), as well as
their anti-holomorphic analog, the charts U i with the super coordinates (z̄i , θ̄i ). When Ui
and U i share a boundary component, we must introduce a transition map that accounts for
the boundary condition, as follows.
   Without loss of generality, we may assume that the chart Ui that meets the boundary is
parameterized by (zi , θi ) with Im(zi ) > 0, and similarly U i is parameterized by (z̄i , θ̄i ) with
Im(z̄i ) < 0. On their overlap, we demand the transition map to be

                                       z̄i = zi∗ ,     θ̄i = ±θi∗ ,                           (14.1)

where ∗ acts as the usual complex conjugation on a complex parameter, and as a formal
complex conjugation upon composition with superconformal maps. The data of the holo-
morphic and anti-holomorphic super coordinate charts subject to the boundary transition
maps of the form (14.1), modulo the equivalence relation of superconformal diffeomorphism
that preserve the boundary condition, define the notion of a super Riemann surface with
boundary (BSRS).
    Note that in our definition of BSRS, the super coordinates on holomorphic and anti-
holomorphic charts that do not meet at the boundary are a priori unrelated, and so the
reduced space is not quite a Riemann surface with boundary. In particular, in the absence
of boundary, the BSRS reduces to a holomorphic SRS C together with an anti-holomorphic
SRS C′ , whose supermoduli space is Mh,ϵL × Mh,ϵR , where h is the genus and ϵL , ϵR label
the holomorphic and anti-holomorphic spin structures. More generally, with b boundary
components and nNS/R the total number of holomorphic, anti-holomorphic, and boundary
punctures of NS/R type, the supermoduli space of the BSRS has dimension 2de |do , where

                                  de = 6h − 6 + 3b + nNS + nR ,
                                                           nR                                 (14.2)
                                  do = 4h − 4 + 2b + nNS +     .
                                                            2
The spin structure ϵ on the BSRS includes the choice of sign in (14.1) associated with each
boundary component (this is the same sign as η̂ appearing in (12.32), (12.41)), as well as
the choice of spinor field periodicity along the boundary circle (this amounts to restricting
the boundary state (12.41) to its (NS,NS) or (R,R) component). The latter is subject to the

                                                     280
constraint that the total number of R type punctures and boundary states must be even.
Therefore, for a given set of puncture types, the total number of distinct spin structures
on the BSRS (with b ≥ 1) is 24h+2b−1 . Note that while a boundary puncture of NS type
does not affect the boundary spin structure, a boundary puncture of R type interpolates
between boundary conditions of + and − spin structures, as is reflected in the cylinder
modular crossing relations (12.49). Moreover, correlation functions of GSO-projected vertex
operators are invariant under simultaneously flipping the spin structure assignments of all
boundary components.

                                                        287
cancellation can be understood as a consequence of the supersymmetry preserved by the

massless (R,R) fields, which exchange gives rise to a repulsive potential that cancels the
Newtonian attraction due to the graviton and dilaton exchange.

(14.32) for A0,2        , but now A0,2      acquires the opposite sign as (14.34). That is, the
anti-Dp-brane carries the opposite (R,R) charge as the Dp-brane, in which case the exchange
of RR fields gives an identical contribution to the attractive potential as the graviton/dilaton
exchange.


14.5     BPS D-brane effective action

14.5.1   Supersymmetry and κ symmetry

We begin by considering a BPS Dp-brane in the 10-dimensional Minkowskian spacetime, in
the absence of nontrivial closed string excitations, and construct an effective action that is
invariant under the super-Poincaré symmetry with 32 supercharges. Similarly to that of the
Green-Schwarz action of the superstring (section 9.3), the 12 -BPS nature of the Dp-brane
is such that the 32 supersymmetries are realized nonlinearly in an effective theory of 16
Goldstinos (which can be identified with the gauginos).
     As in section 13.4, we adopt an arbitrary world volume coordinate system ξ a (a =
0, · · · , p) and parameterize the D-brane configuration in the spacetime with the embed-
ding coordinate fields X µ (ξ), µ = 0, · · · , 9. In addition, we have a U (1) gauge field Aa and
fermion fields θ ≡ (θα , θαb ) that transform in a pair of Majorana-Weyl representations of
so(1, 9) with the same (opposite) chirality in the type IIB (IIA) case. Under the spacetime
supersymmetry generated by a 32-component spinor parameter ϵ ≡ (ϵα , ϵαb ), the fields X µ
and θ transform according to
                                   δϵ θ = ϵ,    δϵ X µ = ϵΓµ θ.                          (14.35)

                             Πµa = ∂a X µ − θΓµ ∂a θ,    Π ≡ Πa dξ a ,                   (14.36)
associated with the spacetime momentum. A supersymmetry invariant that generalizes the
notion of the induced metric (13.47) in the bosonic case is

14.6        Some supersymmetric D-brane configurations

A Dp-brane configuration, as characterized by the κ-symmetric effective action of the mass-
less fields X µ , Aa , θ on the world volume, preserves spacetime supersymmetry if the corre-
sponding supersymmetry variation δϵ of the world volume fields can be undone by a κ gauge
symmetry variation δκ . In the 10D Minkowskian spacetime background, the κ-symmetric
Dp-brane effective action is given by (14.41). As the fermion field θ vanishes for any classical
brane configuration, the condition for preserving the spacetime supersymmetry generated by
a constant spinor parameter ϵ = (ϵα , ϵαb ) is

                                               (δϵ + δκ )θ = 0                                        (14.64)

for some spinor field κ(ξ) on the world volume. According to (14.35) and (14.46), the
equation (14.64) can be put in the form

                                         ϵ + κ(ξ)(1 − Υ(ξ)) = 0,                                      (14.65)

where Υ(ξ) is a certain matrix that obeys (Υ(ξ))2 = 1. A solution κ(ξ) exists if and only if

                                             ϵ(1 + Υ(ξ)) = 0.                                         (14.66)

Restricting to the case of vanishing gauge field strength Fab , Υ(ξ) can be written explicitly
as

          (p + 1)! − det Gab                                        σ3 2 σ1 Γµ1 ···µp+1 (IIB)

     In the on-shell formulation of string perturbation theory, potential ambiguities or scheme dependence
arise from the regularization near the boundary of the moduli space. In the string field theory formulation,
ambiguity in the definition of string coupling arises from the choice of string vertices, or equivalently the
choice of string field frame. In particular, the field redefinition that relates different frames may shift the
dilaton component of the string field, which amounts to a renormalization of gs (see Bergman and Zwiebach,
Nucl. Phys. B 441 (1995), 76 [60]).

14.7     Non-Abelian effective gauge theory of stacked D-branes

The massless effective action described in section 14.5 is a priori applicable to a D-brane
configurations with small extrinsic curvature and slowly-varying gauge field strength, and is
expected to break down when a D-brane folds on itself or multiple D-branes collide, where
new massless open string modes may appear. On the other hand, we know that N coincident
Dp-branes are described by the boundary condition of the worldsheet CFT constructed from
that of a single Dp-brane with Chan-Paton factors, resulting in a U (N ) gauge symmetry on
the world volume, under which all open string states transform in the adjoint representation.
   For N coincident Dp-branes extended in X 0 , · · · , X p directions in Minkowskian space-
time, the massless open string degrees of freedom are captured by a U (N ) gauge theory on
the (p + 1)-dimensional world volume, whose field content includes the gauge potential Aa ,
the scalar fields X i , i = p + 1, · · · , 9, and the fermionic spinor fields λ, all of which are N × N



                                                   298
matrices. The effective action of this gauge theory is constrained by the 16 linearly realized
supersymmetries to be of the form174
            Z          
                          1            1                     1
   S = −Tp d ξ tr (Da X i )2 + (2πα′ )2 Fab F ab − (2πα′ )−2 [Xi , Xj ][X i , X j ]
                p+1
                          2            4                     4
                                                                                      (14.89)
                        a          i     i
                  + λ̄Γ Da λ −        λ̄Γ [Xi , λ] + · · · ,
                                2πα′
where the world volume coordinates ξ a are identified with the spacetime embedding coor-
dinates xa , a = 0, · · · , p, Fab ≡ ∂a Ab − ∂b Aa − i[Aa , Ab ] is the non-Abelian field strength,
and Da ≡ ∂a − i[Aa , · ] is the gauge-covariant derivative in the adjoint representation. The
representation content of the fermion field λ with respect to the so(1, p) Lorentz symmetry
and the so(9 − p) R-symmetry that rotates the transverse directions to the Dp-brane is that
of a Majorana-Weyl spinor of so(1, 9) ⊃ so(1, p) × so(9 − p). In this sense, we can view λ
as an N × N Hermitian matrix whose entries are so(1, 9) Majorana-Weyl spinors. As such,
the contractions of the so(1, 9) spinor indices are understood in the second line of (14.89).
In the special case N = 1, (14.89) reduces to the Born-Infeld action of a single Dp-brane
expanded to quadratic order in the fluctuation fields.
    The couplings in the effective action (14.89) can be organized by assigning mass dimension
1 to Aa and 2πα 1    i       3      1

exhibited on the RHS of (14.89) are of mass dimension 4, whereas the omitted terms · · ·
necessarily involve more derivatives or powers of the fields and are suppressed in the low
energy limit. While all higher corrections can be in principle be determined by matching
with open string amplitudes, there is no simple closed form expression for a non-Abelian
effective action that (nonlinearly) realizes the full spacetime super-Poincaré symmetry, in
contrast to the Born-Infeld action of a single Dp-brane.

14.8      Scattering and bound states of D0-branes

A D0-brane in type IIA string theory is a BPS particle of mass
                                                       1

The massless open string modes on a D0-brane at rest consist of the collective coordinates
X 1 , · · · , X 9 , 16 real fermions λα , and a U (1) gauge field A0 that contains no propagating
degrees of freedom. Upon quantization, λα gives rise to (up to a normalization factor) the
operators θ̂α acting on the world line Hilbert space that obey the canonical anti-commutation
relation
                                             {θ̂α , θ̂β } = δαβ .                         (14.94)

the 10-dimensional super-Poincaré symmetry.

closed string exchanges occur between D0-branes moving at nonzero relative velocity. The

where X̂ ′i , P̂i′ , Θ̂′α are traceless N × N matrices, x̂i is the rescaled center-of-mass coordinate
of the system of N D0-branes, p̂i the rescaled total spatial momentum, whereas θ̂α obey
(14.94) and generate a “center-of-mass multiplet” of 28 states (similarly to that of a single
D0-brane). We can then split the Hamiltonian (14.108) as

                                                     M 2
                                               H=      p̂ + H ′ ,                           (14.113)
                                                     2N i

where H ′ , given by (14.108) with X̂ i , P̂i , Θ̂α replaced by their traceless counterpart, is the
Hamiltonian of the 0 + 1 dimensional maximally supersymmetric SU (N ) gauge theory. The
first term on the RHS of (14.113) is the non-relativistic kinetic energy of a particle of mass
N T0 , whereas H ′ amounts to the interaction energy between the N D0-branes.
    The potential term in H ′ is non-negative and vanishes along the “valleys” where [X̂ ′i , X̂ ′j ] =
0 for all i, j = 1, · · · , 9. Expanding around a valley of the potential at large X ′i , one may
adopt the Born-Oppenheimer approximation and separate X̂ ′i and Θ̂′α into slow and fast
modes, and characterize the low-energy states in terms of wave functions of the slow modes,
while setting the fast modes to their ground states. It is a consequence of the supersymmetry
that the ground state energy of the fast modes vanishes, which gives rise to a continuum of
scattering states whose H ′ eigenvalue range over R+ .
    A normalizable eigenstate of H ′ , on the other hand, would give rise to a low-energy bound
states of N D0-branes. It is believed that H ′ admits a unique normalizable ground state
|Ψ0 ⟩ with
                                           H ′ |Ψ0 ⟩ = 0,                               (14.114)
which is annihilated by all supercharges and is invariant under the so(9) global symmetry.
|Ψ0 ⟩ describes a threshold bound state of N D0-branes, that is, a bound state with zero
binding energy, which will play a crucial role in the connection between type IIA string
theory and the 11-dimensional M-theory in section 18.7. An explicit, global characterization
of the wave function of |Ψ0 ⟩ has been unattainable to date due to its complexity: even in
the simplest N = 2 case, the wave function has 224 components, each of which is a function
of 27 real variables! Nonetheless, it is possible to show that the Witten index of the system,
defined as the trace of (−)F , where F is the fermion number, over normalizable H ′ = 0


                                                       303
states, is equal to 1, thereby proving that there is at least one threshold bound state.176 The
uniqueness has been established in the N = 2 case by analyzing the wave function of the
supersymmetric ground state in the asymptotic region.177




 176
     The computation of the Witten index, which is highly nontrivial due to the gapless continuum of scat-
tering states, is completed in the N = 2 case by Sethi and Stern, Commun. Math. Phys. 194, 675 [61], and
extended to higher values of N by Yi, Nucl. Phys. B 505, 307 (1997) [62].
 177
     Frohlich et al., Nucl. Phys. B 567, 231 (2000) [63].

15.1.3        Witten’s cubic OSFT

A particularly elegant construction of the open string vertices is as follows. On the UHP
with boundary punctures at y1 , · · · , yn ∈ R, consider a quadratic differential φ(z)dz 2 that
is holomorphic everywhere (including the point at infinity) except for double poles at yi . A
horizontal (vertical) trajectory is a curve along which φ(z)dz 2 is real and positive (negative).
We will demand that the boundary of the UHP is a vertical trajectory, i.e. φ(z) is a negative-
real-valued function over the real axis, and
                                      Z p
                                           −φ(z)dz = ±πi                                 (15.21)
                                               γ

for every horizontal trajectory γ with both end points on the boundary.180 We can write
φ(z) = P (z) ni=1 (z − yi )−2 , where P (z) is a degree 2n − 4 polynomial with real coefficients

that is completely determined by the condition (15.21). The Hermitian metric

                                                   ds2 = |φ(z)|dz 2                                     (15.22)

is flat everywhere except for an excess angle π at the n − 2 zeros of φ(z) on the UHP,
and moreover decomposes the UHP into finite or semi-infinite strips of width π foliated

gauge transformations are generated by a Grassmann-even string field Λ of ghost number 0.


15.2     Open string tachyon condensation

We now return to the question of open string tachyon condensation on a D-brane, already
hinted by the effective action (13.25). In the classical OSFT framework, an (a priori off-shell)
open string tachyon profile that is constant on the world volume of a D-brane is represented
by the open string field of the form

                                          |Ψ⟩ = tc1 |0⟩ + · · · ,                         (15.33)

where |0⟩ is the state that corresponds to the identity operator on the boundary of the
worldsheet, t is the magnitude of the tachyon field, and · · · stands for higher oscillator level
states built out of bn , cn , and the cm = 26 matter Virasoro generators Lm n.

15.3      More general solutions of the bosonic OSFT

15.3.1     Marginal deformations

A marginal deformation of the boundary conformal field theory (BCFT) is generated by a
                                                                  R    
weight 1 boundary primary V , and amounts to inserting exp λ ∂Σ V into the correlation
functions of the CFT on the surface Σ. The precise definition of the exponential of the
integrated operators requires the choice of a regularization scheme (e.g. point-splitting),
which a priori may violate conformal invariance beyond the first order in λ. We say that the
deformation is exactly marginal if conformal invariance is preserved to all orders in λ.190
    An exactly marginal deformation of the matter BCFT on the string worldsheet may also
be viewed as a deformation of the corresponding D-brane configuration. The background
independence of OSFT suggests that such a deformation can be equivalently represented by
a solution to the open string field equation (15.31), which admits a perturbative expansion
of the form                                  ∞
                                            X
                                       Ψ=      λn Ψ(n) .                             (15.60)
                                                  n=1

The first order solution is simply
                                                Ψ(1) = cV,                                         (15.61)
where V is a weight 1 matter BCFT primary, and satisfies QB Ψ(1) = 0. It will be useful to
represent the BPZ inner product Ψ(1) with an arbitrary state ϕ in the form

                                    ⟨⟨ϕ|Ψ(1) ⟩ = ⟨[ϕ(0)]s cV (1)⟩W1 ,                              (15.62)

where s is the sliver map (15.44), and Wn stands for the semi-infinite cylinder obtained by
identifying z ∼ z + n + 1 on the UHP.

15.3.2     Rolling tachyon revisited

The rolling tachyon on the ZZ-brane of c = 1 string theory was described from the world-
sheet perspective in section 13.6.1 as the BCFT deformation (13.80), which may be viewed
as the Wick rotation of (15.77) defined by the replacement X → iX 0 in the free boson
sector, together with the decoupled ZZ-boundary condition in the Liouville sector. From
the perspective of on-shell string perturbation theory, it is not immediately obvious how to
define physical observables analogous to the scattering amplitudes of asymptotic states due
to the explicit time-dependence in the spacetime background.194 Some clues can be found
by inspecting the deformed matter boundary state |B⟩ = |B⟩X 0 ⊗ |BZZ ⟩, where

                            |B⟩X 0 ∝ f (X 0 )|0⟩ + g(X 0 )α−1 α
                                                              e−1 |0⟩ + · · · .                    (15.81)

Here · · · stands for higher oscillator level states, and the functions f (X 0 ), g(X 0 ) are given
by
                                         1                    1
                      f (X 0 ) =      X 0           +     −X 0           − 1,
                                      √                    √
                                 1+e   α ′

                          0                           0
                      g(X ) = 1 + cos(2π e   λ) − f (X ).
Heuristically, one expects f (X 0 ) and g(X 0 ) to represent sources for the dilaton and graviton
fields. Indeed, the quantity f (X 0 )+g(X 0 ) which is conserved in time was interpreted, up to a
normalization factor, as the energy of the rolling tachyon by Sen, JHEP 04, 048 (2002) [52],
which is further justified by considering coupling to closed string fields in Sen, JHEP 12
(2004), 053 [74].

    It is somewhat nontrivial to identify the energy of the open string field, however, as the
classical OSFT is formulated through a Lagrangian that contains a priori arbitrarily high
order time derivatives, to which one cannot simply apply the canonical formalism. Nonethe-
less, the Hamiltonian of the OSFT can be constructed indirectly through the covariant phase
                                                                R
space formalism.195 The basic idea is that given an action S = M L where M is the space-

to the equation of motion ea = 0 obtained by varying the Lagrangian with respect to the
fields ϕa ,
                                      δL = ea δϕa + dU.                                (15.83)

15.3.3    The Erler-Maccaferri solutions

Given a pair of matter boundary conformal field theories BCFT0 and BCFT∗ corresponding
to two different D-brane configurations, not necessarily related by marginal deformations,
the expectation of background independence is such that the OSFT based on BCFT0 should
admit a nontrivial solution that is physically equivalent to changing the D-brane configura-
tion into that of BCFT∗ . A remarkable construction for such an open string field solution
was found by Erler and Maccaferri, JHEP 01 (2020), 021 [80], which we now describe.
    Let H0 and H∗ be the space of open string fields based on BCFT0 and BCFT∗ respectively.
We will write Ψtv,0 and Ψtv,∗ for the tachyon vacuum solution, given by (15.51) up to a gauge
transformation, in the two OSFTs respectively. Let H0∗ , H∗0 be the space of open string
fields interpolating between the two boundary conditions. The idea of Erler and Maccaferri
is to construct a solution of the OSFT based on BCFT0 of the form

                                    Ψ∗ = Ψtv,0 − ΣΨtv,∗ Σ.                           (15.99)

Here and below all products between string fields, unless otherwise noted, are understood as
∗-product. Σ ∈ H0∗ and Σ ∈ H∗0 are intertwining fields that obey

                            QΨtv Σ ≡ QB Σ + Ψtv,0 Σ − ΣΨtv,∗ = 0,
                                                                                    (15.100)
                            QΨtv Σ ≡ QB Σ + Ψtv,∗ Σ − ΣΨtv,0 = 0,

and
                                           ΣΣ = I.                                  (15.101)
For convenience of notation we will drop the subscript 0, ∗ on Ψtv . Given the properties
(15.100), (15.101), it is easy to verify that (15.99) solves the equation of motion:

         QB Ψ∗ = QB Ψtv − (QB Σ)Ψtv Σ − Σ(QB Ψtv )Σ + ΣΨtv QB Σ
               = −Ψ2tv + Ψtv ΣΨtv Σ − ΣΨ2tv Σ + ΣΨ2tv Σ − ΣΨ2tv Σ + ΣΨtv ΣΨtv       (15.102)
               = −Ψ2tv + Ψtv ΣΨtv Σ − ΣΨtv ΣΣΨtv Σ + ΣΨtv ΣΨtv = −Ψ2∗ .

It will be useful to consider the homotopy operators A0 ∈ H0 and A∗ ∈ H∗ that satisfy

                                    QΨtv A = I,         A2 = 0,                     (15.103)

where I = Ω0 is the identity string field, in the two OSFTs respectively. The first equation
of (15.103) reflects that the cohomology of QΨtv is trivial, as already seen in (15.55). The
second equation of (15.103) is an extra condition that is also satisfied by (15.55), and will
be used in (15.106) below. The intertwining fields can be constructed as

                            Σ = QΨtv (AΣpre ),         Σ = QΨtv (Σpre A),           (15.104)

                                                 324
where Σpre ∈ H0∗ and Σpre ∈ H∗0 satisfy

                                           Σpre AΣpre = A,                                    (15.105)

Obviously (15.100) is satisfied. It follows from (15.103) and (15.105) that

           ΣAΣ = QΨtv (Σpre A)AQΨtv (AΣpre )
                                                                                              (15.106)
                = Σpre A(QΨtv A)((QΨtv A)Σpre − AQΨtv Σpre ) = Σpre AΣpre = A.

Applying QΨtv to both sides then gives (15.101).

                                              σ ∗ σ = I.                                (15.107)

    As the OSFT is expected to capture all open string excitations on a D-brane, it should in
particular be able to describe the D-brane folding onto itself. A striking feature of the Erler-
Maccaferri solution (15.99) is that it allows for describing multiple D-branes as a solution
of the OSFT based on a single D-brane. For instance, we may take BCFT∗ to be BCFT0
tensored with the U (k) Chan-Paton factor. In this case, the interface operator σ ∈ H0∗ ∼
H00 ⊗ Ck can be represented as a row vector (σ1 , · · · , σk ) where each σi is a boundary
operator of BCFT0 , and σ ∈ H∗0 a constant column vector (σ 1 , · · · , σ k ). We must impose
the condition that the zero weight component of σσ, now represented as a k × k matrix,
to be proportional to the identity matrix operator. In other words, we require the zero
weight component of the OPE σ i (y)σj (0) to be proportional to δij in BCFT0 , and impose
the orthogonality condition
                                        ⟨⟨σ i |σj ⟩ = δij .                            (15.113)
This requires taking σi to be nontrivial boundary operators, but is not hard to satisfy in a
general BCFT0 . The resulting string field solution then represents k coincident D-branes.

2. each ∂Djo ∩ Σ′ is an open geodesic of length Lo , and all open geodesics in Σ′ with ends on

                         0 < Lc ≤ L′∗ ,   sinh(Lc ) sinh(Lo ) ≤ 1,                   (15.125)

where L′∗ is the solution to sinh L2∗ sinh L′∗ = 1, whose numerical value is L′∗ ≈ 1.21876.202
    Interestingly, in the limit Lo → ∞ with Lc ≤ (sinh Lo )−1 , the open string vertices reduce
to that of Witten’s cubic OSFT. That is, the only non-vanishing open string vertex is the
disc 3-point vertex defined in (15.25). In this case, the L-loop Feynman diagrams built out of
Witten’s cubic open string vertex cover precisely the entire moduli space of Riemann surfaces
with at least one boundary component and Euler characteristic χ = 1 − L,203 whereas the
closed string field propagators only serve as counter terms that cancel the UV divergences
from the open string loops. This would amount to a quantum OSFT based on the path
integral over the open string fields only, with Witten’s cubic OSFT action and a suitable
UV regularization. In practice however, the quantum bosonic open+closed string theory
suffers from either closed string tachyon instability, such as in critical bosonic string theory,
or open string tachyon instability, as with the ZZ-brane in c = 1 string theory, or massless
closed string tadpole, as with FZZT-brane in c = 1 string theory, all of which renders the
conventional string perturbation theory ill-defined. Whether the quantum OSFT can be
defined non-perturbatively remains an outstanding open question.

16         D-instantons

16.1         The effect of D-instantons

The construction of the string S-matrix based on the worldsheet path integral and closed
SFT has thus far been organized according to the genus expansion, and is perturbative
with respect to the string coupling gs . Such a perturbative expansion is expected to yield
an asymptotic series that is not convergent at any nonzero value of the string coupling.206
A complete formulation of string theory should include D-branes, perhaps in the form of
open+closed SFT. While the latter has only been defined at the level of perturbation theory
in sections 15.4 and 15.5, one expects that any reasonable non-perturbative completion of
the D-brane path integral should contain saddle points corresponding to Euclidean D-brane
solutions that are localized in spacetime, similarly to the bounce or instanton solutions of
the Euclidean equation of motion that play the role of non-perturbative saddle points in
the path integral formulation of quantum field theory. Such Euclidean D-brane solutions, or
“D-instantons”, are expected to mediate non-perturbative corrections to string amplitudes
of order exp(−C/gs ) where C does not scale with gs . The simplest examples of D-instantons
include the ZZ-instanton in c = 1 string theory (section 16.2) and the BPS D(−1)-brane in
type IIB string theory (section 16.3).
       Our basic postulate is that the closed string scattering amplitude takes the form

                                        A = Apert + AD−inst + · · · ,                      (16.1)

where Apert stands for the perturbative amplitude, AD−inst the contribution from worldsheets
with boundaries that are subject to the D-instanton boundary conditions, and · · · stands
for higher order non-perturbative effects, such as gravitational instanton contributions which
are expected to be of order exp(−C/gs2 ). Strictly speaking, to define Apert requires summing
up the perturbative series in gs , e.g. through Borel resummation with a suitable integration
contour on the Borel plane (Appendix B.5), and the non-perturbative corrections are subject
to potential ambiguities of the resummation procedure. In this chapter we will focus on
examples where the perturbative amplitude can be Borel-resummed (as in c = 1 string
theory) or truncates at a finite order (as for BPS-protected amplitudes in superstring theory),
in which case the D-instanton corrections are unambiguously defined and will turn out to be
essential for the consistency of various string dualities.
   Generally, a D-instanton comes in a continuous family that is parameterized by the
moduli space MD−inst of exactly marginal deformations of the corresponding worldsheet
boundary condition. By analogy with the on-shell formulation of string perturbation theory,
 206

    Strictly speaking, the “empty disc” amplitude is undefined in the formalism of open+closed perturbation

momenta. Similar open string divergences plague the empty worldsheet diagrams Acx|h,b [∅],
whose ambiguities are tied to that of the measure factor dµ(x) on the D-instanton moduli
space.

results up to certain counter term ambiguities. These ambiguities will be resolved through
the open+closed string field theory formulation of D-instantons in section 16.4.

16.3     D-instantons in type IIB string theory

The type IIB superstring theory admits D-instantons in the form of BPS D(−1)-branes. The
effective action of a BPS Dp-brane derived in section 14.5 can be extended to the p = −1


                                                              337
case,210 yielding the (Euclidean) action of a single D(−1)-brane

                                      SD(−1) = T−1 e−Φ − iµ−1 C0 = −2πiτ,                                     (16.13)

where τ ≡ τ1 + iτ2 = gB−1 (C0 + ie−Φ ), C0 is the RR axion background field, and gB is
the type IIB string coupling defined in (14.62). Likewise, the anti-D(−1)-brane has action
SD(−1) = 2πiτ̄ . A more general class of D-instantons is defined by the worldsheet boundary
condition that is the direct sum of that of n D(−1)-branes and m anti-D(−1)-branes, which
we will refer to as an (n, m) D-instanton and has action S(n,m) = −2πi(nτ − mτ̄ ).
    Importantly, while the perturbative type IIB closed string amplitudes are independent
of the RR axion background or the value of τ1 , the D-instantons mediate closed string
interactions that are dependent on τ1 through the instanton action S(n,m) (when n ̸= m).
Moreover, the charge quantization of the D-instanton is such that constant shift of τ1 which
is a symmetry to all orders in string perturbation theory is broken to the discrete shift
symmetry τ1 7→ τ1 + 1. The latter is part of the S-duality symmetry of type IIB string
theory, as will be discussed in section 18.3.
    The simplest massless closed string amplitude affected by the D-instantons is that of four
supergravitons, whose (NS,NS) component takes the form (8.80). Accounting for possible
non-perturbative dependence on τ1 , we will replace the function f (s, t; gs ) in (8.80) with
f (s, t; τ, τ̄ ), whose perturbative and D-instanton expansion is expected to be of the form
                               ∞

given in (8.81), f (n,m)) represents the (n, m) D-instanton contribution, and · · · stands for
other possible non-perturbative corrections (such as gravitational instanton effects).
