    At the next order in the 1/τ2 expansion, we encounter several different worldsheet topolo-
gies: (i) four 1-punctured discs with a 3-holed sphere (i.e. 2-holed disc), (ii) four 1-punctured
discs with a 1-holed torus, (iii) three 1-punctured discs and one 1-punctured annulus, (iv)
two 1-punctured discs and one 2-punctured disc. While we cannot unambiguously compute
the 3-holed sphere and the 1-holed torus amplitudes in the on-shell formalism, assuming
these can be defined with a suitable regularization of the worldsheet moduli space, the con-
tribution from (i) and (ii) to (16.32) would be independent of s, t, i.e. they only contribute
to the R4 effective coupling. Similarly, the annulus 1-point amplitude cannot introduce non-
trivial dependence on the kinematic invariants, and therefore (iii) only contributes to the
R4 effective coupling as well. (iv), on the other hand, introduces nontrivial s, t dependence
through the disc 2-point amplitude, and contributes to effective couplings to all orders in
the momentum expansion.


16.4     Open+closed string field theory of D-instantons

We now turn to a systematic formulation of D-instanton effects based on the open+closed
string field theory. The basic idea is that the Euclidean (effective) action of closed string
fields, Γ[Ψc ], receives a D-instanton contribution of the form
                                                   Z
                                  −Γ[Ψc ]
                                 e        D−inst
                                                 =   dλo e−S[Ψc ,Ψo ] ,               (16.33)
                                                           Lo




                                                         342
where S[Ψc , Ψo ] is the BV action functional of the closed string field Ψc coupled to the open
string field Ψo on the D-instanton, Lo is a Lagrangian submanifold of the open string field
space Ho , and dλo is the measure on Lo defined as in (5.110), (5.111).
    The construction of S[Ψc , Ψo ] follows the same recipes as in section 15.4 for the bosonic
string and as in section 15.5 for the type II superstrings, except that the D-brane is replaced
by the D-instanton and we must include in S[Ψc , Ψo ] a constant term S0 that is the classical
D-instanton action in the absence of closed string field, corresponding to the “empty disc”
worldsheet diagram.
    In contrast to (16.2), the integration over the D-instanton moduli space MD−inst is re-
placed by the integration over open string fields in (16.33). This is reasonable as the latter
includes the open string collective modes (denoted φk ) which are in correspondence with
the D-instanton moduli (denoted xk ). Namely, φk appears in the open string field Ψo in the
form
                                      Ψo = φk cVk + · · · ,                           (16.34)
where Vk are weight 1 boundary primaries that generate marginal deformations of the D-
instanton boundary condition. These collective modes do not appear in the kinetic term of
the open string field
                                           1
                                             ⟨⟨Ψo |QB |Ψo ⟩,                                (16.35)
                                           2
and consequently the integration over φk cannot be treated as a perturbative expansion
around a Gaussian. In the absence of an a priori non-perturbative definition of the functional
integral (16.33), this issue is partially remedied by identifying a field redefinition relating the
open string collective modes φk to the D-instanton moduli xk , following the open string
analog of the notion of background independence introduced in section 5.8. Namely, there
is a diffeomorphism between the open string field space at moduli x and y,
                                             Fx,y : Hxo → Hyo ,                                  (16.36)
that satisfies the open string analog of (5.113). The restriction Fx,x0 |φk =0 can be viewed
as field redefinition that trades φk for xk or vice versa, which allows for converting the
(non-perturbative) integration over φk to an integral over MD−inst .
  There are additional weight zero modes of Ψo that cannot be interpreted as the collective
modes of the D-instanton and require special consideration. In the bosonic string case, these
modes are of the form
                            ρ1 c0 |0⟩ + ζ 2 |0⟩ + ζ1 c−1 c1 |0⟩ + ρ2 c−1 c0 c1 |0⟩,              (16.37)
where |0⟩ is the state that corresponds to the identity boundary operator. In the superstring
case, they are
         ρ1 β− 1 c0 c1 | − 1⟩ + ζ 2 β− 1 c1 | − 1⟩ + ζ1 γ− 1 c1 | − 1⟩ + ρ2 γ− 1 c0 c1 | − 1⟩,   (16.38)
               2                      2                    2                   2



                                                     343
where | − 1⟩ is the state that corresponds to δ(γ) ≃ e−ϕ . Note that the coefficients ρ1 and ρ2
are Grassmann-even, whereas ζ1 and ζ 2 are Grassmann-odd. The BV symplectic form pairs
ρ1 with ζ1 , and ζ 2 with ρ2 .
   The kinetic term of open string fields (16.35) is independent of ρ2 , ζ1 , ζ 2 , and depends on
 1
ρ through the term
                                         −CD2 (ρ1 )2 ,                                      (16.39)
where CD2 is a positive normalization constant associated with the disc diagram that is
proportional to gs−1 .216 Naively, if one adopts Siegel gauge condition on Ψo (by choice of the
Lagrangian submanifold Lo ⊂ Ho ), ρ1 and ρ2 would be set to zero, leaving ζ1 and ζ 2 with
vanishing kinetic term. This appears to make the open string field path integral ill-defined
in perturbation theory.
    The problem originates from the interpretation of ζ1 , ζ 2 in Siegel gauge as the Faddeev-
Popov ghosts associated with fixing the U (1) gauge symmetry on the D-instanton. This is
illustrated more clearly if we regularize the setup by considering instead the analogous open
string modes stretched between a pair of D-instantons separated by some distance in the
spacetime, so that |0⟩ acquires nonzero weight h. In this case, the kinetic term for ζ1 , ζ 2 is217

                                                 CD2 hζ1 ζ 2 .                                         (16.40)

The relevant gauge transformation is generated by the ghost number 0 string field ϑ|0⟩,
whose infinitesimal form is

                               δ|Ψo ⟩ = QB δϑ|0⟩ + · · · = hδϑc0 |0⟩ + · · · .                         (16.41)

That is, ρ1 transforms by δρ1 = hδϑ + · · · , where · · · stands for higher order terms in the
string field. The Gaussian integral over ζ1 , ζ 2 amounts to the Faddeev-Popov determinant
associated with the gauge condition ρ1 = 0. In the limit h → 0, however, the gauge condition
ρ1 = 0 is invalid, and the corresponding FP determinant vanishes. This indicates that the
Siegel gauge condition for the open string fields on the D-instanton is singular.
    The issue is resolved if we relax the Siegel gauge condition on open string modes appearing
in (16.37) or (16.38), replacing the Faddeev-Popov determinant by restoring the integration
over ρ1 divided by the volume of the U (1) gauge group. This amounts to the substitution

    Beyond the leading order in perturbation theory, to compute the volume dϑ we must
account for a potentially nontrivial change of variable relating ϑ to the standard phase angle
of the U (1) gauge group. The latter can be determined by inspecting a mode χ of the open
string stretched between the D-instanton and another “spectator” D-instanton which we will
refer to as the Ds -instanton. Let χ‡ be the BV anti-field conjugate to χ. The BV action of
the D-Ds OSFT contains a term
                                           Kχχ‡ ζ 2 ,                                    (16.44)
where K is calculated at the leading order in perturbation theory by the disc diagram with
the insertions of the three boundary vertex operators corresponding to χ, χ‡ , ζ 2 (with the ap-
propriate assignment of Chan-Paton factors of the D-Ds system). The gauge transformation
of χ is
                               δχ = (S, χ)|ζ 2 →δϑ = Kχδϑ + · · · ,                      (16.45)
where · · · stands for higher order corrections. Comparing this with the standard U (1) gauge
transformation
                                          δχ = iχδϑ0 ,                                (16.46)
where ϑ0 has periodicity 2π, then fixes the relation between ϑ and ϑ0 . The result is moreover
intrinsic to the D-instanton, independent of the choice of the mode χ or the configuration of
the spectator Ds -instanton.
    The open string fields on the D-instanton generally may also contain negative weight or
tachyonic modes, whose kinetic term comes with a negative sign. In this case, the integra-
tion over the tachyonic open string mode should be defined with a suitable contour in the
complexified field space that is in principle dictated by the Borel resummation prescription
of string perturbation theory and the physical interpretation of the D-instanton.

17.1        Unoriented strings

Thus far we have assumed that the fundamental string comes with a preferred orientation,
or equivalently, the string worldsheet is assumed to be an oriented surface. An unoriented
version of string theory would seem to be possible so long as the worldsheet theory is parity
invariant, as one can simply modify the worldsheet path integral, e.g. (2.23) in the bosonic
string case, by including unoriented worldsheet surfaces and demanding that orientation-
reversing diffeomorphisms are part of the gauge redundancies.
    Let us begin by revisiting the propagation of a closed bosonic string, now assumed to
be unoriented. We will parameterize the Euclidean worldsheet cylinder with the complex
coordinate w ≡ σ + iτ , w ∼ w + 2π, and work in the conformal gauge. The effect of gauging
orientation-reversing diffeomorphism leaves the worldsheet (spatial) parity transformation Ω
as a residual gauge symmetry, under which all physical states by definition must be invariant.
Ω acts on the worldsheet fields by

ΩX µ (w, w̄)Ω−1 = X µ (−w̄, −w),          Ωc(w)Ω−1 = −e
                                                      c(w̄′ = −w),
                                                              Ωb(w)Ω−1 = eb(w̄′ = −w),
                                                                                  (17.1)
with Ω = 1. By the state/operator map defined via the conformal transformation z = e−iw ,
       2

Ω acts on the fields in the z-plane as

       ΩX µ (z, z̄)Ω−1 = X µ (z̄, z),   Ωc(z)Ω−1 = ce(z̄ ′ = z),     Ωb(z)Ω−1 = eb(z̄ ′ = z),         (17.2)

where the multiplication of operators is understood in the sense of radial quantization. A
priori, the transformation (17.1) leaves an overall sign ambiguity in Ω as an operator acting
on the space of CFT states. The choice that allows for consistent string interaction (at least
at tree level) turns out to be225
                                     Ω|k; ↓, ↓⟩ = |k; ↓, ↓⟩.                           (17.3)
In other words, the closed string tachyon is Ω-invariant, so are the massless states (3.45)
with symmetric polarization tensor eµν , representing the graviton and the dilaton. On the
other hand, the B-field is odd with respect to Ω and is disallowed in the unoriented string
theory. This is consistent with the expectation that only an oriented string could be charged
with respect to the B-field.
    The interaction of unoriented strings can be formulated through the path integral that
includes oriented as well as unoriented worldsheet surfaces. A general unoriented surface
 225
    In the vertex operator notation, Ω · ce
                                          c(0) = ce
                                                  c(0). Note that this does not contradict (17.2) as Ω cannot
be viewed as a local operation on the plane.


                                                    352
can be constructed by inserting cross caps on a genus h oriented surface. In the absence
of punctures, a surface with genus h, b boundary components, and c cross caps has Euler
characteristic
                                   χ = 2 − 2h − b − c.                             (17.4)
In particular, the surface with (h, b, c) = (0, 0, 1) is the real projective plane RP2 , (h, b, c) =
(0, 1, 1) is the Möbius strip, and (h, b, c) = (0, 0, 2) is the Klein bottle. Note that an unori-
ented surface is topologically classified by χ and b only.226
   In the conformal gauge, the unoriented worldsheet is equipped with the structure of an
unoriented Riemann surface Σ. The latter can be described through its oriented double cover

involution.

cancel the massless tadpole due to the cross cap state by that of space-filling D-branes. We
will defer this analysis to section 17.4 in the context of type I superstring theory.

   Consistency of string perturbation theory requires the massless tadpole due to the cross

examine the worldsheet parity transformation of the open string states. Let us consider the

17.5     Type I string amplitudes

The perturbative type I string S-matrix can be formulated by a straightforward extension of
the open+closed superstring perturbation theory of section 14.1. Starting with the world-
sheet theory of type IIB superstring in the superconformal gauge, we will allow for both
oriented and unoriented surfaces, with boundaries subject to the boundary condition that

density. There are four distinct topologies that contribute: the torus, the Klein bottle, the
cylinder, and the Möbius strip.

supersymmetry of type I string theory.

    As is generally the case for the bulk-brane effective action, (17.49) does not admit a
classical limit with dynamical bulk fields, as the tree-level closed string exchange diagram
can also be viewed as a 1-loop open string diagram. Rather, (17.49) should be viewed
as a quantum effective action in the Wilsonian or 1PI sense. At leading orders in the
derivative expansion, (17.49) is constrained by spacetime supersymmetry to be that of type
I supergravity with SO(32) gauge group. We have already encountered the latter in the
context of heterotic string theory in section 11.2. However, unlike in the heterotic string
theory where the spacetime anti-symmetric 2-form potential arises from the (NS,NS) B-
field, in type I string theory it comes from the (R,R) sector.

17.6.1    BPS D1 and D5-branes

To describe Dp-branes of type I string theory, we begin by analyzing the worldsheet parity
transformation of open strings on a BPS Dp-brane in type IIB string theory, for odd p < 9.
On the strip subject to the boundary condition of a Dp-brane located at X p+1 = · · · = X 9 =
0, the Ω-transformation on the bulk fields (17.18) remain valid. After applying the doubling
trick (12.7), (12.36), the Ω-transformations of XLµ and ψ µ read, in place of (17.20),

       ΩXLµ (z)Ω−1 = XLµ (−z),     Ωψ µ (z)Ω−1 = −iζ̂ η̂ψ µ (−z),              µ = 0, · · · , p,
                                                                                                   (17.52)
       ΩXLi (z)Ω−1 = −XLi (−z),      Ωψ i (z)Ω−1 = iζ̂ η̂ψ i (−z),         i = p + 1, · · · , 9.

We also need to keep track of the Ω-transformation of the spin fields on the strip, in particular
                                                  ϕ
of the spacetime supersymmetry current jα = e− 2 Θα , which in the notation of the doubling
trick (12.36) takes the form

                           Ωjα (z)Ω−1 = − (β p+1 · · · β 9 )−1 j α (−z).
                                                                
                                                                                         (17.53)

Compatibility of (17.53) with Ω2 = 1 requires 9 − p ≡ 0 mod 4. Therefore, it is possible to
gauge the worldsheet parity in the presence of a BPS Dp-brane for p = 1 or 5, which defines
the D1 or D5-brane in type I string theory.
   It remains to determine the Ω action on the Chan-Paton factor of D1 and D5-branes.
Given n coinciding D1-branes, let |ij⟩D1 be the state that corresponds to the identity bound-
ary operator at the interface between the boundary conditions that correspond to the i-th
and j-th D1-brane. By the same consideration of (17.21), Ω acts by
                                                      −1
                              Ω|ij⟩D1 = −(γD1 )jj ′ (γD1 )i′ i |j ′ i′ ⟩D1 ,                       (17.54)

where γD1 is a priori an n × n unitary matrix that is either symmetric or anti-symmetric.
The correct choice can be determined by computing the Möbius strip partition function,
similarly to (17.37) except that the boundary state |B⟩ is now taken to be that of the n
D1-branes (as in type IIB string theory), whereas the cross cap state |⊗⟩ is the same as the
one determined in section 17.4. In the end one finds that γD1 must be symmetric, and thus
can be taken to be γD1 = In .
   In the case of single D1-brane, the Ω-invariant massless NS open string states are

                              ce−ϕ ψ i eik∥ ·X |11⟩D1 ,    i = 2, · · · , 9,                       (17.55)

corresponding to the transverse collective coordinates, where k∥ is a lightlike momentum
along the 1+1 dimensional world volume. Note that crucially, Ω acts on ψ i=2,···9 (subject

                                                  365
to Dirichlet boundary condition) with the opposite sign as on ψ 0,1 (subject to Neumann
boundary condition). The Ω-invariant massless Ramond open string states are
                                           cuα jα eik∥ ·X |11⟩D1 ,                                (17.56)
where the polarization spinor uα obeys
                                 −u = uβ 2 · · · β 9    and k∥µ Γµ u = 0.                         (17.57)
The first condition of (17.57), which follows from Ω-invariance, is equivalent to Γ01 u = −u.
While the momentum k∥ obeys the lightlike mass-shell condition k∥0 = ±k∥1 , the second
condition of (17.57) further requires k∥0 = −k∥1 . Therefore, (17.56) describes 8 negative-
momentum massless fermions on the D1-brane, which transform in a spinor representation
with respect to the SO(8) that rotates the transverse directions. Indeed, the D1-brane
preserves half of the 16 supersymmetries of type I string theory, whereas the massless states
(17.56) can be interpreted as Goldstinos associated with the 8 broken supersymmetries.
    The D1-brane in type I string theory also supports open strings with one end on the
D1-brane and the other end on the space-filling D9-branes. As Ω exchanges the left and
right ends of the open string, it exchanges D1-D9 and D9-D1 string states in the type IIB
theory, and therefore the Ω-invariant states can be identified with those of the D1-D9 string
only. The latter is a special case of the Dp-Dp′ system analyzed in section 12.4.1, where the
lowest level NS and R open string states involve the matter vertex operators (12.66) and
(12.68) respectively. It follows from (12.67) (with dND = 8) that there are no massless D1-D9
string states in the NS sector (as the lowest NS string state has m2 = 2α1 ′ ). The R sector,
on the other hand, contains massless states of the form
                                             ϕ
                                       cΣe− 2 Θ+ eik∥ ·X |1, j⟩D1,D9 ,                            (17.58)
where Σ is a weight 21 operator built out of the product of 8 Z2 twist fields of chiral bosons
(see the discussions around (12.64)), and Θ+ is the weight 81 spin field of the ψ 0 , ψ 1 system,
whose chirality is selected by the GSO projection. The state |1, j⟩D1,D9 accounts for the
Chan-Paton factor associated with the D1-brane and 32 D9-branes (the latter labeled by
j = 1, · · · , 32). The BRST closure condition further restricts the lightlike momentum k∥ to
be such that k∥0 = k∥1 .234 Therefore, (17.58) describes 32 massless fermions that propagate
with positive momentum along the D1-brane, and transform in the vector representation of
the SO(32) gauge group of type I string theory.
   Next we turn to the D5-branes. The analog of (17.54) on n coincident D5-branes of type
IIB string theory is
                                                   −1
                           Ω|ij⟩D5 = −(γD5 )jj ′ (γD5 )i′ i |j ′ i′ ⟩D5 ,         (17.59)

    This is compatible with the invariance of the states (17.58) with respect to the chiral supersymmetries

                                                       366
where the unitary matrix γD5 turns out to be anti-symmetric. To see this from the Möbius
strip partition function would require considering the contributions to (17.37) from the two
spin structures separately, as they sum up to zero in the case of the D5-brane boundary
condition. An easier way to determine the symmetry property of γD5 is to consider the Ω
action on the Chan-Paton factor of the D5-D9 open string,
                                                       −1
                            Ω|ij⟩D5,D9 = −(γD9 )jj ′ (γD5 )i′ i |j ′ i′ ⟩D9,D5 ,                (17.60)
where γD9 is symmetric (and may be set to the identity matrix). The lowest D5-D9 string
states involve matter vertex operator of the form (12.66) and (12.68). In the NS sector,
for instance, the oscillator ground state is built out of chiral spin fields in the system of
dND = 4 fermions, which must transform with phase ±i under Ω by compatibility with the
OPE. In order to maintain Ω2 = 1 on the physical D5-D9 string states, the transformation
on the Chan-Paton factor (17.60) must square to −1, and thus we conclude that γD5 is
anti-symmetric.
    Consequently, the D5-brane system in type I string theory exists only for even n, in
which case the D5-D5 open string states carry Sp(n) Chan-Paton factor. In the simplest
n = 2 case, we may take γD5 = σ2 as in (17.24). With the D5-brane extended in X 0 , · · · , X 5
directions, the massless NS open string states are
                    ce−ϕ eµ ψ µ eik∥ ·X λij |ij⟩D5 ,     ce−ϕ ψ 6,7,8,9 eik∥ ·X λ′ij |ij⟩D5 ,   (17.61)
where eµ is a polarization vector along the world volume direction that obeys e · k∥ = 0, and
λ, λ′ are constrained by Ω-invariance to obey
                                 σ2 λσ2 = −λT ,          σ2 λ′ σ2 = (λ′ )T .                    (17.62)
It follows that λ is a linear combination of the Pauli matrices σ1,2,3 , giving rise to Sp(2) ≃
SU (2) gauge bosons, whereas λ′ is proportional to I2 , corresponding to (a single set of)
transverse collective coordinates. Therefore, the n = 2 D5-brane system, upon Ω-projection,
describe a single D5-brane of type I string theory, with SU (2) gauge fields on its world
volume. The latter combine with the massless R sector D5-D5 string states to form a gauge
multiplet with respect to the 6-dimensional N = (1, 0) supersymmetry.
    The D5-D9 open strings give rise to additionally 2 sets of massless complex scalars that
carry (2, 32) Chan-Paton factor with respect to the SU (2)×SO(32) gauge group from the NS
sector, and an equal number of massless fermions from the R sector. Altogether, the massless
D5-D9 string states form a 6-dimensional hypermultiplet in the (2, 32) representation.

    Note that a parallel Dp-brane in the bulk, i.e. with transverse coordinate (X p+1 , · · · , X 9 ) =
x⊥ ̸= 0, corresponds to a boundary state that is the sum of that of a pair of Dp-branes
at transverse coordinate x⊥ and −x⊥ in the absence of the orientifold. It follows from
(17.78) that the Op± -plane carries ±2p−5 times the tension and RR charge of a bulk Dp-
brane. The tension and RR charge of the orientifold plane can also be understood simply
through T-duality as follows. If we compactify type I string theory on a circle by identifying
X 9 ∼ X 9 + 2πR, and perform a T-duality in the X 9 direction, the worldsheet parity Ω is
mapped to e  Ω = ΩR9 where the spatial reflection R9 has two fixed planes at X 9 = 0 and
X 9 = πR. The T-duality therefore turns the space-filling orientifold into a pair of O8− -planes
of type IIA string theory, each carrying 12 times the tension and RR charge of the O9− -plane
of type I string theory. The 32 D9-branes of type I string theory are turned into D8-branes
transverse to the X 9 direction, that can only move away from the O8-planes in pairs. It
follows that the O8− -plane carries − 21 × 21 × 32 = −8 times the tension and RR charge of a
bulk D8-brane, in agreement with the normalization of the cross cap and boundary states.

and the identification between ℓs,het , gs,het and ℓs,I , gs,I via (18.2), (18.5) for the same values

in fact be equivalent in the sense of a strong/weak coupling duality. Conjecturally, the non-
perturbative completions of the heterotic so(32) and type I string theories share the same
one-parameter family of 10-dimensional Minkowskian vacua with N = (1, 0) supersymmetry,
parameterized by the expectation value of a massless scalar field Φ. The latter may either
be interpreted as the dilaton Φ = Φhet of the heterotic string theory, or minus the dilaton
Φ = −ΦI of type I string theory.
    The identification of the spacetime effective theories in particular maps the B-field of
the heterotic string theory to the RR 2-form potential C2 of type I string theory. The
heterotic/type I duality should therefore map the electrically charged string with respect to
the B-field, namely the fundamental heterotic string itself, to the D1-brane which is charged
with respect to C2 in type I string theory. Indeed, according to (18.2), (18.5), the heterotic
string tension
                                                      5   3
                                    1         2
                                             gYM    2 2 π 2 ℓ2s,I
                                           =      =                                     (18.8)
                                 2πℓ2s,het   8πκ2       gs,I
precisely agrees with the tension of the D1-brane tension in type I string theory. The spec-
trum of massless open string excitations on the D1-brane, as analyzed in section 17.6.1,
consists of 8 massless scalar fields and 8 right-handed fermions coming from the D1-D1
strings, and 32 left-handed fermions coming from the D1-D9 strings. This is in agreement
with that of an (infinitely long) heterotic string, at least at the level of counting the degrees
of freedom and their symmetry properties. In particular, note that the right-handed fermions
described by the open string vertex operators (17.56), which transform in the spinor repre-
sentation of the SO(8) symmetry that rotates the transverse spatial dimensions, should be
identified with not the transverse fermion fields ψei on the heterotic string worldsheet, but
rather the spin fields in the latter system.
    Similarly, the duality maps the magnetically charged object with respect to C2 in type
I string theory, namely the D5-brane, to a magnetically charged object with respect to the
B-field in heterotic string theory. The latter, known as the NS5-brane, will be analyzed in
section 18.2.
    The equivalence between the spacetime quantum effective actions of heterotic so(32) and
type I string theories can be seen beyond the 2-derivative level. In particular, the Green-
                                        R
Schwarz effective coupling of the form B2 ∧ trv (F 4 ) arises in the heterotic so(32) string
theory at one-loop order (11.43), whereas the same effective coupling arises in the type I
string theory at open string tree-level (17.51). Their agreement under the heterotic/type
I duality is necessary for the cancellation of the spacetime gauge anomaly. Related by
supersymmetry, the four-derivative effective gauge coupling of the form t8 tr(F 4 ) that arises


                                                373
from the disc amplitude in type I string theory (by a calculation similar to (14.23)) can also
be shown to agree with the analogous effective coupling that arises from the torus amplitude
in heterotic so(32) string theory.
    The heterotic so(32) string theory admits non-BPS stable particles that transform in the
spinor representations of the SO(32) gauge group, as was analyzed in section 11.3. The
type I string theory, on the other hand, admits stable non-BPS D0-branes. Remarkably, the
quantization of the massless open string modes on the non-BPS D0-brane, as seen in section
17.6.2, give rise to precisely a multiplet of states that transform in the spinor representation
of SO(32). This suggests that the non-BPS D0-brane should be identified with the SO(32)-
spinor heterotic string state. The mass of this object is then expected to interpolate between
the result of section 11.3 at weak heterotic string coupling to the non-BPS D0-brane mass
determined in section 17.6.2 at weak type I string coupling.236


18.2        NS5-branes

In the type II and heterotic string theories, whereas the fundamental string is electrically
charged under the B-field, one also expects a magnetically charged object with respect to
the B-field that extends in 5 spatial dimensions, known as the NS5-brane. By a similar
argument to that of section 14.5.3, the H-flux through the S 3 enclosing the NS5-brane in
the transverse directions obeys the Dirac quantization condition

and anti-chiral components with respect to Γ̂012345 and gives rise to (1, 1) supersymmetry in
6 dimensions. The low energy excitations of a single NS5-brane, which include the Nambu-
Goldstone bosons corresponding to the transverse collective coordinates, are expected to be
governed by a 6-dimensional field theory of a (0, 2) tensor multiplet in the type IIA case,
and of a (1, 1) gauge multiplet in the type IIB case.

or the small instanton solution is strongly coupled near its core, one cannot simply deduce
its excitation spectrum based on a perturbative analysis of the string states. However, at
nonzero thickness R, the massless bosonic excitations of the heterotic gauge instanton can
be identified with the moduli of an SO(32) Yang-Mills instanton. Indeed, the latter can be
shown to agree with the moduli of vacua of the massless effective field theory of the D5-brane
in type I string theory, in which the scalars of the D5-D9 hypermultiplets acquire nonzero
expectation values.239

evidently a symmetry of the bosonic part of the pseudo-action (18.37). The extension of the
SL(2, R) transformation to the fermionic fields, which preserves the complete equation of
motion of type IIB supergravity, can be deduced from the supersymmetry variations and is
given in (N.20).240 The SL(2, R) symmetry is spontaneously broken by the expectation value
of τ in the Minkowskian vacuum configuration to a U (1) subgroup, which may be identified
with the U (1)R outer automorphism of the N = (2, 0) supersymmetry algebra.
   In the type IIB string theory, the low energy SL(2, R) symmetry (as well as its U (1)R
subgroup) is explicitly violated by the α′ -corrections. Indeed, at fixed gravitational coupling
κ, any nontrivial dependence on the axion-dilaton expectation value of say the graviton
scattering amplitudes, which is already evident at the string tree level, breaks the SL(2, R)
invariance. The S-duality is the conjectural statement that an SL(2, Z) subgroup of the
SL(2, R), whose elements are the matrices with integer entries
                              
                              ab
                                   , a, b, c, d ∈ Z, ad − bc = 1,                        (18.40)
                              cd

that acts on τ, B2 , C2 according to (18.38) (and leaves Gµν , C4 invariant) is an exact symmetry
of type IIB string theory. Moreover, we will see in section 18.6 that the S-duality should be
viewed as a (discrete) gauge symmetry of type IIB string theory.

τ̄ respectively), cannot be completed into a supergraviton amplitude that obeys the super-
symmetry Ward identities without poles in the momenta. It follows that ∂τ ∂τ̄ f (τ ), which

18.5      Black p-branes

Similarly to the NS5-brane solution described in section 18.2.1, one may also seek super-
symmetric solitonic p-brane solutions of type II supergravity, also known as black p-branes,
that carry the same RR charge as the Dp-branes. Such solutions can be interpreted as the
spacetime that results from the gravitational backreaction of a stack of Dp-branes.

18.6     D7-branes and F-theory

The D7-brane in type IIB string theory is a peculiar object. One indication is that the
black p-brane solution (18.75), (18.76) with ISO(1, p) × SO(9 − p) isometry no longer exists
for p ≥ 7, as there is no solution for fp (r) (18.77) that respects the asymptotic boundary
condition at r = ∞. Let us consider a more general family of BPS 7-brane solutions assuming
only ISO(1, 7) along its world volume directions, but not necessarily asymptotically flat nor
invariant with respect to the transverse rotations. The supersymmetry conditions are still
solved by (18.75), (18.76) if we replace f7 (r) with a harmonic function

                                       f (z, z̄) = Im(h(z)),                            (18.78)

where z ≡ x8 + ix9 is a complex coordinate that parameterizes the transverse space. The
dilaton and RR axion profile can be expressed as

                                τ ≡ gB (C0 + ie−Φ ) = gB h(z),                          (18.79)

and the metric in the Einstein frame is simply
                                   1

In the presence of a single D7-brane, the magnetic flux with respect to the RR axion is such

naive attempt is to take

z-plane, including at the locus of the brane where it vanishes, the positivity of Im(τ ) implies
that τ (z) is a constant by Liouville’s theorem. In other words, the 7-brane solution with a
globally defined axion-dilaton profile τ (z) does not exist.
   The S-duality of type IIB string theory allows for the possibility that τ (z) undergoes
an SL(2, Z) monodromy as z moves around a closed loop. To understand the monodromy
properties, it will be useful to consider a slightly more general form of the Einstein frame

describes a vacuum configuration of type IIB string theory that preserves 16 supersymme-

and a compact internal space of spherical topology. The non-perturbative consistency of
this spacetime background, also known as “F-theory on elliptic K3”, will be further justified
in section 18.7. This family of vacua is parameterized by the coefficients of f (z) and g(z)
modulo the P SL(2, C) transformations of the Riemann sphere and an overall simultaneous
rescaling of f, g, resulting in 9 + 13 − 3 − 1 = 18 complex moduli, plus 1 additional real
parameter due to the freedom of rescaling ρ(z) by a constant. Note that in particular the
24 7-branes cannot all be moved independently while preserving supersymmetry.

18.7      M-theory

The low energy effective theory of type IIA string theory, namely type IIA supergravity,
coincides with the dimensional reduction of the 11-dimensional supergravity (Appendix N.2).
This is seen by considering an S 1 compactification of the 11D spacetime that is translationally
invariant along the S 1 direction, whose metric can be expressed as

effective theory of a certain quantum theory of gravity, commonly referred to as the M-
theory, which admits the 11D Minkowskian spacetime as a vacuum configuration with 32
supersymmetries, and whose circle compactification is equivalent to (the non-perturbative

approximation. Nonetheless, one expects the spectrum of BPS states such as the KK modes
of the supergraviton to be protected from quantum corrections and thereby agreeing with
the spectrum of the D0-brane and its bound states deduced at weak string coupling.


18.7.1       M2 and M5-branes

The 11D supergravity contains a 3-form gauge field CM N P that descends to the B-field and

string is electrically charged with respect to the B-field, whereas the D2-brane is electrically
charged with respect to C3 . The M-theory, on the other hand, is expected to contain a

18.7.3   From M to F-theory

Let us consider the compactification of M-theory on T 2 , described by the background metric

                             ds2 = ds2R1,8 + dx29 + (dx10 + adx9 )2 ,                   (18.112)

where x9,10 ∼ x9,10 + 2πR9,10 , and a is a real constant. The complex modulus of the T 2 is
                                                           R9
                                  τ ≡ τ1 + iτ2 = (a + i)       .                        (18.113)
                                                           R10
This M-theory background is a special case of (18.96), and should√ therefore be equivalent
to type IIA string theory compactified on the x9 -circle, with gA α′ = R10 and a constant

                                               395
background RR 1-form potential C1 = adx9 . Note that despite the vanishing field strength,
there is a nontrivial gauge-invariant holonomy of the RR potential around the x9 -circle, given
                                             −1
   H
by C1 = 2πR9 a = 2πτ1 /µ0 , where µ0 = R10      is the charge of a D0-brane.
    Next, we consider the T-duality along the x9 -circle, which maps the type IIA string√theory
to type IIB string theory on a circle of radius R e9 = α′ /R9 , with coupling gB = gA α′ /R9
and constant background RR axion C0 = a = gB τ1 . Consequently, the complex modulus of
the M-theory torus (18.113) is precisely identified with the axion-dilaton τ of the type IIB
string theory. The compactification radius of the type IIB string theory, on the other hand,
can be expressed in the 10-dimensional Planck units as
                                                        − 34
                                               R  9 R 10
                                   M10 R
                                       e9 =                    ,                       (18.114)
                                                 M11
where M10 is defined as in (18.42), and we have used (18.102). The decompactification of
the type IIB string theory to the 10-dimensional Minkowskian spacetime is recovered in the
limit R9 R10 → 0, i.e. the limit in which the M-theory torus has vanishing area with a fixed
complex modulus τ .
    The relation between the M-theory compactified on small torus and type IIB string the-
ory can be generalized to the case where the M-theory torus is fibered over a base manifold.
In particular, one can consider M-theory compactified on an elliptically fibered K3 surface,
whose underlying complex manifold is described by (18.88), where f (z) and g(z) are poly-
nomials of degree 8 and 12 respectively. Yau’s theorem implies that the K3 surface admit a
family of Ricci-flat (hyper-)Kähler metrics, giving rise to vacuum solutions of 11D supergrav-
ity of the form R1,6 ×K3 that preserve 16 supersymmetries generated by covariantly constant
Killing spinors. The moduli of the family of solutions, which include the area A of the torus
fiber, give rise to massless scalar fields in the 7-dimensional massless effective theory. The
vanishing of the effective potential for the moduli fields is required by compatibility with the
16 supersymmetries, and hence the existence of this family of vacua is expected to persist in
the M-theory beyond the supergravity approximation. In the limit A → 0, the compactified
M-theory is expected to be equivalent to type IIB string theory on the 2-dimensional base
manifold of the elliptic fibration, with a varying axion-dilaton profile τ as given by (18.88),
which is none other than the F-theory on elliptic K3 described in section 18.6. Moreover,
Sen’s limit corresponds to the case where the K3 is the Kummer surface T 2 × Te2 /Z2 , where
the first T 2 factor is viewed as the elliptic fiber, and the Z2 acts by reflection in all directions.


18.7.4    Corrections to 11D supergravity

The quantum effective action of M-theory is expected to receive corrections beyond that
of the 11D supergravity. In particular, while the scattering amplitudes of supergravitons

dispersion relations.244 For comparison, let us inspect the reduced amplitude of 2 → 2 scat-
tering of gravitons in type IIA string theory, which is constrained by supersymmetry to be

18.8.2     The strong coupling limit of hetE

We can now address the strong coupling limit of hetE by combining the T-duality between
hetE and hetO theories with the strong/weak duality between hetO and type I string theory.
Consider the hetE theory with string coupling gs,hetE , compactified on the X 9 -circle of radius
R with constant background gauge field as in (18.122). On one hand, in the R → ∞ limit,
one recovers hetE in 10-dimensional Minkowskian spacetime, and the background gauge field
becomes negligible. On the other hand, at finite R, the T-duality (18.128) maps hetE to the
circle-compactified hetO theory with constant background gauge field (18.126), whose string
coupling gs,hetO and compactification radius R′ are related by245

sets of SO(16) gauge fields on their respective 9-dimensional world volumes. The latter is
in agreement with the unbroken gauge group of the compactified hetE theory due to the

The pair of O8-planes together with the D8-branes at the end points of the interval of the

stretched along the interval I, suspended between the two boundaries. Indeed, the latter has
an effective string tension πRA TM2 = (2πℓ2s,het )−1 , in agreement with that of the heterotic
string.
    In the limit R → ∞, the M-theory circle decompactifies, and we end up with M-theory
in the spacetime R1,9 × I. The above chain of dualities implies that the latter should be
equivalent to the hetE theory in the 10-dimensional Minkowskian spacetime, whose string
coupling gE is related to the length πRA of the M-theory interval by (18.135). Moreover,
the 10-dimensional E8 × E8 gauge symmetry is restored in the decompactification limit, and
therefore one expects the SO(16) gauge fields living on each of the boundaries of the M-theory
spacetime to be enhanced to E8 gauge fields. We have thus arrived at the striking conclusion
that the hetE theory is equivalent to M-theory “compactified” on an interval, whose length
                                          2/3
in 11D Planck units is proportional to gE . Furthermore, each boundary of the M-theory
spacetime supports E8 gauge fields with 10-dimensional N = (1, 0) supersymmetry, whose
gauge coupling is expressed in terms the 11D Planck mass as

As will be explained in the next subsection, such a 10-dimensional supersymmetric gauge
theory would have been anomalous on its own, but in fact it serves to cancel against the
anomalies that would otherwise arise from the boundary condition on the fields of the 11D
supergravity in the bulk.

18.8.4    Heterotic instanton and M5-brane

We have seen in section 18.2.3 that the heterotic NS5-brane solution is continuously con-
nected to that of the gauge instanton. In the M-theory description, while the heterotic
NS5-brane is expected to uplift to an M5-brane traverse to the interval I, a heterotic gauge
instanton turns into that of the E8 gauge theory residing on either boundary. The latter
is characterized by a 10-dimensional gauge field configuration whose field strength F2 obeys
the self-duality condition F = ∗4 F , where ∗4 stands for the Hodge star operator on a 4-
dimensional submanifold B4 ⊂ M ′ transverse to the world volume of the instanton 5-brane,
whose tension obeys the BPS relation

    Starting from the C2 /Z2 orbifold CFT, the deformation operators M 1,AB (19.23) split

and (0, π). Only one of these points corresponds to the undeformed C2 /Z2 orbifold, which as
we understand is a perfectly regular CFT. The other point is in fact a singular CFT that is
not equivalent to the undeformed orbifold, and is expected to capture the k = 2 NS5-brane
throat (section 18.2.2).


19.2.3    Singular CFT and massless D-branes

It is useful to characterize the type II string theory in R1,5 ×C2 /Zk through the long distance
effective field theory of the massless degrees of freedom, which includes the supergraviton
propagating in the orbifold spacetime, and the massless closed string states that arise from
the twisted sector of the orbifold CFT that are confined to the vicinity of the orbifold fixed
point. We will focus on the type IIA case, where the orbifold background preserves the
6-dimensional (1, 1) supersymmetry. The massless closed string states from each of the k − 1
twisted sectors form a 6D Abelian gauge multiplet, including four (NS,NS) scalar moduli
fields associated with the deformation (19.23), and a gauge boson that arise from the (R,R)
sector. The (1, 1) supersymmetry prevents any correction to the effective action of the gauge
theory at the two-derivative order. This non-renormalization property also applies to the
supersymmetry algebra acting on charged states, where the dependence of the central charges
on the vacuum expectation value of the moduli fields is as in the classical gauge theory.
    A particularly interesting class of charged BPS states correspond to D2-branes wrapping
2-cycles in the Taub-NUT space. Their properties are most easily determined using the
T-dual description as D1-branes suspended between NS5-branes in type IIB string theory,
as in the setup of section 19.1. Let us consider the k = 2 case, with a pair of NS5-branes
separated by ∆⃗x ∈ R3 and angle ∆ψ on the S 1 . The mass of the BPS suspended D1-brane
is
                                         1 p

                                     gB 2πα′

the Taub-NUT space. The mass (19.31) can be expressed in terms of the T-dual frame

with the coordinates on the moduli space M    f2 (19.28). We emphasize that (19.32) is the
exact expression of the BPS D2-brane mass as it is a consequence of the centrally extended
supersymmetry algebra. In particular, the D2-brane mass vanishes at the point (∆⃗x  e, ∆ψ) =
(0, 0), signaling the breakdown of the 6D Abelian effective field theory, as well as string
perturbation theory itself. This is consistent with the expectation that ∆ψ = 0 corresponds
to a singular CFT on the worldsheet, which differs from the C2 /Z2 orbifold theory that arises
at ∆ψ = π.
    There is, nonetheless, a non-singular effective field theory description of the massless
degrees of freedom including the wrapped D2-brane, in the form of an SU (2) gauge theory.
Turning on nonzero ∆⃗xe or ∆ψ amounts to moving to the Coulomb branch of this gauge the-
ory, where the SU (2) gauge group is broken to U (1), and the massive W-boson is none other
than the wrapped D2-brane! In a similar manner, the moduli space M  fk of the marginally de-
formed R1,5 × C2 /Zk background contains a point where the 6D gauge symmetry is enhanced
to SU (k).


19.3     D-branes in orbifolds

There is a general recipe for constructing conformal boundary conditions of an orbifold CFT
of the form M/Zk , starting from a Zk -invariant boundary condition B of the parent CFT
M , as follows. Let g be the generator of the Zk global symmetry of M , and denote by Lg
the corresponding topological defect line operator. By assumption, Lg acts trivially on the
boundary, i.e. g|B⟩ = |B⟩, where |B⟩ stands for the boundary state. It follows that there is
an isomorphism from the Hilbert space on the interval, HBB , to the space of states on the
interval with an Lg -defect, which we denote by HBLg B . The latter can also be viewed as
the space of boundary defect operators with an Lg line attached. In particular, the identity
operator in HBB maps to a state ιg ∈ HBLg B , which as a boundary operator can simply
be viewed as a conformally invariant end point of Lg on the boundary. Inserting ιg on a
boundary component then turns the boundary state |B⟩ into

                                                           417
    Under the exactly marginal deformations that turn the orbifold into the ALE space, the

contractible 2-cycles in the ALE space. In the k = 2 case, for instance, the ALE space
admits only one minimal area non-contractible S 2 . The two kinds of fractional D0-branes
turn into a D2-brane or an anti-D2-brane wrapping the S 2 , whose world volume magnetic
fluxes differ by one unit. When the S 2 is of nonzero size, the D2-brane and the anti-D2-
brane are no longer mutually BPS. Together they can annihilate via condensation of the
open string tachyon, leaving behind an ordinary D0-brane that is then free to move in the
ALE space.

  The validity of the above T-duality prescription relies on the existence of a worldsheet
matter SCFT based on the supersymmetric nonlinear sigma model with target space ge-
ometry (19.47) and dilaton profile as in (19.46). At finite k, the Lagrangian/path integral

                                               419
formulation of this NLSM is strongly coupled, and is expected to receive all-order perturba-
tive as well as non-perturbative corrections in α′ . Remarkably, there is an exact formulation
of this SCFT based on a supersymmetric generalization of the coset models described in
Appendix I.4, of the form252

Here SL(2, R)k and SU (2)k refer to the supersymmetric WZW models based on the group
SL(2, R) and SU (2) at level k, whose definition and properties are elaborated in section
22.6.1. The quotient by U (1) can be defined either through the gauged WZW models or
in terms of intrinsic CFT data by decoupling a subsector based on the U (1) WZW model,
which we now describe in more detail.

The GSO projection further imposes F + q, Fe + qe ∈ 2Z, where F, Fe are the holomorphic and
anti-holomorphic fermion numbers of the R1,5 sector combined with superconformal ghosts.
For the quantum number assignment (19.97) and (19.101), q = qe = 0, and so the GSO
projection restricts the spin fields Sα , Seαb in the R1,5 to be both chiral spinors of so(1, 5) in
the type IIB case and (chiral, anti-chiral) spinors in the type IIA case. In the type IIB case,
these massless RR vertex operators correspond to k − 1 self-dual 3-form field strengths in
6D, in agreement with the (0, 2) world volume theory of k separated NS5-branes in the T-
dual type IIA string description (upon factoring out the center-of-mass degrees of freedom;
cf. section 21.4.3). In the type IIA case, the massless RR vertex operators correspond to
k − 1 2-form field strengths of a 6D U (1)k−1 gauge theory, in agreement with the (1, 1) world
volume theory of k separated NS5-branes in the T-dual type IIB string description.
    From the perspective of the 6D effective theory on the NS5-branes, the DSLST captures
dynamics near the origin of the tensor branch (in the (0, 2) theory of type IIA NS5-branes) or
the Coulomb branch (in the (1, 1) theory of type IIB NS5-branes) moduli space of vacua. The
effective string coupling at the tip of the cigar, due to (19.44), is inversely proportional to ρ0
or the distance from the origin in the tensor/Coulomb branch. In the limit ρ0 → 0 (with fixed
asymptotic string coupling), the DSLST becomes strongly coupled and approaches the little
string theory of section 18.2.2. In the type IIA DSLST, a set of D0-branes become massless
in this limit; they play the role of W-bosons, and enhance the U (1)k−1 gauge symmetry to
SU (k) on the k coincident type IIB NS5-branes.265 In the type IIB DSLST, a set of D1-
strings that are charged with respect to the aforementioned massless (R,R) fields become
tensionless. This is a characteristic feature of the (0, 2) little string theory, whose infrared
superconformal theory will be discussed further in section 21.4.
 265
   For a detailed analysis of the boundary state of D-branes in the DSLST, see Israel, Pakman and Troost,
Nucl. Phys. B 722, 3-64 (2005) [107].

The logarithmic divergence as L → ∞ indicates that the complex structure deformation
of the conifold is not quite a normalizable mode. Nonetheless, it is useful to work in the
effective field theory framework, treating L as a large but finite parameter, as a local model
of Calabi-Yau compactifications that develop a conifold singularity.
   As already mentioned, the complex scalar fields ϕα that arise from the complex structure
deformation belong to 4D N = 2 vector multiplets. Any quantum corrections to the NLSM
metric would introduce dependence on either the Kähler moduli or the dilaton background,
both of which are expectation values of 4D hypermultiplet scalars in the type IIB string
compactification. It is a consequence of the 4D N = 2 supersymmetry that the vector
multiplets and uncharged hypermultiplets decouple at the 2-derivative level (see Appendix
N.5). Therefore, ds2MC as determined from the Kähler potential (19.131) is the exact NLSM
metric that governs the kinetic term of vector multiplets in the 4D quantum effective action.
    The singularity of the metric (19.143) at Z 1 = 0 indicates that the 4D massless effective
theory breaks down near the conifold point, in a manner that cannot be resolved by quantum
corrections to the massless effective action (as the metric on MC is exact!). The resolution
to this apparent puzzle is that new massless degrees of freedom appear in the Z 1 → 0 limit,

As the minimal S 3 is a special Lagrangian subspace and the wrapped D3-brane is BPS

from quantum corrections and hence valid for any |Z 1 |.
    The key idea, due to Strominger,273 is that there is a non-singular 4D Wilsonian effective
field theory that contains both the vector multiplet corresponding to the complex modulus of
the deformed conifold, and the charged hypermultiplet corresponding to a D3-brane wrapping
the S 3 , that governs the low energy dynamics near Z 1 = 0. In the language of 4D N = 1
superspace (Appendix M.2), the N = 2 vector multiplet is described by a U (1) N = 1 vector
superfield V and a neutral chiral superfield Φ, whose scalar component is the aforementioned
complex moduli field ϕ. The hypermultiplet is described by a pair of chiral superfields Q
and Q e that carry +1 and −1 unit of U (1) charge respectively. Their complex scalar field
components will be denoted q, qe. The 2-derivative Lagrangian of this effective theory is an
extension of (M.39) by including the charged hypermultiplet coupling, which in the N = 1
formalism involves a generalization of (M.30) that accounts for a hyperkähler metric on the
target space of (q, qe),274 and a superpotential of the form (as a special case of (M.38))

                                             W = QΦQ.

Due to the noncompactness of the conifold, the vector multiplet kinetic term comes with a
divergent coefficient. This leads to a simplified form of the scalar effective potential

of the Coulomb branch parameterized by nonzero ϕ with q = qe = 0, and the Higgs branch
parameterized by nonzero (q, qe) with ϕ = 0.

manner, the transition between the (topologically distinct) deformed and resolved conifold

The cubic polynomial form of (19.167) can also be understood as a consequence of the
Peccei-Quinn (PQ) symmetry that shifts the B-field by a closed 2-form, which holds to all
perturbative orders in the α′ -expansion (recall discussion around (9.25)). As the preserved
supersymmetries pair up gij̄ and Bij̄ into the complex scalars of vector multiplets, the PQ
symmetry amounts to shifting ϕ1 by an arbitrary real constant. Under ϕ1 → ϕ1 + ϵ for
infinitesimal real ϵ, the preservation of G11̄ requires Im(F ′′′ (ϕ1 )) = 0, and hence F ′′′ (ϕ1 )
must be a real constant, as seen in (19.167).
    Moreover, we learn that (19.167) cannot be modified by the higher-derivative corrections
to the 10-dimensional supergravity effective theory beyond the α′3 order (corresponding to
the R4 effective coupling). This is because any corrections to F(ϕ1 ) that involve extra powers
of α′ must be accompanied by inverse powers of ϕ1 by dimension analysis. A correction to
F(ϕ1 ) beyond α′3 order would necessarily involve negative powers of ϕ1 and therefore violate
the cubic polynomial form as required by the PQ symmetry.279
   Beyond the perturbative α′ -expansion, however, the PQ symmetry is violated by world-
sheet instanton effects. In particular, the shift symmetry of the form B 7→ B + φ holds
supergravity corresponds to (see e.g. Candelas and de la Ossa [109]).

takes the same form as (9.12). The resulting superconformal field theory is simply related

19.5.5     The singular CFT at the conifold point

The (2, 2) superconformal NLSM with the resolved conifold target space can be realized
as the IR fixed point of the GLSM (Appendix K.3) of a U (1) vector superfield V , chiral
superfields A1 , A2 of charge +1, B1 , B2 of charge −1, and vanishing superpotential. The
classical moduli space of vacua of the GLSM is
                    n

where r is the Fayet-Iliopoulos parameter as defined in (K.10). Indeed, in terms of the
gauge-invariant variables Wab ≡ Aa Bb , Mcl for r > 0 and r < 0 can be identified with the
two different resolutions (19.113) and (19.119) of the conifold det(Wab ) = 0 respectively.
     Applying the dualization procedure of Appendix K.4 to the GLSM, one finds a low
energy effective theory described by the vector superfield coupled to twisted chiral superfields

19.6     Singularities in M-theory

19.6.1    Orbifold singularities in M-theory

Despite a wealth of evidence for the existence of M-theory as seen in sections 18.7 and
18.8, an intrinsically 11-dimensional formulation has thus far been limited to the leading
few orders in the derivative expansion of the low energy effective field theory. However, the
generic M-theory vacua may involve singular spacetime geometries, and exhibit dynamical
phenomena that are not captured by the 11-dimensional effective field theory. A basic class
of admissible singularities in M-theory, as we now consider, are those of the C2 /Zk orbifold.
    M-theory in the orbifold spacetime R1,6 × C2 /Zk may be obtained as the infinite string
coupling limit of the configuration of k coincident D6-branes in type IIA string theory,
as described in section 18.7.2. The massless degrees of freedom localized at the orbifold
singularities are characterized by the world volume effective theory of the D6-branes, namely
the 7D (N = 1) supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory with gauge group SU (k). Note that the
7D gauge coupling gYM can be expressed in terms of the 11D Planck mass M11 as

    An alternative way of arriving at the same M-theory orbifold spacetime is to take the
infinite coupling limit of type IIA string theory in R1,5 × C2 /Zk . As seen in section 19.2.3,
the orbifold singularity supports massless excitations that arise from closed string states in
the twisted sectors as well as the fractional D0-branes, which are moreover characterized by
a 6D (1, 1)-supersymmetric SU (k) gauge theory. The codimension-4 Yang-Mills instanton
solution of the 6D gauge theory describes a BPS solitonic string, which is in fact none other
than a fundamental type IIA string extended along R1,1 ⊂ R1,5 at the orbifold singularity.
Uplifting to M-theory, one finds a 7D supersymmetric SU (k) gauge theory, whose Yang-
Mills instanton solution describes an M2-brane located at the orbifold singularity. Indeed,
it follows from (19.217) that M2-brane tension (18.103) agrees with the instanton action,
namely
                                                 4π 2

                                                 gYM
    The construction of a massless effective theory that couples the bulk supergravity to the
degrees of freedom localized at the orbifold singularity is somewhat subtle. Similarly to a
brane-bulk effective theory, a fully consistent treatment of the orbifold-bulk effective theory
is only expected at the quantum level, e.g. through a Wilsonian effective action with a UV
cutoff scheme. Unlike the brane-bulk effective theory, however, the orbifold-bulk effective
theory is not subject to a nonlinearly realized bulk Poincaré symmetry and is in particular
not of the Born-Infeld form. An explicit construction of the orbifold-bulk effective action at
the two-derivative order is given by Anderson, Barrett and Lukas, Phys. Rev. D 73 (2006),
106011 [117], and some of the subleading corrections in the low-energy expansion have been
determined from the perspective of gluon-graviton scattering amplitudes in Chester et al.,
JHEP 06 (2024), 001 [118].


19.6.2   G2 holonomy and singularities

Now we turn to M-theory in spacetime of the form R1,3 × M , where M is a 7-dimensional
manifold. In the weak curvature approximation, and in the absence of G4 flux or background
fermion field, the condition for preserving supersymmetry i.e. the vanishing of the super-
symmetry variation of the gravitino (as in (N.5)) amounts to the existence of covariantly
constant spinors of the form ϵ = ϵ(4) ⊗ ξ, where ϵ(4) is a constant so(1, 3) spinor in R1,3 ,
and ξ is a covariantly constant so(7) spinor ξ on M . The holonomy group K ⊂ SO(7) on
M , defined as the group of parallel transport along all closed paths that begin and end at a
point x ∈ M , leaves ξ(x) invariant. It follows that K lies in a G2 subgroup of SO(7), under
which the 8-dimensional spinor representation splits into the direct sum of the 7-dimensional
fundamental representation of G2 and a singlet. Moreover, the metric on M is Ricci-flat.

                                             453
   On the G2 -holonomy manifold M , we can also construct covariantly constant p-forms via

similarly to that of a 4D N = 1 effective field theory, is expected to be a 1-dimensional

parameterized by the complex coordinates ηi = eℓi +ieαi , where ℓi is a certain linear function
of (f1 , f2 , f3 ), subject to the constraint

                                          η1 η2 η3 = −1.                                   (19.238)

The triality symmetry generated by (19.229) demands that M is invariant under cyclic
permutation of (η1 , η2 , η3 ), and is invariant under (η1 , η2 , η3 ) 7→ (η3−1 , η2−1 , η1−1 ).
   In the large volume regime, say in the branch where [D1 ] is filled, we have η2 ∼ e2πit ,
η3 ∼ e−2πit , where t is defined as in (19.235). The classical moduli space would amount to

                                         η1 = −η2 η3 = 1.                                  (19.239)

(19.239) cannot be the exact description of the quantum moduli space, as it would seem
to imply the existence of spacetime of the form (19.231) with large negative r03 . Instead, a
consistent proposal for the quantum moduli space is the curve

                                         η2 (1 − η3 ) = 1.                                 (19.240)

Indeed, one can easily verify that this curve is invariant under triality: (19.238) and (19.240)
imply η3 (1 − η1 ) = η1 (1 − η2 ) = 1 as well as η2−1 (1 − η1−1 ) = 1. It follows from (19.240) that
the three branches of the quantum moduli space are smoothly joined with one another.

20      The AdS/CFT correspondence

20.1     The decoupling limit of the black p-brane

The physical equivalence between the black p-brane solution of the massless effective theory
of type II superstring and the Dp-branes defined in terms of the open strings, as anticipated
in section 18.5, can be sharpened in the low energy limit where the massless open string
excitations on a stack of N Dp-branes are captured by the (p + 1)-dimensional maximally
supersymmetric U (N ) gauge theory (a.k.a. super-Yang-Mills, or SYM). The effects of mas-
sive open as well as closed string exchanges are suppressed by powers of ℓ2s E 2 , where E is the
energy scale of the open string excitations. The coupling to the bulk massless closed string
degrees of freedom, on the other hand, is suppressed by powers of κ2 N Tp E 7−p ∼ gN (ℓs E)7−p ,
where g is the dimensionless string coupling constant. Both effects are suppressed in the limit
                                                1
                                    ℓs E, (gN ) 7−p ℓs E ≪ 1,                             (20.1)

where the SYM theory based on the 2-derivative Lagrangian, to the extent that the latter
defines a UV-complete quantum field theory, potentially captures the entirety of the low
energy dynamics of the Dp-branes.
    In the black p-brane description (18.75), the second condition of (20.1) is equivalent to
E ≪ R−1 , where R is the gravitational radius of the p-brane solution. At this energy scale,
the bulk modes at r ≳ R decouple from the near horizon modes at r ≪ R, the latter being
                                                       1
subject to the gravitational redshift factor (fp (r))− 4 . This suggests that the near horizon
modes should capture the same degrees of freedom as those of the low energy open strings
on the stack of Dp-branes, leading to the conjecture that the type II string theory in the
background of the near-horizon or decoupling limit of the black p-brane, defined by the
solution (18.75), (18.76) with fp (r) replaced by
                                                    7−p

                                                   r
should be somehow equivalent to the (p + 1)-dimensional maximally supersymmetric U (N )
gauge theory, at least in the case p ≤ 3 where the SYM Lagrangian defines a UV-complete
quantum field theory.
    For p ≤ 2, the decoupling geometry appears to be singular at the horizon r = 0 as well as
at the asymptotic infinity (or boundary), whereas the effective string coupling, proportional
                   3−p

do not necessarily invalidate the solution, but indicates large quantum corrections at small
r and stringy corrections in the asymptotic region. The case of p = 2, 1, 0 will be analyzed
in sections 21.3, 26.4, and 26.1 respectively.

the AdS5 × S 5 solution.

The key conceptual leap, based on the observation that the path integral quantization of
action (20.6) defines N = 4 SYM as a UV-complete (3+1)-dimensional quantum field theory,
is that the latter should provide an exact characterization of the quantum D3-brane dynamics
in the decoupling limit. The consistency of this proposal relies crucially on the property that
the N = 4 SYM is a scale-invariant QFT, with gYM being an exactly marginal coupling
parameter. While the vanishing of the beta function has been confirmed by computations of
perturbative and instanton contributions, a relatively simple non-perturbative argument can
be made based on supersymmetry as follows. The basic idea is to extend (20.6) by promoting
the complexified coupling τ (20.7) to the scalar component of an N = 1 chiral superfield,
and consider the effective action that results from the path integral with a Wilsonian cutoff,
assuming a regularization scheme that preserves N = 1 supersymmetry. The effective gauge
coupling appears in the Wilsonian effective action through a chiral superspace integral that
can only depend holomorphically on τ , and is severely constrained by the anomaly in the
U (1)R symmetry (see Appendix M.3 for further details). In the end, one finds that the
effective gauge coupling can at most receive a 1-loop correction, which vanishes in the case
of the N = 4 SYM. A more intrinsic argument for the exact marginality of gYM based on
consistency with the superconformal representation theory will be given in section 20.6.
     While the scale invariance of N = 4 SYM implies that the trace of its stress-energy tensor

The supercharges QI α , QI α̇ that generate the N = 4 supersymmetry, on the other hand,
obey the (anti-)commutator relations

  {QI α , QJ β̇ } = −2δJI γαµβ̇ Pµ ,      {QI α , QJ β } = {QI α̇ , QJ β̇ } = 0,
                                                          i                        i
  [Pµ , QI α ] = [Pµ , QI α̇ ] = 0,      [Jµν , QI α ] = − (γµν )α β QI β ,
                                                                 [Jµν , QI α̇ ] = − (γµν )α̇ β̇ QI β̇ .
                                                          2                        2
                                                                                              (20.12)
The non-commutativity of P with K implies that Q cannot commute with K either. As P
and K carry weight +1 and −1 with respect to the dilatation operator, Q has weight + 21 , it
follows that [K, Q] is an operator of weight − 12 . Therefore, we can write

                                                        I β̇
                             [K µ , QI α ] = −γαµβ̇ S ,              [K µ , QI β̇ ] = −γαµβ̇ SIα ,           (20.13)

                    I β̇
where SIα and S are weight − 12 operators known as the special supercharges. As P and K
are related by the inversion map, so are Q and S. It follows that
                              β̇               I                                    J β̇
        [P µ , SIα ] = γαµβ̇ QI ,      [P µ , S β̇ ] = γαµβ̇ QIα ,        {SIα , S } = −2δIJ γαµβ̇ Kµ .      (20.14)

Finally, to close the algebra by consistency with Jacobi identities, we have
                                                                                              J
   {QI α , SJβ } = 2iδJI (γ µν )αβ Jµν − 2iδJI ϵαβ D − 4ϵαβ RI J ,

A novel feature here is that {Q, S} necessarily involves R J , the generators of the su(4) ≃
so(6) R-symmetry, that obey RI I ≡ 0 and
                                                                                 1

Altogether, P, J, D, K, Q, S, R generate the N = 4 superconformal algebra, which is isomor-
phic to the Lie super-algebra psu(2, 2|4).289

20.3      Vacuum configurations

The N = 4 SYM in the Minkowskian spacetime R1,3 admits a family of “Coulomb branch”293
vacua that spontaneously break the conformal symmetry and the SO(6) R-symmetry, while
maintaining the N = 4 super-Poincaré symmetry. In the classical limit, the vacua can be
understood as the minima of the scalar potential appearing in the action (20.6), and are
parameterized by the vacuum expectation values of the scalar fields ⟨ϕi ⟩ that obey

                                   [⟨ϕi ⟩, ⟨ϕj ⟩] = 0,         i, j = 1, · · · , 6,                   (20.26)

modulo the gauge equivalence ⟨ϕi ⟩ ∼ g⟨ϕi ⟩g −1 , for all g ∈ U (N ). We can use the gauge
transformation to simultaneously diagonalize ⟨ϕi ⟩ and write

                                ⟨ϕi ⟩ = diag φi1 , · · · , φiN .

    The AdS5 ×S 5 spacetime (20.3) as a vacuum configuration of type IIB string theory, which
arises in the decoupling limit that involves a stack of N coincident D3-branes, corresponds
to the vacuum of N = 4 SYM that preserves the full psu(2, 2|4) superconformal symmetry,
i.e. the origin of the moduli space M. To understand the dual description of the other
vacua in M from the AdS5 perspective, let us begin with the picture of N D3-branes before
taking the decoupling limit, and consider separating one of the D3-branes from the remaining
stack of N − 1. An equivalent description of this system would be to replace the stack of
N − 1 D3-branes with the black 3-brane solution (18.74) that carries N − 1 units of RR
5-form flux, leaving a single D3-brane probing the black 3-brane background at a nonzero
transverse coordinate ⃗x⊥ = (x4 , · · · , x9 ). Assuming that r = |⃗x⊥ | is sufficiently small so
as to be in the throat region of the black 3-brane geometry, after taking the coupling limit
one finds a D3-brane located at radial coordinate r and a point on the S 5 in the AdS5 × S 5
geometry (20.3). Evidently, this configuration can be interpreted as the dual description of
a vacuum of N = 4 SYM where the gauge group is broken to U (N − 1) × U (1). In the
classical limit of N = 4 SYM, this vacuum is described by the scalar fields acquiring the
vacuum expectation value of the form (20.27) with φi1 = · · · = φiN −1 = 0 and φiN ̸= 0. In the
strong ’t Hooft coupling regime that corresponds to the supergravity background with large
curvature radius, we can nonetheless characterize this vacuum in terms of an effective field
theory in which a U (1) gauge multiplet, whose scalar components can be identified with φiN ,
is coupled to the N = 4 SYM with gauge group U (N − 1) through irrelevant operators (as
constrained by supersymmetry) that are suppressed at energy scale E ≪ |⃗       φN |.

fields give rise to massive particles, which we will refer to as “W-bosons” by a standard
abuse of terminology, that carry ±1 unit of charge with respect to the U (1) gauge field.
These W-bosons are dual to open strings stretched from the probe D3-brane to the AdS5
horizon at r = 0. In the large radius regime, the mass of the open string can be deduced

                        ds2 = R2 (− cosh2 ρ dt2 + dρ2 + sinh2 ρ dΩ23 ).                (20.36)

Following the same chain of Wick rotations and conformal transformation on the CFT side,
one is led to the proposal that the type IIB string theory in the global AdS5 ×S 5 spacetime is
equivalent to the N = 4 SYM on the Lorentzian cylinder R × S 3 . In particular, one expects
the Hilbert space of quantum states of the type IIB string theory in the global AdS5 × S 5 to
be identified with that of the N = 4 SYM on S 3 , or equivalently the space of gauge invariant
local operators at a point in R4 via the state/operator map. The Hamiltonian with respect
to the global time coordinate t as appearing in (20.36) is identified with the Hamiltonian of
N = 4 on S 3 , or equivalently the dilatation operator (up to a factor of i by convention) on
the space of local operators at a point.
