The above analysis can be generalized to free fields that transform in any tensor or spinor rep-
resentations of the local Lorentz group, whose quantization lead to a Hilbert space spanned
by Fock states, and the 1-particle states form an irreducible representation of the isome-
try/conformal group SO(2, 4) whose lowest energy states are a set of conformal primaries
that transform in a representation of the SO(4) rotation group.
    In the dual N = 4 SYM on S 3 , the Fock space structure of the Hilbert space emerges in
the infinite N limit as a consequence of the large N factorization, in the following sense. A
priori, at the level of perturbative gauge theory, a basis of gauge invariant local operators
can be constructed as regularized and renormalized products of single-trace operators of the
form
                                      O = tr (Φ1 Φ2 · · · ) ,                          (20.46)
where Φ1 , Φ2 , · · · stand for adjoint-valued fields ϕi , λIα , λI α̇ , Fµν and their gauge-covariant
derivatives. While the regularization and renormalization generally introduce anomalous
dimensions as well as operator mixing, a standard counting of N -scaling in Feynman dia-
grams shows that in the limit of large N with finite ’t Hooft coupling λ, the mixing between
single-trace and multi-trace operators is suppressed. A single-trace operator, or equivalently
its corresponding state in HS 3 , is dual to a 1-particle state in AdS5 , and likewise multi-trace
operators are dual to multi-particle states. The large N factorization of correlation functions,
via the holographic dictionary described in the next section, will lead to the suppression of
the interaction between particles in the said limit.
    Whereas in perturbative theory, it is sensible to characterize the states of a gravitational
theory through particles or field excitations that propagate in a given spacetime background,
at the non-perturbative level one should allow for excitations that alter the spacetime topol-
ogy at least in a semi-classical sense, such as in a process that involves the formation of
black hole horizon. The Hilbert space of a quantum gravitational theory in the global AdS
spacetime, in particular, should capture all finite energy excitations that preserve the AdS
geometry at the asymptotic infinity i.e. the conformal boundary. This is sensible particu-
larly due to the confining nature of the global AdS geometry. In sections 20.6 – 20.9, we will

                                                      469
examine the map between the quantum states of type IIB string theory in AdS5 × S 5 and
the operator spectrum of N = 4 SYM in detail.


20.5     Holographic correlators

The identification between the space of local operators in the N = 4 SYM and the Hilbert
space of type IIB string in the global AdS5 × S 5 can be extended to a holographic dictionary
between correlation functions of the gauge theory in the Euclidean R4 and the partition
function of string theory in EAdS5 × S 5 subject to suitable asymptotic boundary conditions.
For the sake of generalization to other examples (Chapter 21), we will describe this holo-
graphic dictionary in the context of the AdSd+1 /CFTd correspondence. The latter amounts
to the assertion that a certain theory of quantum gravity (QG) in the AdSd+1 spacetime
is equivalent to a d-dimensional conformal field theory (CFTd ). In particular, the Hilbert
space of the QG in the global AdSd+1 is identified with the Hilbert space of the CFTd on
S d−1 , or equivalently the space of local operators in the CFTd .
    By a Wick rotation and a conformal transformation, we may view a local operator O(x0 )
of the CFT, inserted at x0 ∈ Rd , as creating a state |O⟩ in the Hilbert space of the QG
associated with the totally geodesic hypersurface Sx0 ,u in EAdSd+1 defined by

                                         (x − x0 )2 + z 2 = u2 ,                               (20.47)

for any u > 0. In other words, Sx0 ,u can be viewed as the constant time slice with respect to
the Euclidean time coordinate log(u), the latter being equivalent to the Euclidean global time
by an isometry of AdSd+1 . At least at the level of a perturbative path integral formulation of
the QG, we may represent the state |O⟩ by a wave functional ΨO of field configurations on
the hypersurface Sx0 ,u . Furthermore, we can represent a correlation function of a set of local
operators O1 (x1 ), · · · , On (xn ) inserted at different points in Rd by the QG path integral in
EAdSd+1 with the regions Bxi ,ui = {(x, z) : (x−xi )2 +z 2 < u2i } excised, all the while inserting
the wave functionals ΨOi on Sxi ,ui = ∂Bxi ,ui . This is sensible so long as the ui ’s are chosen
to be sufficiently small so that the hypersurfaces Sxi ,ui do not overlap with one another. In
particular, we may take the limit ui → 0, and view the effect of integrating against the wave
functional ΨOi on Sxi ,ui as a modification of the asymptotic boundary condition of the QG
in EAdSd+1 at the point (xi , z = 0). This leads to a formal holographic dictionary

                ZQG,EAdSd+1 [O1 (x1 ), · · · , On (xn )] = ⟨O1 (x1 ) · · · On (xn )⟩CFT,Rd ,   (20.48)

where the LHS is the QG partition function with the modification of the boundary condition
at (xi , z = 0), or “boundary source”, as specified by the quantum state ΨOi . In principle
(20.48) is sensible also at the non-perturbative level, to the extent that ZQG,EAdSd+1 is defined,

                                                   470
say by a sort of path integral over all gravitational field and brane configurations that are
asymptotically EAdSd+1 .
   In an effective field theory framework for QG in AdS, the LHS of (20.48) can be evaluated
using the perturbative path integral. The relevant boundary conditions for the bulk fields
and the subsequent computations of holographic correlators are discussed in Appendix R.


20.6       Supergraviton states

All quantum states of type IIB string theory in AdS5 × S 5 can be organized according to
irreducible unitary representations of the psu(2, 2|4) super-isometry or superconformal alge-
bra. The lowest weight states in such a representation are superconformal primaries, which
are states that are annihilated by the special supercharges SIα , S I α̇ (and hence also by the
special conformal generator Kµ ), and all remaining states in the representation are obtained
by acting on the primaries with QI α , QI α̇ . Special classes of superconformal primaries, also
known as chiral primaries, are such that their QI α , QI α̇ descendants obey nontrivial linear
relations (i.e. null states) and thereby give rise to shortened (BPS) representations. It is a
consequence of the superconformal algebra relation {Q, S} ∼ D + J + R that the confor-
mal weight of a chiral primary (or the energy of the corresponding state in the global AdS)
is determined by a linear combination of its SO(4) spin and SO(6) R-symmetry quantum
numbers.297
    The 1-particle states of the supergraviton fall into the simplest class of shortened rep-
resentations of psu(2, 2|4), known as the 12 -BPS representations. The chiral primaries of
these representation, somewhat surprisingly, come from linear combinations of the fluctua-
tion modes of the volume element of the S 5 and the RR 5-form flux.298 It is easier to examine
instead the axion-dilaton field τ whose linearized equation of motion is simply the massless
Klein-Gordon equation in the AdS5 × S 5 spacetime. We can decompose

                                  τ (x, y) =    τI (x)YI (y),                           (20.49)
                                                        I

where x and y stand for coordinates on the AdS5 and S 5 respectively, and YI (y) is a ba-
sis of scalar spherical harmonics on S 5 . In terms of the embedding coordinate ⃗
                                                                                Ω of S 5 as

20.8     Giant gravitons

The quantum states of type IIB string theory in the global AdS5 × S 5 include those of the
D-branes, which typically arise at energy scale or scaling dimension ∆ of order N . This is
elegantly illustrated through a special class of D3-brane configurations in AdS5 ×S 5 that solve
the Euler-Lagrange equation of the Born-Infeld effective action, known as giant gravitons.
   We begin by writing the metric on the S 5 in the Hopf coordinates as

subgroup of SO(6)R . Now consider a D3-brane wrapping the S 3 in the Ω3 direction, moving
in the ϕ direction, while sitting at constant θ and at the center (ρ = 0) of the global AdS5 .

The saturation of the BPS bound ∆ ≥ J indicate that these D3-brane solutions preserve

angular momentum due to the coupling to the background magnetic RR 4-form potential.

and may appear indistinguishable from a BPS supergraviton that carries the same energy
and angular momentum quantum numbers. The latter is dual to the chiral primary operator

                                         tr(X J ),      X ≡ ϕ1 + iϕ2 .                         (20.72)

As (20.72) is the only single-trace operator in the N = 4 SYM that obeys ∆ = J, one is
tempted to identify a supergraviton that carries large J quantum number with the giant
graviton D3-brane solution (hence the name).
   One should be cautious, however, as the mixing between single-trace and multi-trace
operators is no longer suppressed when the operator scaling dimensions are of order N , and
the planar diagrams no longer dominate in the large N limit. This can be illustrated by
comparing the single-trace operator

                                                  Oℓ := tr(Φℓ )                                (20.73)

with the double trace operator Oℓ1 ,ℓ2 := Oℓ1 Oℓ2 in the theory of a free Hermitian N × N
matrix-valued field Φ, for ℓ = ℓ1 + ℓ2 . The normalization of (20.73) is such that the planar
contributions to the two-point functions scale as

        ⟨Oℓ Oℓ ⟩planar ∼ ℓN ℓ ,   ⟨Oℓ1 ,ℓ2 Oℓ1 ,ℓ2 ⟩planar ∼ ℓ1 ℓ2 N ℓ ,
                                                                ⟨Oℓ Oℓ1 ,ℓ2 ⟩planar ∼ ℓℓ1 ℓ2 N ℓ−1 .
                                                                                                (20.74)
If we set ℓ1 = ε1 N , ℓ2 = ε2 N and consider the limit of large N with finite ε1 , ε2 , the estimate
(20.74) violates Cauchy-Schwarz inequality ⟨Oℓ Oℓ1 ,ℓ2 ⟩2 ≤ ⟨Oℓ Oℓ ⟩ ⟨Oℓ1 ,ℓ2 Oℓ1 ,ℓ2 ⟩, indicating
that the planar approximation breaks down (even if ε1 , ε2 are parametrically small). The
large mixing between single and multi-trace operators is expected to persist in the interacting
gauge theory at any value of the ’t Hooft coupling. From the bulk perspective, this does
not come as a surprise. For instance, given that the gravitational coupling κ in AdS units
 301

distinct from the spherical D3-brane.

20.9         Black holes in AdS and thermodynamics

The states at energy scale ∆ ∼ N 2 in the global AdS5 × S 5 can no longer be characterized in
terms of weakly coupled strings or D-branes as they necessarily involve strong gravitational
interactions. In the long distance effective field theory description, such states produce order
one backreaction on the local spacetime geometry, which typically lead to the formation of
black holes with horizons.
    A “small” black hole is characterized by a solution to the supergravity equation in asymp-
totically AdS5 × S 5 spacetime that is localized in all spatial dimensions, with a horizon of
size rH ≪ R. It can be approximated by the more familiar black hole (e.g. Schwarzschild)

                     7
hole scales as M ∼ rH  /κ2 , which translates to operator scaling dimension

                                       ∆ ∼ N 2 (rH /R)7 .                               (20.81)

The quantum interpretation of the black hole, at the semi-classical level, is understood
through the quantization of field fluctuations in the black hole background, which famously
lead to the Hawking radiation. The standard dogma is that the black hole should be viewed
as metastable quantum states that decay through Hawking radiation, or alternatively as a
thermal ensemble of quantum states that is in statistical equilibrium with a thermal bath of
gravitons and other particles.
                                                                               −1
    The Hawking temperature TH of the small black hole scales as TH ∼ rH          , and the life
time of the black hole (in units of the AdS radius) as estimated from the power of Hawking
radiation scales as ∼ N 2 (rH /R)9 . As such, the small black holes are expected to be dual to
an ensemble of metastable states in the N = 4 SYM on S 3 at large N and strong ’t Hooft
coupling. The small black hole cannot reach thermal equilibrium with its decay product,
and therefore cannot be detected by reasonable means from the thermal partition function
of the dual gauge theory. Short of a direct diagonalization of the Hamiltonian which has
been computationally intractable, there is no currently known method to effectively identify
the small black hole states in the gauge theory description.
   The “large” black holes, whose horizon size is of order R and is delocalized on the S 5 ,
have qualitatively different features. The simplest class of large black holes are described by
the AdS-Schwarzschild solution, as follows. It will be convenient to express the global AdS5
metric as
                                                      dr2

                            2     2         2  2                2  2

                                                    1 + r2
where r is related to the radial coordinate ρ in (20.36) by r = sinh ρ. Assuming the same RR
5-form flux, the absence of other background fields, and SO(6)R symmetry, the supergravity

21.2      The 3D N = 8 SYM and SCFT

The 3D N = 8 SYM, which arises as the low-energy effective theory on a stack of N D2-
branes, consists of the U (N ) gauge field Aµ , the Hermitian N × N matrix-valued scalar fields
ϕi , i = 1, · · · , 7, and the N ×N matrix-valued fermion fields λIα , where α is an so(1, 2) spinor
doublet index, and I = 1, · · · , 8 is a spinor index with respect to the so(7) R-symmetry. The
action is given by
             Z

the gauge coupling gYM has mass dimension 12 , the theory is strongly coupled in the infrared
and is expected to described by a superconformal field theory at the IR fixed point. Similarly
to the analysis in section 20.2, the 16 supercharges QIα do not commute with the special
conformal generator Kµ . Their commutator produces 16 additional special supercharges
SIα , and together they generate the Lie super-algebra osp(8|4). In particular, the anti-
commutators between Q and S take the form

                         {QIα , SJβ } = 2iδIJ (γ µν )αβ Jµν − iδIJ ϵαβ D − ϵαβ RIJ ,              (21.11)

and necessary consequence of the closure of the superconformal algebra.
   It is instructive to examine the mechanism of the symmetry enhancement through the
Coulomb branch effective theory in the N = 2 case. As the diagonal U (1) gauge theory
decouples, it suffices to consider the theory defined by the Lagrangian (21.10) with SU (2)
gauge group, with ϕi and λI taken to be traceless 2 × 2 matrices. A generic point in the
moduli space of vacua is parameterized by the expectation values of ϕi that are mutually
commuting matrices and be simultaneously diagonalized via a global gauge transformation

constant and that A is a well-defined 1-form. The third term on the RHS evaluates to 2πkn, where n ∈ Z
is the winding number of g as a map from the spacetime manifold M3 to the gauge group G. Therefore, the
weighting factor eiSCS [A] in the path integral is gauge invariant if and only if k is an integer.

The ABJM theory can be viewed as a special case of the N = 3 Chern-Simons-matter
theory which is defined more generally for any gauge group G and matter representation R.
In the case of U (N ) × U (N ) gauge group with Chern-Simons levels (k, −k), and a pair of
matter hypermultiplets in the bifundamental representation, the SU (2) R-symmetry of the
N = 3 supersymmetry algebra is enhanced to SU (4), and consequently the supersymmetry
is enhanced to N = 6. The Chern-Simons-matter theory is moreover conformally invariant,
at the classical as well as the quantum level due to the non-renormalization property of the
Chern-Simons level. In particular, the ABJM theory is a superconformal field theory with
the symmetry algebra osp(6|4).
    As will be explained in section 21.3.4, in the special cases k = 1, 2, the ABJM theory
is equipped with additional conserved supercurrents built out of monopole operators, which
enhances the supersymmetry to N = 8. This will also be seen from the holographic dual
that follow from the brane construction of section 21.3.1.


21.3.1    Brane construction

We begin with the type IIB string in the flat spacetime with the X 6 direction compactified,
and consider the system of N coincident D3-branes extended in 0126 directions, and a pair
of NS5-branes extended along 012345 directions, intersecting the D3-branes at two points on
the X 6 -circle. This brane configuration preserves 8 supersymmetries. The massless degrees
of freedom propagating in the 012 directions shared by the world volumes of the D3 and
NS5-branes are thus expected to be characterized by a 3-dimensional N = 4 effective field
theory in the low energy limit. As a D3-brane can end on the NS5-brane, the N D3-branes
break into two stacks of N D3-branes suspended between the pair of NS5-branes along two
halves of the X 6 -circle.
   The open string spectrum on the suspended D3-branes are not straightforwardly de-
termined from the worldsheet description which is strongly coupled in the vicinity of the
NS5-brane. Nonetheless, they can be inferred by applying T-duality to the X 6 -circle, which
as analyzed in section 19.1 leads to a C2 /Z2 orbifold singularity in the e
                                                                          6789 directions. In

                                                   490
the T-dual frame, the suspend D3-branes turn into fractional D2-branes that support 3-
dimensional N = 4 U (N ) × U (N ) gauge multiplets with two bifundamental hypermultiplets.
The gauge multiplets can be interpreted in the original frame as the massless modes of open
strings stretched between the same stack of suspended D3-branes, whereas the bifundamen-
tal hypermultiplets come from the open strings stretched between different stacks of the
suspended D3-branes across an NS5-brane.

independent ϵ0 ’s that are invariant under (21.70). This is in agreement with the dual ABJM
theory preserving 3D N = 6 supersymmetry.
    In the special cases k = 1 (obviously) as well as k = 2, the phase factor on the RHS of
(21.70) vanishes for all components of ϵ0 . This indicates that the ABJM theory with k = 1, 2
should admit 3D N = 8 supersymmetry, and hence necessarily osp(8|4) superconformal sym-
metry. In particular, the extra symmetry generators include a pair of supercharges Qα , Qα
and a pair of special supercharges Sα , Sα that are charged with respect to a “topological”
U (1)T symmetry that amounts to translation in the M-theory circle of (21.50) (parameter-
ized by the coordinate y). The microscopic origin of the enhanced symmetries from the
gauge theory path integral perspective will be explained in section 21.3.5.


21.3.5    Topological charge and monopole operators

The ABJM theory admits a U (1)T symmetry generated by the current

gether, these ∆ = 1 scalars transform in the 35-dimensional rank-4 anti-symmetric self-dual
tensor representation of the SO(8) R-symmetry of the N = 8 SCA, whose superconformal
descendants include the stress-energy tensor.


21.4     The 6D (0, 2) SCFT

The low energy limit of the world volume theory of N coincident M5-branes, dual to M-
theory in the AdS7 × S 4 spacetime (21.9), is believed to be a 6D local quantum field theory
with (0, 2) superconformal symmetry. There is no known UV-complete Lagrangian or path
integration description of this theory. Nonetheless, many of its properties can be inferred
based on a combination of symmetries, unitarity and locality, and consistency with string
dualities, as we now describe.


21.4.1    The superconformal algebra and multiplets

The 6D (0, 2) superconformal algebra, isomorphic to osp(2, 6|4), is generated by the super-
charge QI α and special supercharge SI α , where the upper and lower index α are associated
with the chiral and anti-chiral spinor representation of so(1, 5). I = 1, · · · , 4 is an index for
the fundamental representation of sp(4) R-symmetry (or equivalently the spinor representa-
tion of so(5) R-symmetry), and can be raised or lowered using the invariant anti-symmetric




                                                 501
tensor ΩIJ or ΩIJ . The nontrivial (anti-)commutation relations are319

momentum that obey the commutation relation (20.11) (adapted to the 6D case), and RI J
are sp(4) R-symmetry generators.
    By the state/operator map, the space H of local operators in the (0, 2) SCFT can be
identified with the Hilbert space of the (conformally coupled) theory on S 5 × R. As such,
the local operators can be organized into irreducible representations of the superconformal
algebra that are unitarity with respect to the inner product on H. Note that the Hermitian
conjugation with respect to the inner product is such that (QI α )† = SI α . The irreducible
unitary representations are determined by the dimension ∆, the so(6) spin, and the sp(4)
R-symmetry quantum numbers of the superconformal primaries, and have been completely
classified.320 A particularly important class of BPS (i.e. shortened) representations, known
as D-type multiplets, are characterized by a scalar superconformal primary that admits a
null state at level 21 , and saturates the BPS bound ∆ = 2(r1 + r2 ), where [r1 , r2 ] are the
Dynkin labels of the corresponding sp(4) representation.321

    For instance, the multiplet D[0, 1] contains ∆ = 2 scalars in the 5-dimensional vector
representation of so(5), which would necessarily be free fields. These are indeed realized by
the collective coordinates of a single M5-brane in Minkowskian spacetime. In the low energy
limit of N coincident M5-branes, the supermultiplet that contains the overall transverse
collective coordinates is described by a free field theory that decouples from the interacting
sector of the (0, 2) SCFT. The latter will be referred as the AN −1 (0, 2) SCFT.
   The multiplet D[0, 2], on the other hand, contains a set of ∆ = 4 superconformal primaries
Φij in the 14-dimensional symmetric traceless tensor representation of so(5), along with
conserved currents of spin 1, 23 , and 2 at descendant level 1, 23 , 2 respectively. This multiplet
indeed appears (with multiplicity 1) in the spectrum of the AN −1 (0, 2) SCFT, and contains
among its descendants the R-symmetry current, the supersymmetry currents, and the stress-
energy tensor. We will henceforth refer to D[0, 2] as the stress tensor multiplet.
    From the dual bulk perspective, the stress tensor multiplet contains the lowest KK modes
of the supergraviton in AdS7 × S 4 . More generally, the KK modes of a single supergraviton
comprise the BPS representations D[0, k] for k = 2, 3, · · · .322 The corresponding super-
conformal primaries Φi1 ···ik , of weight ∆ = 2k and transforming in the rank k symmetric
traceless tensor representation of the so(5) R-symmetry, play a special role in characterizing
the moduli space of vacua as will be discussed in section 21.4.3.

22     D1-D5 system and AdS3/CFT2

22.1     The D1-D5 system and its low energy effective theory

Consider type IIB string theory in R1,5 × M4 , where M4 is a compact hyperkähler manifold,
namely either T 4 or the K3 surface, and the system of Q1 D1-branes extended in the X 1 -
direction and Q5 D5-branes extended in X 1 and wrapping M4 . In the case M4 = T 4 , the D1
and D5-branes are described by their respective Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions
on the worldsheet, and the system preserves 8 out of the 32 supersymmetries by the same
consideration of intersecting branes as in section 12.4.1.
    In the case M4 = K3, the D1 and D5-branes are defined through Dirichlet and Neumann
boundary conditions in the supersymmetric nonlinear sigma model with the K3 target space.
In particular, the NLSM on K3 admits holomorphic spin fields Θ± that generate ± 12 unit
of spectral flow of the N = 4 superconformal algebra (see comment at the end of section
19.2), as well as their anti-holomorphic counterpart Θ e ± . In the large radius regime, Θ± can
be represented through a pair of spinor fields ζ± of the same chirality on the K3 in the form
(9.27). On the upper half plane Im(z) ≥ 0, the relevant boundary conditions are such that
                                       h                  i
                                  lim Θ± (z) − Θ  e ± (z̄) = 0,                           (22.1)
                                Im(z)→0

for both D1 and D5 boundary conditions. Consequently, Θ± and e   Θ± can be combined with
                        1,5
the spin fields of the R and βγ ghost system to construct spacetime supercharges similarly
to (12.35), yielding once again a total 8 supersymmetries.
    The low energy dynamics of the D1-D5 system can be characterized from several different
perspectives. Starting from the configuration where the Q1 D1-branes are coincident and lie
within the world volume of the Q5 coincident D5-branes, in the large radius regime of M4 , the
D1-D1 open strings give rise to a (1 + 1)-dimensional U (Q1 ) gauge theory on R1,1 , the D5-D5
open strings give rise to a (5 + 1)-dimensional U (Q5 ) gauge theory on R1,5 × M4 , and the
D1-D5 open strings give rise to massless fields that propagate in the D1-brane world volume
and transform in the bifundamental representation of U (Q1 )×U (Q5 ). The vacuum structure
of the D1-D5 system is somewhat involved. One class of vacuum configurations, known as
the Coulomb branch, amounts to separating the D1-branes from the D5-brane world volume
in the 4 transverse spatial dimensions. Another class of vacuum configurations, known as
the Higgs branch, amounts to condensing the massless scalar modes of the D1-D5 string,
which may also be equivalently viewed as dissolving the D1-branes into the D5-branes as
Yang-Mills instantons of the U (Q5 ) gauge theory on M4 (for Q5 ≥ 2).
   In the weak string coupling and large M4 volume limit, the massless effective theory of
D1-D1 and D1-D5 strings is a 2D (4, 4) supersymmetric U (Q1 ) gauge theory, whose coupling

    The low energy dynamics of the D1-D5 system can be characterized by an effective
field theory of fluctuations around the vacuum configurations, which takes the form of a
supersymmetric nonlinear sigma model whose target space is MC or MH at tree level.
Constraints from (4, 4) supersymmetry on the 2-derivative effective action are such that the
quantum-corrected low energy effective action remains a NLSM, and while the target space
geometry of MC may be deformed, MH is expected to be free from quantum corrections.
    In the Q1 = 1 case (for any Q5 ≥ 1), the target space Mqu  C of the quantum-corrected
effective nonlinear sigma model in the Coulomb branch is equipped with a Riemannian metric
that is constrained by the global symmetries to be

of (18.77).331 A consequence of (22.10) is that the singularity at r = 0, where the Coulomb
branch is expected to meet the Higgs branch, is at infinite distance as measured by the target
space metric of the quantum effective NLSM.
   Let us now turn to the Higgs branch. In the simplest case Q1 = Q5 = 1, the equations
on the RHS of (22.43) imply that qA = 0, and the Higgs branch disappears. In the next
simplest case Q1 = 1, Q5 = 2, with the notation (q11 , q21 , q12 , q22 ) ≡ (z1 , z2 , w1 , w2 ), we may
write the Higgs branch equation as

                                  |z1 |2 + |w1 |2 − |z2 |2 − |w2 |2 = 0,
                                                                                                 (22.11)
                                  z1∗ z2 + w1∗ w2 = 0.

The second equation is solved by setting z1 = u∗ y ∗ , z2 = xv, w1 = −u∗ x∗ , w2 = vy, for
which the first equation reduces to (|u|2 − |v|2 )(|x|2 + |y|2 ) = 0. The nontrivial solution
requires |u| = |v| > 0. We are free to set u = 1, and then use the U (1) gauge redundancy to
set v = 1. There is a residual Z2 subgroup of the U (1) gauge transformations that acts on
(x, y) ∈ C2 by
                                      (x, y) 7→ (−x, −y).                             (22.12)
Thus we can identify MH as R4 × (C2 /Z2 ), where the first R4 factor is the decompactified
M4 parameterized by yAI . This is the same as the moduli space of an SU (2) Yang-Mills
instanton on R4 , where the C2 /Z2 factor parameterizes the size and the gauge orientation of
the instanton. The low energy effective theory on the Higgs branch should therefore include
the superconformal NLSM on the orbifold C2 /Z2 . As was analyzed in section 19.2.2, the
orbifold CFT comes with a conformal manifold M     f2 of exactly marginal deformations of
the form (19.28). In the present context of the D1-D5 system, such marginal deformations

22.3      The conformal manifold and U-duality

The AdS3 × S 3 × M4 vacua of type IIB string theory that are holographically dual to the
2D CFT that arise in the low-energy limit of the D1-D5 system, which we will refer to as
the D1-D5 CFT, are parameterized by a moduli space MQ1 ,Q5 that can be identified with
the conformal manifold of exactly marginal deformations of the D1-D5 CFT that preserve
the 2D (4, 4) superconformal symmetry.
    Some of the possible moduli deformations include changing the string coupling or equiva-
lently the background value of the dilaton τ2 = gB−1 e−Φ , as well as turning on a constant RR
axion τ1 = gB−1 C0 .335 Under a continuous deformation that changes τ ≡ τ1 + iτ2 to τ ′ = aτ    +b
                                                                                             cτ +d
                                                                                                   ,
where a, b, c, d ∈ Z and ad − bc = 1, the D1-D5 system of charge (Q1 , Q5 ) undergoes an
SL(2, Z) monodromy (as discussed in section 18.4) and turns into a D1-F1-D5-NS5 system
in the S-dual frame, whose (R,R) charges (Q′1 , Q′5 ) and (NS,NS) charges (K1′ , K5′ ) are related
by
                       Q′1 = dQ1 , K1′ = bQ1 , Q′5 = aQ5 , K5′ = −cQ5 .                    (22.29)
Therefore, upon taking the decoupling limit, the resulting AdS3 × S 3 × M4 spacetime sup-
ported by (Q′1 , Q′5 ) units of (R,R) fluxes and (K1′ , K5′ ) units of (NS,NS) fluxes should lie in
the same connected component of the moduli space MQ1 ,Q5 .
   One may also consider deformations of the hyperkähler geometry of M4 as well as turning
on a flat B-field. For the D1-D5 system in asymptotically R1,5 × M4 spacetime (i.e. before
taking the decoupling limit), these deformations may be characterized through those of the
worldsheet NLSM with M4 target space. In the case M4 = T 4 , this deformation space is
characterized by the moduli space of the Narain lattice Γ4,4 ⊂ R4,4 which is isomorphic
to Aut(Γ4,4 )\SO(4, 4)/SO(4) × SO(4).336 Monodromies in this moduli space include the
T-duality in all 4 dimensions of the T 4 , which amounts to swapping the D1-branes with D5-

     Note that in the near-horizon solution (22.21) supported by purely (R,R) fluxes, turning on a nonzero

     Here Aut(Γn,m ) stands for the discrete subgroup of SO(n, m) that preserves the embedded lattice Γn,m ⊂

branes, the T-duality in 2 dimensions of the T 4 that turns the D1-D5 system into D3-branes,
as well as more general T-duality transformations that includes integral shifts of B-field that
results in a BPS D1-D3-D5 system. In the case M4 = K3, the analogous moduli space of
the worldsheet NLSM with K3 target space is isomorphic to Aut(Γ20,4 )\SO(20, 4)/SO(4) ×
SO(4),337 which again admits monodromies that map the D1-D5 system to the more general
D1-D3-D5 system.
    A generic R1,5 × M4 vacuum of type IIB string theory involves turning on additionally
flat RR 2-form and 4-form potentials on the M4 . For M4 = T 4 , the 17 (NS,NS) moduli from
the dilaton, the metric and the B-field combine with the 1 + 42 + 1 = 8 (R,R) moduli from
                                                                 

the 0,2,4-forms to give a total of 25 moduli. In the 6D low energy effective theory namely the
(2, 2) supergravity, the moduli are in correspondence with the massless scalar fields whose
kinetic term is that of a nonlinear sigma model with the 25-dimensional coset target space338
                                   SO(5, 5)/(SO(5) × SO(5)).                           (22.30)
Note that the S-duality of type IIB string theory and the T-duality group Aut(Γ4,4 ) of the
T 4 compactification do not commute. Together they generate a large “U-duality” symmetry
that can be identified with the group Aut(Γ5,5 ), and the full moduli space of R1,5 × T 4 vacua
of type IIB string theory is isomorphic to
                             Aut(Γ5,5 )\SO(5, 5)/(SO(5) × SO(5)).                      (22.31)
For M4 = K3, the 1 + 80 (NS,NS) moduli from the dilaton, the metric and the B-field on
the K3 combine with 1 + 22 + 1 = 24 (R,R) moduli from the 0,2,4-forms to give a total of
105 moduli. The corresponding 6D low energy effective theory is a (2, 0) supergravity theory
with 21 tensor multiplets, whose scalar fields are governed by a nonlinear sigma model with
the 105-dimensional target space SO(21, 5)/SO(21) × SO(5). The U-duality group in this
case is Aut(Γ21,5 ), and the full moduli space of R1,5 × K3 vacua of type IIB string theory is
isomorphic to Aut(Γ21,5 )\SO(21, 5)/(SO(21) × SO(5)).339
    We will focus on the M4 = T 4 case for the rest of this section. A continuous deformation
in the moduli space of type IIB string vacua can implement the monodromy associated
with any element of the U-duality group Aut(Γ5,5 ). Of particular interest is a subgroup
Aut(Γ2,2 ) ≃ SL(2, Z)L × SL(2, Z)R that acts on the D1-F1-D5-NS5 charges (Q1 , K1 , Q5 , K5 )

follows that all D1-D5 systems with the same values of Q1 Q5 and gcd(Q1 , Q5 ) are related by
continuous moduli deformations!
    Not all moduli of the asymptotic R1,5 × M4 spacetime survive the decoupling limit of
the D1-D5 system. This is already seen in the example of (22.17), where the volume of M4
at the horizon ends up being fixed by the charges as in (22.22). The moduli of AdS3 ×
S 3 × M4 vacua can be identified with marginal deformations of the dual 2D (4, 4) SCFT,
which are descendants of weight ( 12 , 12 ) BPS primaries according to (19.23) and come in
multiples of four. Moreover, the local geometry i.e. the Zamolodchikov metric (19.25) of the
conformal manifold is constrained by the 2D (4, 4) superconformal symmetry to be that of the
quaternionic-Kähler symmetric space SO(5, 4)/(SO(5) × SO(4)), the latter being identified
with a subspace of (22.30). The global form of the moduli space of the AdS3 × S 3 × M4
vacua, or equivalently the conformal manifold of the D1-D5 CFT, is340

    Returning to the D1-D5 system on T 4 , one expects that in the Q5 = 1 case the infrared
CFT is given by an exactly marginal deformation of the supersymmetric nonlinear sigma
model with target space SymQ1 (T 4 ). At certain loci in the conformal manifold MQ1 ,1 , the
D1-D5 CFT is exactly given by the orbifold of the product of Q1 copies of (4, 4) NLSM on
T 4 with respect to the permutation group SQ1 . We will refer to the latter theory as the
symmetric product orbifold CFT, denoted once again by SymQ1 (T 4 ). It must be emphasized
that the symmetric product orbifold CFT has perfectly regular, discrete, operator spectrum,
and is clearly distinct from the singular D1-D5 CFT at Re(τ ) = 0 discussed at the end of
section 22.3. On the other hand, the SymQ1 (T 4 ) CFT is invariant with respect to a parity
symmetry that is inherited from the orientifold parity of type IIB string theory. As the RR
axion C0 = gB Re(τ ) is odd under the orientifold parity, the invariant configurations must
have either Re(τ ) = 0 or Re(τ ) = 21 . Therefore a natural proposal is that the SymQ1 (T 4 )
CFT occurs at Re(τ ) = 12 in the subspace T ⊂ MQ1 ,1 described around (22.37).
    For any positive integer Q5 that is coprime to Q1 , the U-duality monodromy of the

The physical interpretation of these representations can be understood by inspecting the
classical limit of the AdS3 sigma model. In the conformal gauge, a family of solutions that
describe a short string oscillating about the center of the AdS3 are given by

                                                                                tan(ατ )
         ϕ = wσ,    ρ = arcsinh(sinh ρ0 sin(ατ )),         t = wτ + arctan               ,   (22.79)
                                                                                 cosh ρ0
where α, ρ0 are arbitrary constants. These can be obtained by spectral flow from the solution
with w = 0, which describes a pointlike string moving along a timelike geodesic. The latter
can be viewed as the classical limit of principal discrete representation states. Therefore we
expect the spectral-flowed discrete representations (22.77) to give rise to the quantum states
of a short string.
   A different family of classical solutions that describe a long string contracting from and
expanding to spatial infinity are given by

  ϕ = wσ,     ρ = arcsinh(cosh ρ0 sinh(ατ )),         t = wτ + arctan(tanh(ατ ) sinh ρ0 ).   (22.80)

These can be obtained by spectral flow from the solution with w = 0, which describes a
pointlike string moving along a spacelike geodesic. The latter corresponds to the classi-
cal limit of principal continuous representation states. Thus we expect the spectral-flowed
continuous representations (22.78) to give rise to the scattering states of a long string that
approaches spatial infinity in the far past and future.

22.7.1   Semi-classical limit

background B-field. Assuming that the string is static in S 3 × M4 and moves in the global

22.7.2   String field theory description of the RR flux deformation

A fully quantum description of the string dynamics perturbatively with respect to the RR
flux parameter µ (22.127) is given by the closed superstring field theory. Following the
general prescription of section 10.3, one begins with the SFT description by the worldsheet
theory of the purely (NS,NS) AdS3 × S 3 × M4 background as described in section 22.6, and
represent the RR flux deformation as a nontrivial solution to the SFT equation of motion.

23.1     Single-trace operators as spin chains

Before systematically analyzing the spectrum of single-trace operators of the N = 4 SYM in
the planar limit, we need to set up a few conventions. The dilatation operator will be written
as D = iH, where H is the Hamiltonian of the gauge theory on S 3 whose eigenvalues are
the scaling dimensions ∆. Given a pair of scalar operators O(x) and O′ (y), the two-point
function can be expressed as
                                                           1
                                ⟨O′ (x)O(y)⟩ = ⟨O′ |             |O⟩.                    (23.1)
                                                       |x − y|2H

We will group the six adjoint scalar fields ϕi of the gauge theory into the complex scalars

                                X A = ϕ2A−1 + iϕ2A ,      A = 1, 2, 3,                   (23.2)

that transform in the fundamental representation of U (3) ⊂ SO(6)R . Let R1 , R2 , R3 be the
three Cartan generators of SO(6)R that assigns charge 1 to X 1 , X 2 , X 3 respectively. The
chiral fermions λIα are re-organized as (λAα , χα ) that transform in the anti-fundamental and
the singlet of the U (3) symmetry. Moreover, we consider an N = 1 subalgebra of the N = 4
supersymmetry algebra generated by the supercharges Qα , Qα̇ that act as

                Qα · X A = 0,      Qα · X A = λAα ,
                                                                                         (23.3)
                Qα · λAβ = ϵαβ ϵABC [X B , X C ],     Qα · χβ = (γ µν )αβ Fµν ,   etc.

The symmetrized single-trace operators tr(X (A1 · · · X An ) ) are BPS primaries, as they are
                                                                    I
annihilated by Qα as well as all of the special supercharges SIα , S α̇ . On the other hand, the
unsymmetrized single-trace operators

                                         tr(X A1 · · · X An )                            (23.4)

are generally not BPS primaries, but can only mix among themselves in perturbation theory,
as they are the only operators of classical dimension n that carry R-charge R1 + R2 + R3 = n.
The space spanned by this set of operators will be referred to as the “SU (3) sector”.
   For now we will simplify our task by further restricting to the “SU (2) sector”, which is
spanned by the operators of the form (23.4) for Ai = 1 or 3, and denote X ≡ X 1 , Z ≡ X 3 .
Let L be the classical dimension, or “length”, of the operator, and M ≡ R1 that counts the
number of X’s. It suffices to analyze the operator mixing problem at fixed L and M . At

                                                539
M = 0, the only operator is tr(Z L ), a BPS primary. At M = 1, the only operator tr(XZ L−1 )
is automatically symmetrized, hence also a BPS primary. The first nontrivial case is M = 2,
where the operator tr(XZ ℓ XZ L−2−ℓ ) generally does not have definite anomalous dimension.
It will be convenient to identify an operator of the form tr(Z ℓ1 −1 XZ ℓ2 −ℓ1 −1 XZ · · · ) with the
spin chain state
                                    | ↓ · · · ↓↑ ↓ · · · ↓↑ ↓ · · · ⟩,
                                      | {z } | {z }                                            (23.5)
                                          ℓ1     ℓ2 −ℓ1

where ↓ represents Z and ↑ represents X. The cyclicity of the trace means that the spin
chain is closed, i.e. there is a gauge redundancy of simultaneously shifting all spins to the
right (or left) by one site.
   In the planar limit, it is evident from the structure of the perturbative computation of
the LHS of (23.1) that the Hamiltonian H takes the form
                                                ∞
                                                X
                                          H=          λn Hn ,                                 (23.6)
                                                n=0

classical dimension. Moreover, the planar diagrams are such that when acting on the basis
states (23.5), Hn can involve interactions between spins separated by a distance of no more
than n sites along the chain.
   At the 1-loop order, the only planar diagrams that can move the position of a spin (by
one site) are those that contain a single interaction vertex, coming from the scalar potential
term proportional to

Of course, due to the cyclicity of the trace, the state of a single magnon with nonzero
momentum p does not exist. Nonetheless, (23.12) correctly captures the contribution from
a single magnon to the 1-loop Hamiltonian in the limit of an infinitely long spin chain with
the magnons separated at large distances.
    To characterize the states that involve multiple magnon excitations a priori requires ac-
counting for the interactions between the magnon. The integrability property of the spin
chain Hamiltonian (thus far observed in H1 ) is such that there are infinitely many lin-
early independent conserved charges that generate symmetries that amount to momentum-
dependent spatial translations of the individual magnons, thereby relating any excited state
of the infinite spin chain to a linear combination of states that describe magnons separated
at large distances from one another. The latter can be characterized by asymptotic wave
functions of identical particles, say in the case of a 2-magnon state, of the form

                 Ψ(x1 , x2 ) = eip1 x1 +ip2 x2 + S(p1 , p2 )eip2 x1 +ip1 x2 ,   x1 ≪ x2 ,   (23.13)

                                                    541
and a similar expression with x1 , x2 exchanged on the RHS in the case of x1 ≫ x2 , where x1
and x2 label the positions of the two magnons. S(p1 , p2 ) is a phase that can be viewed as
the S-matrix element of 2 → 2 scattering. Demanding that Ψ(x1 , x2 ) is the wave function of
eigenvalue E with respect to H1 gives in particular

            8π 2 EΨ(x, x + 1) = 2Ψ(x, x + 1) − Ψ(x − 1, x + 1) − Ψ(x, x + 2).                                  (23.14)

(23.13) solves (23.14) with

and solve the spectral problem in the infinite length chain limit. To capture the finite size
effects beyond the 1-loop order, however, will require additional ingredients to be introduced
in section 24.1.


23.2         The BMN/pp-wave limit

The spectral problem of massive string states in AdS5 × S 5 simplifies dramatically in the
Berenstein-Maldacena-Nastase (BMN) limit [170], also known as the pp-wave limit, defined
by zooming in near the null geodesic that corresponds to the world line of a massless particle
sitting at the center of global AdS5 , namely ρ = 0, and moving along the equator of the S 5
at θ = 0 with dϕ/dt = 1 in the coordinate system (20.68). This can be accomplished by
redefining (t, ϕ, ρ, θ) in terms of the new coordinates (x+ , x− , r, y) via

                                       x−                            x−             r           y
                     t = µx+ +             ,          ϕ = µx+ −          ,     ρ=     ,    θ=     ,   (23.22)
                                      2µR2                          2µR2            R           R
where R is the AdS radius and µ is an arbitrary positive parameter, and then take the
R → ∞ limit. The AdS5 × S 5 metric reduces to

            ds2 = −2dx+ dx− + dr2 + r2 dΩ23 + dy 2 + y 2 dΩ
                                                          e 2 − µ2 (r2 + y 2 )(dx+ )2 ,
                                                            3                                         (23.23)

with the RR 5-form flux

                                 F5 = 4µdx+ ∧ (r3 dr ∧ ωS 3 + y 3 dy ∧ ωSe3 ).                        (23.24)
 353
       This can be derived using the transfer matrix formalism. See e.g. Faddeev, arXiv:hep-th/9605187 [169].



                                                             543
This is precisely the pp-wave background as seen in (10.52), (10.51). The momenta P±
conjugate to x± are related to the energy ∆ and angular momentum J conjugate to ϕ by
                                                         ∆+J
                            P+ = −µ(∆ − J), P− = −            .                   (23.25)
                                                         2µR2
Therefore, a closed string state of finite P± in the pp-wave background is expected to be
         √ of the single-trace operators in the N = 4 SYM in the limit N, λ, J → ∞ with
dual to that
finite J/ λ and ∆ − J.
    In principle, the string spectrum in the pp-wave background can be determined by solving
the linearized closed superstring field equation of motion around the background solution
(10.50), perturbatively with respect to the deformation parameter µ.354 A more efficient
approach is based on the quantization of the Green-Schwarz (effective) action of type IIB
string in the pp-wave background, which turns out to take a simple form in the lightcone
gauge. The formulation of the GS action in a general massless background (9.44) involves the
super-metric GM N and the super-B-field BM N which are not easy to solve either based on
a supergravity solution expressed in terms of the bosonic fields, or from the super geometry
torsion constraints (9.59), (9.60). In the case of the pp-wave (and more generally AdS5 × S 5 )
background, however, it is possible to construct the GS action directly from a sigma model
with a supercoset target space that manifests the super-isometry and admits the desired
κ-symmetry.

23.3     The all-order magnon dispersion relation

  In fact, it is possible to also identify the dual description of the magnon at finite mo-
mentum p on the infinite chain, in the λ ≫ 1 regime, as a semi-classical string solution in

                                                  551
AdS5 × S 5 . As discussed around (20.72), the operator tr(Z L ) is dual to a supergraviton that
carries angular momentum L with respect to ϕ in the Hopf coordinate system (20.68) of
the S 5 , and is at rest in the global AdS5 . In the limit L → ∞, the wave function of the
supergraviton is localized at the equator θ = 0, and may be viewed as the point-particle limit
of a closed string moving along the equator at the speed of light, namely ϕ̇ = 1. Adding
magnon excitations to the spin chain corresponds to exciting oscillator modes on the closed
string, pulling the latter away from the point-particle configuration. Consider in particular
the motion of a classical string within an equator S 2 parameterized by θ, ϕ that occupies a
pair of antipodal points on the S 3 in (20.68), and sitting at the center of the global AdS5
(ρ = 0). The relevant spacetime metric is that of R × S 2 ,

                             ds2 = R2 (−dt2 + dϑ2 + sin2 ϑdϕ2 ),                       (23.70)

where we have adopted the more standard polar coordinate convention with ϑ = π2 − θ. We
will seek a solution that describes a string moving at constant angular velocity ϕ̇ = 1, whose
end points at ϑ = π2 move at the speed of light and carry infinite angular momentum. It is
thus convenient to identify the worldsheet coordinates (τ, σ) as

                                       τ = t,     σ = ϕ − t,                           (23.71)

so that the string configuration will be parameterized by ϑ(σ) together with the range of σ.

As the relation (23.69) holds at both weak and strong ’t Hooft coupling, one might suspect
that it is in fact exact at all λ. Such a claim would be contingent on the regularization
scheme through which the planar perturbation theory or path integral of N = 4 SYM is
defined, as different schemes are generally expected to be related by a redefinition of the
coupling constant. It turns out that (23.69) exactly agrees with the scheme defined through
supersymmetric localization (see comments in section 25.3).


23.4        The magnon S-matrix: su(2|2) invariance, analyticity, and
            crossing

The elementary magnons (23.58) of momentum p on the infinite chain, transforming ac-
cording to (23.66), form a short representation with respect to the centrally extended

                                                     553
su(2|2)L ⊕ su(2|2)R algebra, where the subscript L, R refers to the left and right tensor
factors of (23.58) respectively. To avoid clutter in notation, we will for now omit the right
tensor factor and simply denote the magnon states as |φA (p)⟩ and |ψα (p)⟩, which transform
in the (2|2) (i.e. fundamental) representation of su(2|2)L . The (asymptotic) states of a pair
of magnons, say of momenta p1 and p2 , transform in the representation (2|2) ⊗ (2|2). The
latter is in fact a single irreducible long representation of su(2|2)L , a key property that ties
all components of the 2-magnon S-matrix to one another.
    Explicitly, the action of the S-matrix on (the left tensor factor of) the 2-particle asymp-

from the gauge theory perspective.

the strong coupling expansion (23.107) is asymptotic (but Borel summable).

23.7           Nested Bethe ansatz

Before getting a handle on more general operators in the planar N = 4 SYM, we will
need to formulate the asymptotic Bethe ansatz for factorized scattering with multiple types
of particles. This is particularly nontrivial when the types of particles can change in the
scattering process. We begin by writing the M -particle asymptotic wave function as
                                     X              P
      Ψa1 ···aM (x1 , · · · , xM ) =   Caσ1 ···aM ei j pσ(j) xj , x1 ≪ x2 ≪ · · · ≪ xM , (23.137)
                                          σ∈SM

where the index ai labels the type of the i-th particle, and the coefficients Caσ1 ···aM obey
   X                                                        X

Faddeev (ZF) algebra, defined by the relation
                                           X

the out-particles of type b1 , b2 .

24       Strings from N = 4 SYM II: mirror TBA and the

24.1     Mirror model and thermodynamic Bethe ansatz

The all-loop asymptotic Bethe ansatz is not expected to capture the spectrum of a finite
closed chain due to the presence of interactions between spins at a range that is longer than
the chain itself. A hint comes from relativistic integrable quantum field theories, in which a
double-Wick rotation exchanging the roles of space and Euclidean time relates the spectrum
of the system on a finite spatial circle to the thermal observables at finite temperature in
infinite space. This is not directly applicable to the spin chain of planar N = 4 SYM, as the
dispersion relation between the energy E and momentum p of the magnon is not invariant
under the double Wick rotation (E, p) → (ip, iE). Instead, the double Wick rotation relates
the magnons on the spin chain to those of a mirror model, in which the energy E         e and
momentum pe of the mirror magnon are related by

                                     E = ie
                                          p,          p = iE.
                                                           e                           (24.1)

It follows from (23.68) that the dispersion relation of the mirror magnon is
                                                  p
                                                          2
                                    e = 2arcsinh 1 + pe
                                    E                                                  (24.2)
                                                     4h

The idea is that the thermal observables of the mirror model at inverse temperature βe will
capture the spectrum of the original theory on a finite closed chain of length L = β.
                                                                                    e As
a sanity test, consider the contribution of a single mirror magnon to the thermal partition
function,
                                          √                          L

Remarkably, it admits a weak coupling expansion that begins at the L-loop order, which
could conceivably capture wrapping interactions on a chain of length L.

24.9.1       Weak coupling limit

                                       ∆ = J + K + h2 γ1 + O(h4 ),                   (24.145)

24.9.2   Small spin expansion

A useful approach to solving the Pµ-system at any ’t Hooft coupling is based on the assump-
tion of analyticity in the Lorentz spin K and the expansion at small K. Formally, the K → 0
limit approaches the BPS vacuum state of the spin chain, and we expect ∆ − J = O(K).
 389
   See section 2.3 of Belitsky, Gorsky and Korchemsky, Nucl. Phys. B 748, 24-59 (2006) [182], and
Appendix C of Eden and Staudacher, J. Stat. Mech. 0611, P11014 (2006) [204].


                                                  600
                                                                                       1
(24.144) implies A1 A4 , A2 A3 ∼ O(K), which suggests that Pa ∼ O(K 2 ). It then follows
from the Pµ-system equations (24.128) that µ   eab − µab = O(K). Therefore, in the K → 0
limit, we expect that µab (u) has no branch cuts and is a function of periodicity i on the
entire u-plane. To find nontrivial solutions it is necessary to relax the large u asymptotics
on µab (u) at a given order in the small K expansion, so long as it is compatible with (24.126)
and (24.128). It turns out that up to a symmetry transformation of the Pµ-system, the
K → 0 limit of µab can be set to

         µ12 = −1,      µ13 = 0,     µ14 = µ23 = 1,          µ24 = − sinh(2πu),     µ34 = 0.   (24.155)

The second set of equations of (24.128) then give

                                     P

24.9.3   Konishi at strong coupling

The key idea that allows for extrapolating the small spin expansion to integer spin is that
the spin K can be expressed as an analytic function of ∆ (at given twist J). Consideration

admits a power series expansion in (4πh)−1 = 1/ λ = α′ /R2 and in ∆2 /λ (as ∆ scales like

25.1     Maldacena-Wilson lines in N = 4 SYM

A natural notion of generalized Wilson line operator in N = 4 SYM, known as the Maldacena-
Wilson line [206], is defined through the world line of a W-boson on the Coulomb branch of
the theory with U (N + 1) gauge group, where the scalar fields ϕ     ⃗ ≡ (ϕ1 , · · · , ϕ6 ) acquire the
vacuum expectation value
                                   ⟨ϕi ⟩ = diag{0, · · · , 0, y i },                             (25.1)
thereby breaking the gauge group to U (N ) × U (1). In the limit |⃗y | → ∞, the W-boson
becomes infinitely massive and can be viewed as a classical quark that couples to the fields
(Aµ , ϕi ) of the U (N ) gauge theory via the insertion of the operator
                                         Z                            
                        W(C) = trP exp                  µ       ⃗

                                                               ⃗
Wilson line (1.10), the additional term proportional to ŷ · ϕ(x)      in the integrand accounts for
the coupling of the W-boson to the scalar fields.
    In the bulk dual description, the W-boson corresponds to an open string that stretches

condition that a worldsheet of the fundamental string ends on (C, z = 0, ŷ). In the classical
limit i.e. N → ∞ and λ ≫ 1, W(C) is evaluated by the saddle point approximation,

in the 5D gauge theory, which are subject to anti-periodic boundary condition on the y-circle,
give rise to a tower of KK modes of mass (n+ 21 )MKK , n ∈ Zn≥0 . As supersymmetry is broken
entirely, the lightest scalar fields are expected to acquire nonzero mass ms at the quantum

25.5      Sakai-Sugimoto model of holographic QCD

As an extension of Witten’s model of holographic confinement, Sakai and Sugimoto proposed
to add D8-branes to the spacetime background (25.39) whose effect is to introduce dynamical

                                   √ intersecting the D4-branes along a (3+1)-dimensional
world volume. So long as L ≫ α′ , all D8-D8 open string modes are massive and the
system is free from open string tachyon instability. The D4-D8 open strings can be analyzed
as in section 12.4.1 in the case dND = 6. According to (12.67), all NS D4-D8 string modes
are massive, whereas a set of massless fermions arise in the R sector as represented by the
vertex operator (12.68) combined with the appropriate Chan-Paton factors. These massless
fermions transform in the chiral spinor representation of so(1, 3), and simultaneously in the
fundamental representations of the U (N ) gauge group associated with the D4-branes and of
the U (Nf )L gauge group associated with the D8-branes. Similarly there is a set of massless
fermions from the R sector of D4-D8 open strings that transform in the anti-chiral spinor
representation of so(1, 3), and in the fundamental representations of the U (N ) associated
with the D4-branes and of the U (Nf )R associated with the anti-D8-branes.
    The massless effective theory of the D4-D8-D8 system, upon reduction with respect to
the y-circle, is a (3+1)-dimensional U (N ) gauge theory with Nf flavors of massless Dirac
fermions (quarks), on which the U (Nf )L × U (Nf )R act as chiral flavor symmetry.400 As
discussed in section 25.4, all U (N ) adjoint fermion KK modes are massive due to the anti-
periodic boundary condition on the y-circle, whereas the lightest SU (N ) adjoint scalar KK
modes also become massive through their 1-loop self-energy. There are nonetheless 6 massless
scalar fields coming from the KK modes of the diagonal U (1) components of the 5D gauge
field and scalars, which couple to the D4-D8 and D4-D8 quarks via Yukawa coupling. In the
large N limit however, these massless scalar fields are expected to be unimportant, and will
henceforth be ignored. In the limit of weak ’t Hooft coupling, by an RG flow analysis similar
to (25.46), (25.47), there is an exponentially large separation between ΛQCD and ms , MKK ,
and the effective theory approaches the U (N ) QCD with Nf massless Dirac quark fields ψI
at energy scale µ ≪ ms , MKK , described by the Lagrangian density

                                           Z

the D8-branes, the F1-strings attached to the D4-brane would necessarily extend to the
asymptotic boundary (r = ∞), resulting in a state of infinite energy. In the presence of
Nf (≥ 1) D8-branes, the F1-strings can end on the D8-branes, resulting in a baryonic state
that may be viewed as a bound state of N quarks. The mass M of the baryon can be
estimated as that of the minimal spherical D4-brane at r = r0 ,

Note that by condensing the 4-8 strings (similarly to the D1-D5 system discussed in section

volume gauge theory.


25.6        Klebanov-Witten theory

The Klebanov-Witten theory is a family of 4D N = 1 SCFTs that are dual to type IIB string
theory in the spacetime AdS5 × T 1,1 .405 It serves as the starting point for the construction
 405
       Klebanov and Witten, Nucl. Phys. B 536 (1998), 199 [220].


                                                     620
of 4D N = 1 holographic gauge theories that exhibit a variety of dynamical phenomena,
including RG cascade, chiral symmetry breaking, and confinement.


25.6.1    D3-branes on the conifold

We begin by considering type IIB string theory in the spacetime R1,3 × C, where C is the
conifold geometry (19.102), and a D3-brane extended in the R1,3 and located at a generic
point on C. The massless effective theory of the D3-brane is a 4D N = 1 gauge theory that
consists of a U (1) vector superfield and 3 neutral chiral superfields whose kinetic term is
governed by a nonlinear sigma model with target space C. That is, there is no superpotential,
and the Kähler potential of the NLSM in the sense of (M.15) coincides with the Kähler
potential of the conifold (19.105). In other words, C can be identified as the moduli space of
vacua of this effective gauge theory.
    At the conifold singularity r = 0, recall from (19.144) that there are additional massless
degrees of freedom coming from D3-branes wrapping the S 3 of the deformed conifold. As
argued following (19.147), the wrapped D3-brane gives rise to a 4D N = 2 hypermultiplet,
whose scalar components account for the size of the S 2 of the resolved conifold, as well as
the modes of a flat B-field and the RR potentials C2 , C4 on the S 2 . The RR charge of
the wrapped D3-brane, which we will refer to as the “baryon number”, is associated with
a global symmetry U (1)B of the 4D effective theory.406 With respect to the 4D N = 1
supersymmetry preserved by the D3-brane extended along R1,3 , the hypermultiplet of the
wrapped D3 splits into two chiral multiplets. One of these chiral multiplets controls the
size of the S 2 , and therefore couples nontrivially to the 3 chiral multiplets on the extended
D3-brane at the level of the Kähler potential. Together, they can be described in terms of
the chiral superfields A1 , A2 of baryon number +1, and B1 , B2 of baryon number −1. The
U (1)B -neutral combinations Wij ≡ Ai Bj form a 2 × 2 matrix W that obeys det W = 0.
We can therefore identify the scalar components of W as the matrix appearing in (19.103),
whose entries are complex coordinates on the conifold C.
    The low energy effective theory on N coincident D3-branes at the singularity r = 0 of the
conifold, proposed by Klebanov and Witten, is constructed as follows. Omitting an overall
decoupled U (1) gauge multiplet, one considers the 4D N = 1 super-Yang-Mills theory with
gauge group SU (N )×SU (N ) and matter chiral superfields A1 , A2 and B1 , B2 that transform
in the bifundamental representations (f , f ) and (f , f ) respectively. The bare Lagrangian of

                                    W = 2λρ tr ([A1 , A2 ]B2 ) .                       (25.104)

is tied to the gauge coupling, resulting in none other than the N = 4 super-Yang-Mills theory
describing the low energy limit of N coincident D3-branes at a point away from the origin
on the conifold.

the singular conifold, where the low energy excitations of N D3-branes at r = 0 are captured

in the holographic dual description wraps S 2 ⊂ T 1,1 and extends in the radial coordinate z
of the Poincaré AdS5 , intersecting the conformal boundary along R1,2 ⊂ R1,3 . This D5-brane
can be viewed as a domain wall that separates two different boundary theories. Crossing the
domain wall, the magnetic F3 flux on the S 3 ⊂ T 1,1 changes by one unit. Suppose on one
side of the domain wall we have the KW SCFT described by the SU (N ) × SU (N ) gauge
theory, where an S 3 -wrapped D3-brane is dual to a baryon operator of the form (25.107).
On the other side of the domain wall, the S 3 -wrapped D3-brane acquires one unit of electric
charge with respect to its world volume U (1) gauge field, due to the Chern-Simons coupling
with the background F3 flux. To satisfy the Gauss law constraint, this electric charge must
be canceled by that of a fundamental string attached to the D3-brane. The other “free”

                                              627
end of the fundamental string is such that the dual baryon-like operator is no longer gauge-
invariant, but should rather carry the gauge index of a classical quark. This is indeed realized
if the dual gauge theory has gauge group SU (N +1)×SU (N ) or SU (N )×SU (N +1). In the
former case, for instance, a baryon-like operator is ϵa1 ···aN aN +1 ϵb1 ···bN (Ai1 )a1 b1 · · · (AiN )aN bN ,
which transforms in the fundamental representation of SU (N +1) due to the free index aN +1 .
    These arguments lead to the proposal that adding M fractional D3-branes to the system of
N D3-branes at the conifold singularity gives rise to a 4D N = 1 SU (N +M )×SU (N ) gauge
theory, with the same bifundamental matter chiral superfields Ai , Bi as in Klebanov-Witten
theory. A surprisingly simple supergravity solution describing the backreacted spacetime was
discovered by Klebanov and Tseytlin,408 with vanishing dilaton and RR axion Φ = C0 = 0,

26.4.4     The matrix string theory conjecture

Analogously to the BFSS conjecture (26.24), a natural proposal is that the correspondence
between the leading order matrix string theory amplitude and the type IIA string amplitude
(26.73) should hold in the N → ∞ limit for any n-point scattering amplitude, to all orders
in perturbation theory with respect to the string coupling gA (26.32) (related to conformal
perturbation theory coupling via (26.47), (26.74)), and conceivably at the non-perturbative
level as well.
    At least in the perturbation theory, one expects a basis of asymptotic in- or out-states
of matrix string theory to be labeled by those of the SymN (R8 ) SCFT, generalizing (26.53),
(26.54), in correspondence with free type IIA string states. For instance, an asymptotic state
of n gravitons |N1 , k1⊥ , e1 ; · · · ; Nn , kn⊥ , en ⟩in/out is labeled by the lightcone momenta ki+ = Ni ,
       (ki⊥ )2
ki− = 2N    i

form (26.67), i = 1, · · · , n, with ni=1 Ni = N . The matrix string amplitude AMST is defined

B.3     Tunneling and instantons

Consider the quantum mechanical model (B.5), where the potential V (q) is taken to be of
the form
                                               1        ∂h(q) ∂h(q)
                                     V (q) = Gab (q)                ,                        (B.34)
                                               2         ∂q a ∂q b
for a function h(q) which we will refer to as the Morse function. V (q) acquires minimal value
0 at a critical point of h(q), i.e. where ∂a h(q) = 0. Suppose that there are several critical
points qα , α = 1, 2, · · · . In the classical limit, the lowest energy states |α⟩ are characterized
by wave functions localized at q ≈ qα . The quantum tunneling leads to nonzero matrix
elements of the propagator between these states,
                                                  X
                                  ⟨β|e−HT |α⟩ =       e−En T ⟨β|n⟩⟨n|α⟩,                     (B.35)
                                               n

where {|n⟩} is an orthonormal basis of energy eigenstates with energy En . In the case of one
degree of freedom, this can be analyzed using the WKB approximation. More generally, the
matrix element (B.35) can be formulated as the Euclidean path integral
                                                 q( T2 )=qβ
                                          Z

                          Z T

                              − T2

In the model (B.5) with (B.34), S E [q] subject to the boundary condition q(− T2 ) = qα ,

                 Z T                                                  
             E

In particular, in the T → ∞ limit, the action is minimized by the solutions to the first order

                                 ∂τ q a ± Gac (q)∂qc h(q) = 0,                          (B.39)
where the sign is + (or −) for h(qβ ) < h(qα ) (or h(qβ ) > h(qα )), with q(−∞) = qα , q(+∞) =

to the Morse function h(q). These solutions will be referred to as “instantons” or “bounces”.
   For large but finite T , the above instanton solution does not quite satisfy the boundary
condition, but nonetheless approximates a saddle point of the path integral, on which the
Euclidean action evaluates to
                                  S E ≈ Sβα ≡ |h(qβ ) − h(qα )|.                       (B.40)
In the semi-classical approximation, it will also be necessary to calculate the Gaussian (i.e.
1-loop) functional determinant of fluctuations around the instanton, which is further com-
plicated by the presence of a zero mode that corresponds to the time translation of the
instanton. We will defer a more careful analysis to the next section in the context of a su-
persymmetric model, and for now simply assume that the Gaussian functional determinant
of the nonzero modes gives rise to a factor Kβα , whereas the integration over the zero mode
associated with time translation gives a factor T . The instanton contribution to (B.36) is
then e−Sβα Kβα T , from which we conclude
                                        ⟨β|H|α⟩ ≈ e−Sβα Kβα .                          (B.41)
To recover the spectral decomposition (B.35), it will be necessary to sum up the contributions
from the approximate saddle points that correspond to a sequence of alternating instanton
and anti-instantons at large separation in Euclidean time (this is often referred to as the
“instanton gas”).

B.6     Lefschetz thimbles

The treatment of the previous section can be generalized to the multi-dimensional integral
                                         Z

where S(ϕ) is assumed to be an analytic function over CN with isolated critical points.
Moreover, we assume that the Hessian of S(ϕ) at each critical point ϕ = ϕi is non-degenerate.
As such, the Hessian of the height function h(ϕ, ϕ∗ ) ≡ Re(S(ϕ)) at ϕi is a 2N ×2N Hermitian
matrix whose eigenvalues come in pairs that are equal in magnitude with opposite signs. It
follows that ϕi lies at the intersection between a stable submanifold or a Lefschetz thimble
Ci ⊂ CN , consisting of all steepest ascent paths with respect to h(ϕ, ϕ∗ ) that begin at
ϕ = ϕi , and an unstable submanifold or anti-thimble Ci⊥ ⊂ CN consisting of all steepest
descent paths that begin at ϕ = ϕi . Up to a small perturbation of S(ϕ) such as the phase
rotation (B.92), we may assume that each thimble or anti-thimble contains only a single
critical point.

C.2       Batalin-Vilkovisky quantization of gauge theory

Now let us consider an action S[ϕ] that is invariant under infinitesimal gauge transformations
of the general form
                                        δϕi = ζ α fαi [ϕ].                               (C.9)
As in (3.1) our notation is such that the repeated index α comes with integration with respect
to a suitable measure on α-space. For simplicity of discussion we will assume that both ϕi
and ζ α are Grassmann-even. Similar to the BRST quantization prescription of section 3.1, we
will associate a Grassmann-odd ghost field cα with the gauge parameter ζ α . We will further
introduce a Grassmann-odd “anti-field” ϕ‡i that is paired with ϕi , as well as a Grassmann-
even “anti-ghost” field c‡α that is paired with the ghost field cα . We will assign ghost number
1 to cα , 0 to ϕi , −1 to ϕ‡i and −2 to c‡α . The BV action is a functional S[ϕ, c, ϕ‡ , c‡ ] of ghost
number zero, whose expansion in the Grassmann-odd ghost and anti-fields takes the form

separated, then the correlation function is independent of the ordering of the operators.

to imaginary values −iτi , and obtain the Euclidean correlation function (also known as

that the ordering of Oi (xi )’s does not affect the value of the Wightman function. Moreover,

the latter are separated points in R . Starting from the Euclidean correlation function, we
can also go back to the Lorentzian Wightman function by analytic continuation in τi . We
expect singularities when a pair of points xi and xj become null-separated, and therefore
the analytic continuation must be performed in a way that avoids the singularities, e.g. by
maintaining the condition Im(x0i − x0j ) < 0 in the vicinity of the Lorentzian kinematic region.
In particular, we can approach the Lorentzian configuration while maintaining the separation
of the points in imaginary (or Euclidean) time and nonzero (xi −xj )2 = (⃗xi −⃗xj )2 −(x0i −x0j )2 .
If xi and xj are to become timelike separated, i.e. (xi −xj )2 goes from a positive real value to
a negative real value, the operator ordering between Oi and Oj in the resulting Lorentzian
correlator is specified by whether (xi − xj )2 goes around zero from above or below the real
axis in the analytic continuation procedure (Figure 26).




                                                   678
D.3      Conformal symmetry

The trace of the stress-energy tensor, T a a , is a scalar operator. Typically, one expresses it
as a linear combination of a basis of scalar operators OI ,
                                                X
                                       T aa =       βI OI ,                              (D.14)
                                                      I

where the coefficients βI are known as beta functions.
    A conformal field theory (CFT) is a quantum field theory whose stress-energy tensor Tab
is traceless, namely
                                         T a a = 0.                                 (D.15)
It follows from (D.15) that there are new conservation laws

                           ∂a (xb T a b ) = 0,   ∂a (T ab x2 − 2T a c xb xc ) = 0.               (D.16)

The symmetries generated by a conserved current of the form Ja (x) = Tab (x)v b (x) obey
the same algebra as those of the vector fields v a (x)∂a , which generate the infinitesimal
diffeomorphism
                               xa 7→ x′a = xa + ϵv a (x).                            (D.17)
In this sense, we can organize the symmetries generated by the conserved currents appearing
in (D.8), (D.9), (D.16) according to the diffeomorphisms generated by the vector fields

                           ∂a ,   xa ∂b − xb ∂a ,   xa ∂a ,   x2 ∂a − 2xa xb ∂b .                (D.18)

(D.18) generate the d-dimensional conformal group, which is isomorphic to SO(d, 2) for
conformal symmetry in d-dimensional Minkowskian spacetime, or SO(d + 1, 1) for conformal
symmetry in Euclidean spacetime.


D.4      Operator product expansion

In the Euclidean signature, rather than working with constant time slices, we may consider
any (d − 1)-dimensional oriented hypersurface S in Rd , and consider a suitable space VS of
states on S. In a path integral formulation, such states may be specified by wave functionals
on S. Generally, there isn’t a natural inner product defined on VS , and so VS is not quite a
Hilbert space (unless S is time-reflection symmetric).429 Rather, we have a bilinear pairing
between states in VS and those in VS , where S is S with the opposite orientation.
 429
    For a more rigorous treatment see Kontsevich and Segal, Quart. J. Math. Oxford Ser. 72 (2021) no.1-2,
673 [237].


                                                    679
    In a conformal field theory, however, if we take S to be a (d − 1)-dimensional sphere
centered at the origin, the inversion map gives rise to a natural isomorphism between VS and
VS (known as BPZ conjugation), and thereby an inner product on VS . Such an inner product
is positive definite if the conformal field theory is unitary or equivalently reflection-positive.
A class of states in VS can be constructed as the wave functionals produced by the path
integral on the ball B enclosed by S, with a set of local operators Oi (xi ) inserted within B;
such a state will be denoted by
                                            Q
                                           | i Oi (xi )⟩S .                               (D.19)
The completion of VS with respect to its inner product, denoted by HS , will be referred
to as the Hilbert space associated with S. The Noether charge associated with dilatation
symmetry,                               Z
                                 H = − dσ nµ xν Tµν (x),
                                 b                                                (D.20)
                                             S

where dσ is the volume element of S and ⃗nµ is the unit normal vector pointing outward,
can be identified as the Hamiltonian operator on HS .430 In particular, H
                                                                        b is Hermitian and
                                431
typically has discrete spectrum, in which case the eigenstates of Hb form a complete basis
of HS .
    Any state |ψ⟩ in HS can be viewed as the state created by a certain, a priori non-local,
operator supported in B. Upon a dilatation symmetry transformation, e−Hτ |ψ⟩ is created
                                                                                 b

by an operator supported in a ball whose radius is e−τ times that of B. When |ψ⟩ is an
eigenstate of bH, we can take τ to be arbitrarily large and conclude that |ψ⟩ is in fact created
by a local operator supported at the origin. Moreover, the corresponding local operator has
definite scaling dimension. It follows that the set of states |Oi (0)⟩S created by local operators
Oi of definite scaling dimension at the origin form a complete basis of HS .
   Given a pair of local operators Oi (xi ) and Oj (xj ) inside B, the state |Oi (xi )Oj (xj )⟩S can
be expanded in the aforementioned basis of HS as
                                                X
                          |Oi (xi )Oj (xj )⟩S =   Cijk (xi , xj )|Ok (0)⟩S ,                  (D.21)
                                                 k


where Cijk (xi , xj ) are real analytic functions in xi and xj , away from the locus xi = xj . This
is known as the operator product expansion (OPE). (D.21) can be viewed as an operator
equation                                            X
                                 Oi (xi )Oj (xj ) =   Cijk (xi , xj )Ok (0),                (D.22)
                                                 k

 430 b
    H agrees with the Hamiltonian on the cylinder R × S d−1 up to a Casimir energy.
