in the sense that (D.22) is expected to hold when inserted into a (Euclidean) correlation
function, with a convergent sum over correlators involving Ok on the RHS, provided that all
other local operators in the correlation function lie outside of B.
   We can of course also shift the origin of the ball B, and write the OPE of a pair of
operators around any given point y ∈ Rd ,
                                         X
                      Oi (xi )Oj (xj ) =   Cijk (xi − y, xj − y)Ok (y),         (D.23)
                                         k

provided that the minimal sphere centered at y that encloses xi and xj does not enclose

                                             681
E     General properties of 2D CFTs

E.1     2D conventions

In 2D Lorentzian signature, we typically denote by σ the spatial coordinate and t the time
coordinate, and define the lightcone coordinates as σ ± ≡ σ ± t. The Wick rotation to
Euclidean signature is defined by t = −iτ . We define the complex coordinates (z, z̄) as

                                    z = σ + iτ,        z̄ = σ − iτ.                           (E.1)

In other words, the Wick rotation takes (σ − , σ + ) to (z, z̄). Our convention for the measure
in complex coordinate z is such that

                                      d2 z ≡ 2dRe(z)dIm(z).                                   (E.2)

In the notation of differential forms, the integration measure dz 2 is equivalent to idz ∧ dz̄.
The conventions for 2D spinors will be stated in Appendix G.3.


E.2     2D conformal symmetry

In two-dimensional spacetime, the conformal group is automatically enhanced to an infinite
dimensional one. This is most easily seen by working in lightcone coordinates (σ − , σ + ), in
which the traceless stress-energy tensor obeys

                           ∂− T++ = ∂+ T−− = 0,             T+− = T−+ = 0.                    (E.3)

Consequently, we have an infinite set of conservation laws

                           ∂+ (v(σ − )T−− ) = 0,             v (σ + )T++ ) = 0,
                                                         ∂− (e                                (E.4)

for any functions v(σ − ) and ve(σ + ). In Euclidean signature, (σ − , σ + ) are replaced by complex
coordinates (z, z̄). The non-vanishing components of the stress-energy tensor are

                                T (z) ≡ Tzz (z),         Te(z̄) ≡ Tz̄z̄ (z̄),                 (E.5)

where we have indicated the conservation laws by declaring that T (z) is holomorphic and
Te(z̄) is anti-holomorphic.
   Let us note that the holomorphy of T (z), like the conservation equations for any symmetry
currents in a quantum field theory, should be understood as an operator equation, in the
                                                                     ¯ vanishes,
sense that any correlation function of local operators that involve ∂T
                               ¯
                               ∂T (z)O1 (z1 , z̄1 ) · · · On (zn , z̄n ) = 0,                 (E.6)

                                                   682
provided that the points z1 , · · · , zn are separated from z. This means that the correlation
function
                                  ⟨T (z)O1 (z1 , z̄1 ) · · · On (zn , z̄n )⟩             (E.7)
is a holomorphic function in z, away from z1 , · · · , zn . Generally, (E.7) will have singularities
when z coincides with one of the zi ’s.
    As a simple example, a linear conformal transformation amounts to a combination of
translation, rotation, and dilation, which may be characterized by the linear holomorphic
diffeomorphism
                            z 7→ z ′ = λz + u, z̄ 7→ z̄ ′ = λ̄z̄ + ū,              (E.8)
where λ, u are complex constants, with λ nonzero. If we set u = 0, then (E.8) would fix the
origin, and the associated dilation/rotation maps an operator at the origin, O(0), to another
operator at the origin O′ (0). Typically, it is possible to find a basis of operators O on which
dilation and rotation act diagonally, namely

                                      O′ (0) = λ−h λ̄−h O(0),                                 (E.9)
                                                      e



for a pair of constants h and e h. We will refer to h and eh as the holomorphic and anti-
holomorphic (or left and right) conformal weights of O. For nonzero u, the linear conformal
transformation takes O to O′ , such that

                                      O′ (u) = λ−h λ̄−h O(0)                                 (E.10)
                                                      e



   There is a conformal transformation that maps the punctured complex plane C× =
C − {0} to the Euclidean cylinder, parameterized by w = σ + iτ , σ ∼ σ + 2π, via the
holomorphic diffeomorphism
                                       z = e−iw .                             (E.11)
Heuristically, we then expect that a CFT on the plane, possibly with a singularity at the
origin, to be equivalent to the same CFT on the Euclidean cylinder. The singularity at the
origin can be characterized by an insertion of a local operator on the plane. The Euclidean
cylinder is related to the Lorentzian cylinder by analytic continuation in τ , and characterizes
time evolution of the CFT defined on a spatial circle.
   This leads to the state/operator correspondence, that is, there is a canonical 1-1 corre-
spondence between the space of local operators in a CFT at a given point (here taken to
be the origin of the complex plane) to the space H of states of the CFT on a circle of unit
radius. Given a local operator O(0), we will write the corresponding state as |O⟩.
   The dilation and rotation symmetry (E.8) on the plane corresponds to time and space
translation on the cylinder under the state/operator map. Thus, we expect that an operator

                                                683
O(0) of conformal weight (h, e
                             h) to map to a state |O⟩ on the cylinder with energy h + e h and
spatial momentum h − e h. We will see in section E.3 that this is correct up to a shift of the
ground state energy-momentum that is fixed by the conformal symmetry.
    We may equivalently think of the state |O⟩ as defined by a wave functional on the
unit circle S : |z| = 1 in the plane, obtained by performing the path integral on the disc
|z| ≤ 1 with the insertion of O(0), as described in section D.4. The conformal symmetry
corresponding to the inversion map z ′ = 1/z gives a natural identification between HS and
HS , known as BPZ conjugation, thereby defining a bilinear inner product on HS . The
Hermitian inner product on HS is related by a further complex conjugation on one of the
two states in the bilinear pairing.
   The operator product expansion in a CFT can be organized according to the conformal
weights. Namely, given a basis of local operators Oi (z, z̄) of weight (hi , e     hi ), we can write the

full conformal symmetry leads to a much more refined version of the OPE, with far stronger
convergence properties.

namely states obtained by acting on |ϕ⟩ with an arbitrary set of L−n and L

    In a unitary CFT, there is a positive definite Hermitian inner product on the Hilbert space
of local operators. In particular, L0 and Le0 are Hermitian operators, whose spectra (namely

                                                688
the set of conformal weights) are real and bounded from below. The Hilbert space can be
decomposed into irreducible representations of Virasoro algebra, each of which is generated
by a lowest weight state of definite conformal weight (h, e
                                                          h). Thus, all local operators can be
expressed as linear combinations of Virasoro descendants of primaries.
   The representations of Virasoro algebra will be analyzed in more detail in section E.5.
We will see in section E.6 and F.4 that the spectrum of primaries together with their 3-point
functions determine all correlation functions of the CFT on any surface.


E.4     Weyl anomaly

In this section we consider 2D CFT on a curved Euclidean worldsheet. Suppose S is the ac-
tion of a classical field theory coupled covariantly to a background metric gab . A deformation
of the metric leads to the variation of the action
                                                    √
                                             Z
                                           1
                                    δS =        d2 σ g δgab T ab .                       (E.41)
                                          4π
In the quantum theory, a deformation of the metric amounts to inserting
                                                          
                                            2 √
                                        Z
                                      1                 ab
                              exp −        d σ g δgab T                                         (E.42)

into the path integral or into a correlation function. If the metric changes by a Weyl trans-

worldsheet, then the CFT coupled to the background metric would be Weyl invariant.
   We must be cautious in dealing with expressions like (E.42), which involves integrating
products of local operators at coinciding points, and could potentially receive contributions
from contact terms that would have been missed if we naively integrate the operator identities
that govern Green functions of operators at separated points.433 For instance, applying ∂¯z̄ to
the OPE of the holomorphic stress-energy tensors (E.24), and keeping track of the contact

E.5     Representations of Virasoro algebra

Let us now examine the lowest weight representations of Virasoro algebra in some detail. We
will focus on the holomorphic Virasoro algebra. Consider a primary state |νh ⟩ that obeys

                            L0 |νh ⟩ = h|νh ⟩,   Ln |νh ⟩ = 0,   n ≥ 1.                  (E.54)

A representation is spanned by the Virasoro descendants

                                 L−N |νh ⟩ = L−n1 · · · L−nk |νh ⟩,                      (E.55)

where N stands for a sequence of positive integers {n1 , n2 , · · · , nk } in descending order
n1 ≥ n2 ≥ · · · ≥ nk . We will refer to |N | ≡ kj=1 nj as the level of the state (E.55). The
                                              P

level n Gram matrix is defined as the matrix whose entries are inner products of pairs of
level n descendants of |νh ⟩,
                         (n)
                       GN M = ⟨νh |(L−N )† L−M |νh ⟩,      |N | = |M | = n.              (E.56)

Recall that L†−N = Lnk · · · Ln1 . The Gram matrix elements can be computed by moving all
the positively graded Virasoro generators to the right of the negatively graded ones using the
Virasoro algebra; the results are generally polynomial functions of h and the central charge
c.
   Of particular use is the determinant of the Gram matrix, known as the Kac determinant,
which is given by formula
                                            Y
                            det G(n) = Kn       (h − hr,s )P (n−rs) .              (E.57)
                                             1≤rs≤n

Here Kn is a positive constant, having to do with the (somewhat arbitrary) choice of basis
(E.55). The product is taken over a pair of positive integers r, s that obey rs ≤ n. P (m)
is the partition number, i.e. the total number of positive integer partitions of m. It can be
computed as coefficients of the generating function
                                   X             Y 1
                                        Pm q m =          .                            (E.58)
                                    m≥0
                                                   1 − qk
                                                   k≥1


                                                 691
Finally, hr,s , which may be real or complex, are given by
                                      Q2 1
                                          − (rb + sb−1 )2 ,
                                      hr,s =                                                     (E.59)
                                       4     4
where Q and b are related to the central charge c by
                                    c ≡ 1 + 6Q2 ,          Q ≡ b + b−1 .                         (E.60)
The significance of (E.57) is that a primary νhr,s of weight h = hr,s admits a Virasoro
descendant at level rs that is a null state. That is, there is a state of the form
                                           X
                                  |χrs ⟩ =     χN
                                                rs L−N |νhr,s ⟩                    (E.61)
                                                !N |=rs

that has zero norm,
                                               ⟨χrs |χrs ⟩ = 0.                                  (E.62)
                                  N
Equivalently, the coefficients {χrs   } form a zero eigenvector of the Gram matrix. The nor-
                                {1,··· ,1}
malization is chosen so that χrs           = 1, i.e. the coefficient of (L−1 )rs |νhr,s ⟩ in (E.61) is 1.
At a higher level n > rs, there will be P (n − rs) descendants of the form L−M |χrs ⟩ with
|M | = n − rs that also have zero norm, giving rise to an order P (n − rs) zero of the Kac
determinant.
   Now let us consider a unitary representation generated by the primary |νh ⟩. In a unitary
representation, any null sate must vanish identically. It follows from ⟨νh |L1 L−1 |νh ⟩ = 2h
that h ≥ 0; the h = 0 case corresponds to the identity/vacuum representation of Virasoro
algebra.
    If c > 1, hr,s are either non-positive real numbers (for c ≥ 25) or complex (for 1 < c < 25);
in this case, det G(n) being a real function of h cannot have zeroes on the positive real axis,
and therefore must be positive for all h > 0. Consequently, all representations with c > 1 and
h > 0 are unitary and do not contain null Virasoro descendants. The vacuum representation
h = 0 is also unitary for c > 1, but contains a null state at level 1, namely L−1 |0⟩ = 0.
   In the case c = 1, det G(n) is non-negative for h ≥ 0, but it does have zeroes along the
positive real axis, at hr,s = 41 (r − s)2 for r ̸= s. Consequently, while all c = 1, h ≥ 0
representations are unitary, for the special values h = 41 n2 , n ∈ Z≥0 , the representation
admits null state relations starting at level n + 1.
    For c < 1, one can show that if h is not equal to one of the hr,s ’s, det G(n) will be negative
for some n and violate unitarity. A careful analysis, which we shall not reproduce here, leads
to the following discrete set of possible unitary representations with c < 1:
             6                        ((m + 1)r − ms)2 − 1
c=1−               ,     h = hr,s =                        ,          with 1 ≤ r ≤ m − 1, 1 ≤ s ≤ m,

where m = 2, 3, · · · . The unitary CFTs with c = ce < 1 come in discrete families as well;
they are known as minimal models, and are completely classified and exactly solvable.


E.6     Conformal correlators and conformal blocks

Let us begin with correlation functions of local operators on the Euclidean plane. In a general
quantum field theory, as discussed in section D.2, these are defined as (analytic continuation)
of vacuum correlation functions. For a 2D CFT, the plane is conformally equivalent to the
cylinder or the Riemann sphere, and we may equivalently speak of correlators on the cylinder
or the sphere. In particular, correlation functions on the sphere should be invariant under
conformal transformations that are globally defined on the sphere; as will be elaborated in
section F.1, these correspond to Möbius transformations on the plane of the form
                                                             αz + β
                                              z 7→ z ′ =            ,                                 (E.64)
                                                             γz + δ
where α, β, γ, δ are complex numbers, that may be taken to obey αδ − βγ = 1. Such
transformations form the group P SL(2, C), which is a finite dimensional subgroup of the
full Virasoro symmetry group. Under such a conformal transformation, a primary ϕ(z, z̄) of
           h) transforms to ϕ′ (z, z̄), related by
weight (h, e

                                ϕ′ (z ′ , z̄ ′ ) = (γz + δ)h (γ̄ z̄ + δ̄)h ϕ(z, z̄).                  (E.65)
                                                                          e

for any set of local operators Oi and the conformally transformed operators Oi′ under (E.64).
Note that in writing (E.66) the conformal symmetry is viewed as acting actively on the op-
erators, leaving the coordinates invariant. Furthermore, (E.66) only captures the P SL(2, C)
invariance and not the full Virasoro symmetry; the implication of the latter will be discussed
later in this section.

The BPZ conjugate of a Virasoro descendant L−N L
    In a unitary CFT, there is an anti-unitary map I that takes the Hermitian conjugate
state ⟨O| to the BPZ conjugate ⟨⟨O|,

                                                ⟨⟨O| = ⟨O|I.                              (E.74)

Typically, we can find a Hermitian basis of operators on which I acts as the identity map,
in which case the distinction between ⟨⟨O| and ⟨O| can be omitted. Here by a Hermitian
operator we mean one that is Hermitian on the Lorentzian cylinder; for instance, the stress-
energy tensor components T and Te are both viewed as Hermitian operators, even though

                                                    694
on the Euclidean plane they are complex conjugations of one another. Note that in the free
boson CFT, the oscillator ground state eikX is not a Hermitian operator; in this case we have
⟨⟨k| = ⟨−k|.
    We say that a CFT is compact if there are finitely many linearly independent states
whose conformal weights are below any given finite value.434 In a compact unitary CFT, we
can further choose a Hermitian basis of primaries ϕi that obey (E.73) with Dij = δij . In a
noncompact unitary CFT, we often need to deal with delta-function normalizable states. For
instance, in the free boson CFT, the oscillator ground state |k⟩ obeys ⟨k|k ′ ⟩ = CX 2πδ(k − k ′ )
for some convention-dependent normalization constant CX .
    Next, let us consider the three-point function of primaries. There is a P SL(2, C) trans-
formation that maps three distinct points z1 , z2 , z3 on C ∪ {∞} to any three other distinct
points. This allows us to determine

the three operators is an integer. Cijk is either completely symmetric or completely anti-

   In a unitary CFT, reflection positivity further demands that, for a Hermitian basis of
primary operators ϕi (in the sense of Hermiticity on the Lorentzian cylinder), the structure
constants Cijk must be real if the sum of three spins is even, and purely imaginary if the
sum of spins is odd.

well as the structure constants.


E.7      Recurrence formulae and analytic property of conformal blocks

In practice, the Virasoro conformal block Fc can be evaluated efficiently to high accuracy
through Zamolodchikov’s recurrence relation. The idea is to consider the analytic continu-
ation of Fc in the central charge c. For fixed weights, the c → ∞ limit of Fc is finite and
reduces to the corresponding conformal block of the global conformal group SL(2, R), that

                                                  703
F     Riemann surfaces and modular invariance

F.1    The sphere

We begin with the genus h = 0 case, in which case the Riemann surface is topologically a
sphere. The Riemann sphere has no moduli, and every metric on the sphere can be put to
the form of the Euclidean metric
                                      ds2 = dzdz̄                                  (F.1)
by a Weyl transformation. More precisely, the z coordinate chart U covers the sphere minus
one point. There is another coordinate chart V , parameterized by the complex coordinate
w, such that on the overlap U ∩ V , the two coordinates are related by w = 1/z.
  The conformal Killing vector (CKV) is a linear combination of a (globally defined) holo-
morphic vector field and an anti-holomorphic vector field,

                                      v z (z)∂z + vez̄ (z̄)∂z̄ .                          (F.2)

On a different coordinate chart parameterized by w, the vector field is expressed as v w (w)∂w +
vew̄ (w̄)∂w̄ , where v w (w) is related to v z (z) on the overlap of the coordinate charts by

                                                          ∂w
                                      v w (w) = v z (z)      .                            (F.3)
                                                          ∂z
On the Riemann sphere, a holomorphic vector field of the form v z (z)∂z on the chart U would
be written as
                                   −w2 v z (1/w)∂w                                      (F.4)
on the chart V . v z (z) should be holomorphic on the entire complex z-plane, as is −w2 v z (w)
on the entire complex w-plane. This restricts v z (z) to be a quadratic polynomial,

                                   v z (z) = a0 + a1 z + a2 z 2 .                         (F.5)

These CKVs generate a finite conformal Killing group transformation of the form
                                                    αz + β
                                       z 7→ z ′ =          ,                              (F.6)
                                                    γz + δ
where α, β, γ, δ can be taken to be complex numbers with αδ − βγ = 1. Further, flipping the
signs of α, β, γ, δ simultaneously does not change the transformation (F.6), and preserves
the condition αδ − βγ = 1. Therefore, the conformal Killing group of the Riemann sphere
is isomorphic to P SL(2, C).



                                                704
F.2    The torus

Next consider the genus h = 1 case, where the Riemann surface is topologically a torus. Up
to a Weyl transformation, the metric on the torus can always be put to the Euclidean form
ds2 = dzdz̄, but with the coordinate z subject to the periodic identification

                                    z ∼ z + 2π ∼ z + 2πτ,                                (F.7)

where τ = τ1 + iτ2 for τ1 , τ2 ∈ R, τ2 > 0. We could equivalently describe the torus via coor-
dinate charts, but that would not be necessary. An alternative coordinate system (σ 1 , σ 2 ),
where σ 1 and σ 2 are of periodicity 2π, is related by

                                z = σ1 + τ σ2,      z̄ = σ 1 + τ̄ σ 2 ,                  (F.8)

so that the metric can be written as

                                     ds2 = |dσ 1 + τ dσ 2 |2 .                           (F.9)

τ is a complex parameter of the moduli space M1 of the torus as a Riemann surface.
   The only diffeomorphism that preserves the Euclidean metric up to a Weyl transformation
with an identification of the form (F.7) for some τ is a linear holomorphic map, of the form
                                                       z
                                       z 7→ z ′ =          ,                            (F.10)
                                                    cτ + d
where c and d are a pair of coprime integers. Note that z ′ is identified with z ′ + 2π, and is
also identified with z ′ + 2πτ ′ , for
                                                 aτ + b
                                            τ′ =        ,                                (F.11)
                                                 cτ + d
for another pair of integers a, b such that ad − bc = 1. Indeed, the torus with modulus τ and

σ a coordinates, it can be expressed as a map (σ 1 , σ 2 ) 7→ (σ ′1 , σ ′2 ), with
                                       ′1            1
                                       σ         a −b       σ
                                         ′2 =                   ,                        (F.12)

                               ds2 = |cτ + d|2 |dσ ′1 + τ ′ dσ ′2 |2 .                  (F.13)

Thus, we learn that the modulus τ should be identified up to P SL(2, Z) transformations of
the form (F.11). The moduli space of the torus is then

                            M1 ≃ {τ ∈ C | Imτ > 0}/P SL(2, Z).                          (F.14)

                                                705
M1 can be parameterized by τ in the fundamental domain (4.83), with the boundary ∂F
identified using either τ → τ + 1 or τ → −1/τ . The resulting space M1 may be viewed
topologically as a sphere with a puncture at τ = i∞, corresponding to a singular limit of
the torus modulus, and two special points τ = i and τ = e2πi/3 where the torus develops a
Z4 and Z6 discrete rotation symmetry respectively.
   The conformal Killing vector fields on the torus are easy to describe: they are simply
constant vector fields. The conformal Killing group of the torus with generic τ is T 2 ⋊ Z2 ,
where the T 2 is the group of translations along the torus, and the Z2 is the orientation-
preserving reflection symmetry z 7→ −z.


F.3     Genus h ≥ 2

A general Riemann surface of arbitrary genus may be constructed by gluing together Rie-
mann surfaces of lower genera using the “plumbing fixture”. Given two Riemann surfaces
Σ1 and Σ2 , of genus h1 and h2 respectively, we can choose a coordinate chart U ⊂ Σ1 pa-
rameterized by z on the unit disc, and another coordinate chart V ⊂ Σ2 parameterized by
w on the unit disc, and identify a pair of annulus regions on the two discs using the map

                                           w = q/z,                                       (F.15)

for a nonzero complex parameter q with |q| ≤ 1. The identification produces a new Riemann
surface Σ of genus h = h1 + h2 .
   Similarly, one may start with a single Riemann surface Σ of genus h, pick two coordinate
charts U and V , and cut out a hole on each and identify them along a pair of annulus regions
using the map (F.15), thereby producing a new Riemann surface Σ′ of genus h′ = h + 1.
    We can give a rough count of the dimension µh of the moduli space Mh of the genus h
Riemann surface based on the plumbing construction. We can choose the center of the pair
of discs U and V on Σ1 and Σ2 , and the complex parameter q, giving a total of 3 complex
parameters, or 6 real parameters. Thus, we expect µh1 +h2 = µh1 + µh2 + 6, which leads to
µh = 6h − 6. This answer is obviously incorrect for h = 0 or 1, but is in fact the correct
number of real moduli for h ≥ 2.
   A more explicit description of the genus h Riemann surface, obtained by plumbing to-
gether Riemann spheres, is as follows. We begin with the Riemann sphere C ∪ {∞}, and
consider a set of h loxodromic P SL(2, C) elements γ1 , · · · , γh . Each γi acts on the complex
coordinate z by
                                                 ai z + b i
                                   z 7→ γi (z) =            ,                              (F.16)
                                                 ci z + d i


                                              706
                                                               
                                                        ai b i
with ai di − bi ci = 1, such that the SL(2, C) matrix             has a pair of distinct eigenvalues
                                                         ci d i
qi , qi−1 with |qi | < 1. Generically, there are no group relations among γ1 , · · · , γh . Together
they generate a free group Γ, known as the Schottky group, that acts on the Riemann
sphere. The set Λ of accumulation points of Γ on the Riemann sphere is a certain Cantor
set of measure zero. The quotient

                                     Σ = (C ∪ {∞} − Λ)/Γ                                     (F.17)

is a Riemann surface of genus h. The Schottky group involves 3h complex parameters, but
an overall conjugation by P SL(2, C), the conformal Killing group of the Riemann sphere,
produces an equivalent Schottky group action. Thus the moduli space of Σ is parameterized
by 3h − 3 independent complex parameters. In fact, each point of the genus h Riemann
surface moduli space Mh can be realized by a Schottky group through (F.17). However,
each Schottky group not only determines a Riemann surface, but also specifies a particular
pair-of-pants decomposition of that Riemann surface. A given Riemann surface admits many
different pair-of-pants decompositions, leading to discrete identifications of the Schottky
parameters. One must also be careful with the boundary of the moduli space where the
Riemann surface degenerates. As a result, the full geometry of the moduli space Mh is
generally rather complicated for h ≥ 2.
   Another useful characterization of the moduli of a genus h Riemann surface Σ is through
the period matrix. Pick a basis of 1-cycles αI , βJ , such that their intersection numbers are

                        αI · αJ = βI · βJ = 0,      αI · βJ = −βJ · αI = δJI .               (F.18)

F.4    Modular invariance of 2D CFT

There is a natural way to extend the definition of correlation functions of local operators in
a 2D CFT to any compact oriented surface Σ equipped with a Riemannian metric, at least
in the case c = ce where gravitational anomalies are absent, as follows.
   Firstly, note that up to the Weyl anomaly factor (E.52) which depends only on the central
charge c and not any further details of the CFT, the partition function on Σ depends only
on the equivalence class of metrics with respect to Weyl transformation, i.e. the structure of
Σ as a Riemann surface. Likewise, under a Weyl transformation of the metric, a correlation
function of local operators O1 , · · · , On on Σ acquires the same Weyl anomaly factor, provided
that the Weyl transformation is trivial in a small neighborhood of the local operators. For
our purpose, it suffices to assume that each operator Oa is inserted at the origin of a disc
Da ⊂ Σ on which the metric is flat, so that there is no ambiguity with regard to the state
created by Oa in radial quantization on Da .

                                                 708
    If Σ is a surface of genus h > 1, we can decompose it into 2h − 2 “pairs of pants”,
joined along their boundary circles Ck , k = 1, · · · , 3h − 3. If Σ has genus h = 1 then it
suffices to represent Σ as a cylinder with two boundary circles identified. The metric in a
neighborhood of each circle Ck , up to a Weyl transformation, can be put in the form of a
standard Euclidean cylinder parameterized by (τ, σ), σ ∼ σ + 2π, τ ∈ (−ϵ, ϵ) for some ϵ > 0,
such that Ck corresponds to the equal time slice τ = 0. We can then insert a complete basis
of states along Ck , and express the correlation function ⟨O1 · · · On ⟩Σ in terms of correlation
functions of local operators on pairs of pants or cylinders, with appropriate CFT states
assigned to the boundary circles. The correlation functions on pairs of pants or cylinders are
conformally equivalent to correlators on the sphere or the plane, which are then determined
by the structure constants as described in section E.6.
    Equivalently, we may view the surface Σ with n local operator insertions as a surface with
n “punctures”. We can decompose the punctured surface into 2h − 2 + n pairs of pants, with
n of the boundary circles shrunk to points. The n-point function on Σ is then decomposed
into the product of 2h − 2 + n three-point functions, suitably Weyl transformed, summed
over the basis of states inserted along 3h − 3 + n circles.
   The consistency in defining correlation functions on Σ requires that different pair-of-pants
decompositions of the n-punctured surface Σ result in the same answer for the correlation
function. If Σ is topologically a sphere, this consistency condition is equivalent to the
crossing equation for the conformal block decomposition of sphere 4-point functions, or the
associativity of the OPE.




Figure 29: The crossing move relating two different pair-of-pants decompositions of the four-
holed sphere.

into a sum of sphere three-point functions. More explicitly, as will be discussed in detail
in section F.2, the torus may be parameterized by the complex coordinate z, subject to
periodicity z ∼ z + 2π ∼ z + 2πτ , for a complex modulus parameter τ = τ1 + iτ2 with
τ2 > 0. We can write the 1-point function of an operator O(z, z̄) on the torus of modulus τ ,

    It can be shown that any two different pair-of-pants decompositions of the n-punctured
surface Σ can be related by a sequence of simple crossing moves: either the crossing move on
the 4-punctured sphere (Figure 29), or that of the 1-punctured torus (Figure 30).436 Con-
sequently, the consistency of the n-point function on Σ follows from the crossing invariance
of all sphere 4-point functions together with the modular invariance of all torus 1-point
functions.

     The relation between the torus 1-point function and the trace on the RHS of (F.26) will be modified in
ghost CFTs. For instance, in the bc system to be discussed in section 3.2, one must insert (−)Nbc into the
trace, where Nbc is the bc ghost number.
 436
     Hatcher and Thurston, Topology 19, 221 (1980) [241].


                                                           710
      Modular invariance puts highly nontrivial constraints on a CFT. For instance, while free
boson CFT is a modular invariant theory, its k = 0 sector, generated by operators of the form
∂ n ∂¯m X and their normal order products, closes under OPE but is not modular invariant.
    The integer spin (NS,NS) sector states of the free fermion CFT close under OPE, but is
not modular invariant by itself. A modular invariant CFT with c = ce = 12 , known as the
critical Ising model, can be constructed by combining the integer spin (NS,NS) sector and
(R,R) sector states (Appendix H.1). Such a construction is known as the diagonal Gliozzi-
Scherk-Olive (GSO) projection. The worldsheet CFT of type II superstrings, on the other
hand, is a non-unitary theory defined with the chiral GSO projection (section 6.4.2) on the
free fermions as well as superconformal ghosts, in which a subset of integer spin states in the
(NS,NS), (NS,R), (R,NS), (R,R) sectors are included in the spectrum.

A priori there is an ambiguity in the choice of periodic boundary condition for the field
ψ± (σ), namely we only need to demand that T++ and T−− are periodic under the shift
σ → σ + 2π, whereas ψ+ and ψ− may independently be either periodic or anti-periodic.
If the fermion field is periodic in a given state, we refer to that state as belonging to the
“Ramond sector”, or R sector. If the fermion field is anti-periodic, we refer to the state
as in the “Neveu-Schwarz sector”, or NS sector. A priori, the Hilbert space of the free
fermion theory on the cylinder may involve states in either (NS,NS), (NS,R), (R,NS), or
(R,R) sectors, where the notation is such that (NS,R) for instance refers to a sector in which
ψ+ is anti-periodic and ψ− is periodic. In order for the CFT to have closed OPE algebra and

                                              718
the property of modular invariance, the actual Hilbert space of the CFT on the circle, which
is in correspondence with local operators, should only include a subset of all possible states
in the various sectors. Those states excluded from this Hilbert space may be interpreted as
defect operators (Appendix H.2).

whereas in the presence of an R sector operator OR (0), ψ(z) has a branch cut.

state/operator correspondence. The entire NS sector Fock space maps to operators formed
by normal ordered products of ψ and its derivatives.

H.1     The Ising CFT

A basic family of unitary CFTs are the minimal models, whose central charge takes value
in the discrete set (E.63). The minimal models are distinguished by the property that they
only admit finitely many Virasoro primaries, which would not be the case for unitary CFTs
with c ≥ 1. In this section we will consider the first nontrivial minimal model, of central
charge c = 21 , also known as the 2D critical Ising model or the Ising CFT.
    As outlined in section F.4, the essential consistency criteria of a 2D CFT are crossing
invariance of the sphere 4-point functions and modular covariance of torus 1-point functions.
We now consider the 4-point function of nontrivial primaries (i.e. other than the identity
operator) in the Ising CFT. There are only three possible primary weights for unitary rep-
resentations of the c = 12 Virasoro algebra, namely

H.2      Topological defect lines

A topological defect line L in a 2D CFT is a line operator whose correlation functions
are invariant under continuous deformations of the line, as long as it does not pass other

                                                      725
operators or defects. Generally L can end on point-like defect operators, which span a defect
Hilbert space HL . By state/operator mapping, we can also think of HL as the Hilbert space
of the CFT on the circle, in the presence of a defect point of type L. While states in HL
still form representations of the left and right Virasoro algebra, they need not have integer
spins.




Figure 31: Left: a defect operator (black dot) attached to a topological defect line L (blue).
Right: the corresponding state on the cylinder in the presence of the defect (blue, extended
in time).

    Given two topological lines L1 and L2 , one can construct their direct sum L1 ⊕ L2 , which
obeys HL1 ⊕L2 = HL1 ⊕ HL2 . Topological defect lines that cannot be reduced to a direct sum
will be referred to as “simple”. One can also fuse a pair of topological lines L1 and L2 , by
bringing them next to each other, which results in a new topological line L1 ▷ L2 . The fusion
operation is associative but need not be commutative. The fusion of simple topological lines
can be decomposed into a direct sum, via
                                               M
                                    Li ▷ Lj =      Nijk Lk ,                            (H.17)
                                                   k

where Nijk are non-negative integers and represent the number of copies of Lk in the direct
summand.
    The possibility of fusion also means that topological lines can form junctions. A junc-
tion of three (ordered) topological lines L1 , L2 , L3 is itself a (topological) defect operator;
such operators span a vector space VL1 L2 L3 , which is the subspace of weight (0, 0) states in
HL1 ▷L2 ▷L3 . For simple lines Li , dimVLi Lj Lk is equal to the fusion coefficients Nijk , where Lk
is the orientation reversal of Lk .
    Given a pair of junctions operators in VLi Lj Lm and VLk Lℓ Lm , we can form a 4-way “H-
junction” by connecting the Lm line with Lm . The H-junction operator can be expressed in
                             L
a cross-channel as a state in n VLj Lk Ln ⊗ VLℓ Li Ln . This defines a linear map
                           M                           M
                   Kijℓk :   VLi Lj Lm ⊗ VLk Lℓ Lm →      VLj Lk Ln ⊗ VLℓ Li Ln ,     (H.18)
                            m                            n


                                                726
which we refer to as the H-junction crossing kernel. The Kijℓk ’s obey a set of consistency
relations that follow from a sequence of H-junction crossing moves on a 5-way junction,
known as the pentagon identity.
   A basic class of topological defect lines are “symmetry lines” or “invertible lines”, which
are associated with symmetries of the CFT. Let G be the symmetry group, it is expected
that every element g ∈ G comes with a simple topological line Lg , such that the fusion is
governed by group product, namely Lg1 ▷ Lg2 = Lg1 g2 . This is a special case of (H.17) where
only one of the fusion coefficients is nonzero (and is equal to 1). The junction operator space
VLg1 Lg2 Lg3 is isomorphic to C when g1 g2 g3 = 1, and trivial otherwise. We can pick a basis
vector vg1 ,g2 ∈ VLg1 Lg2 L(g g )−1 for each junction, and express the crossing kernel (H.18) as
                                          1 2

                           −1 ,g
             Kg(g1 ,g
                   1 g2 g3 )

                                       (vg1 ,g2 ⊗ vg3 ,(g1 g2 g3 )−1 ) = eiθ(g1 ,g2 ,g3 ) (vg2 ,g3 ⊗ v(g1 g2 g3 )−1 ,g1 ).   (H.19)

The pentagon identity implies the following relation of the crossing phase θ,

         θ(g1 , g2 , g3 g4 ) + θ(g1 g2 , g3 , g4 ) = θ(g2 , g3 , g4 ) + θ(g1 , g2 g3 , g4 ) + θ(g1 , g2 , g3 ).              (H.20)

On the other hand, if we rotate the phase of the basis vector vg1 ,g2 by eiφ(g1 ,g2 ) , θ changes by

                       δθ(g1 , g2 , g3 ) = φ(g1 , g2 ) + φ(g1 , g2 g3 ) − φ(g1 g2 , g3 ) − φ(g1 , g2 ).                      (H.21)

The set of possible crossing phases θ that obey the consistency condition (H.20) modulo the
ambiguity (H.21) defines the group cohomology H 3 (G, U (1)). If the G-symmetry lines in a
CFT have crossing phases that represent a nontrivial class in H 3 (G, U (1)), we say that the
symmetry is subject to ’t Hooft anomaly. A consequence of the ’t Hooft anomaly will be
discussed in section H.3.
   The Ising CFT admits a Z2 symmetry ηb that flips the sign of the spin field σ while leaving
the energy operator ε invariant. We will denote the associated symmetry line η. It follows
from the modular property

H.3      Orbifolds

If a CFT M admits a discrete symmetry group G that is free of ’t Hooft anomaly, it is then
possible to gauge G to produce a new CFT, known as the orbifold CFT, denoted by M/G.
We begin with the Hilbert space Hg of defect operators attached to the symmetry line Lg ,
for an element g ∈ G. In the absence of ’t Hooft anomaly, the crossing phase θ(g1 , g2 , g3 )
in (H.19) can be removed via (H.21) by choosing a (not necessarily unique) set of junction
vectors, and so the 4-way junction of Lh , Lg , Lh−1 , Lhg−1 h−1 can be consistently defined by
splitting into a pair of 3-way junctions. This allows for defining the action of the symmetry
group element h,
                                       h : Hg → Hhgh−1
                                       b                                                 (H.25)
by encircling the defect operator with an Lh loop.

H.4            Narain lattice

Let XLi (i = 1, · · · , nL ) be a set of holomorphic free boson fields, with the OPE

                                          XLi (z)XLj (0) ∼ −δ ij log z,                     (H.39)
           ′
and XRi (i′ = 1, · · · , nR ) a set of anti-holomorphic boson fields. The Narain lattice CFT is
                                                                                                ′
defined by including all operators constructed out of normal order products of ∂ n XLi , ∂ m XRi ,
and the exponential operators

                                            Ok = : eikL ·XL +ikR ·XR :,                     (H.40)

for vectors k ≡ (kL , kR ) in a lattice Γ ⊂ RnL ,nR . The operators Ok and Ok′ have single-valued
OPE provided that
                                   k ◦ k ′ ≡ kL · kL′ − kR · kR′ ∈ Z.                      (H.41)
This amounts to saying that Γ is an integral lattice with respect to the pairing induced by
the inner product on RnL ,nR . Ok has integer spin if

                                                  k ◦ k ∈ 2Z.                               (H.42)

This condition amounts to saying that Γ is an even lattice. Finally, demanding that the
torus partition function is modular invariant, namely
                                                                2    2
                                            1           X      kL   kR
                      Z(τ, τ̄ ) =                             q 2 q̄ 2 = Z(−1/τ, −1/τ̄ ),   (H.43)
                                    (η(τ ))nL (η(τ ))nR k∈Γ

requires that Γ is a self-dual lattice, namely Γ = Γ∗ , where

                                    Γ∗ ≡ {ℓ ∈ RnL ,nR |ℓ ◦ k ∈ Z, ∀k ∈ Γ}.                  (H.44)

The self-duality condition is equivalent to saying that Γ is unimodular, that is, given any
integral basis {ei }i=1,··· ,nL +nR , the matrix (Aij ) = (ei ◦ ej ) has determinant ±1. One can
further show that when this condition is satisfied, the torus 1-point function of a general
primary in the Narain lattice CFT is modular covariant.
   A standard theorem438 asserts that such Γ exists only when nL − nR ≡ 0 mod 8. Fur-
thermore, if both nL , nR are positive, the integral pairing (Aij ) is unique up to a change of

I.1    Weyl anomaly in the nonlinear sigma model

To quantize the nonlinear sigma model based on the action (3.71) in a manner that respects

I.5    Liouville CFT

The Liouville theory is defined, at least at the semiclassical level, by the action
                                       √
                                Z
                              1
                                   d2 σ g g ab ∂a ϕ∂b ϕ + QRϕ + 4πµe2bϕ ,
                                                                          
                   SL [ϕ] =                                                             (I.37)
                             4π
where R is the scalar curvature of the background metric g. To define the quantum theory
via the path integral requires specifying a regularization scheme. One approach is to view
Liouville theory as a deformation of the linear dilaton CFT (section 3.8) with background
charge Q and central charge c = ce = 1 + 6Q2 . The operator e2bϕ in the linear dilaton theory
(as defined by free field normal ordering) has conformal weight h = e  h = b(Q − b), and is
marginal when
                                        Q = b + b−1 .                                   (I.38)


                                              739
With this choice of b, one finds that the coupling µ has vanishing beta function,441 indicating
that the Liouville theory is in fact a CFT.
    One may equivalently formulate the quantum Liouville theory via canonical quantization.
This amounts to starting with the linear dilaton theory on the cylinder, whose Hamiltonian
                                                                             R
is identical to that of a free boson, and deforming the Hamiltonian by µ dσ e2bϕ (where the
operator e2bϕ is defined by the free field normal ordering). A generic energy eigenstate takes
the form of a scattering state in the field configuration space parameterized by the Fourier
modes of ϕ(σ) = n∈Z ϕn einσ , whose wave functional in the asymptotic region ϕ0 → −∞ is a
                   P

superposition of incoming and outgoing waves related by reflection off the Liouville potential
wall. In particular, the wave functional of a typical primary state has the asymptotic form
                                               −2iP ϕ0
                                                        − P∞ nϕn ϕ−n
                 Ψin
                   P [ϕ] ∼   e 2iP ϕ0

where the dependence on ϕn̸=0 takes the form of the oscillator ground state of the free boson.
Here P ∈ R≥0 is the target space momentum of the incoming wave, and S(P ) is a scattering
phase. We will denote the corresponding vertex operator of the Liouville theory by VPin . In
the asymptotic region, VPin may be expressed as a vertex operator of the linear dilaton CFT
in the form
                             VPin ∼ e(Q+2iP )ϕ + S(P )e(Q−2iP )ϕ .                       (I.40)
The conformal weight of VPin in the Liouville theory is the same as that of the RHS of (I.40)
                                              2

J     Superconformal symmetry in two dimensions

J.1     (1, 1) superspace

The free field action (6.5) can be formulated in the language of (1, 1) superspace on the
worldsheet, by extending the coordinates (z, z̄) to include formal Grassmann-odd coordinates
(θ, θ̄), and packaging X µ , ψ µ , ψeµ into a “real superfield”,
                                            r                 r
             µ                  µ             α′ µ              α′ eµ                            (J.1)
            X (z, z̄, θ, θ̄) ≡ X (z, z̄) + i    θψ (z, z̄) + i     θ̄ψ (z, z̄) + θθ̄F µ (z, z̄),
                                              2                  2
where F µ will play the role of an auxiliary field that does not carry independent propagating
degrees of freedom. The action (6.5) can be equivalently written as the superspace integral
                                           Z
                                      1
                                S=            d2 zd2 θ Dθ̄ Xµ Dθ Xµ ,                    (J.2)
                                     2πα′
where Dθ and Dθ̄ are super-derivatives, defined as

                                 Dθ = ∂θ + θ∂z ,       Dθ̄ = ∂θ̄ + θ̄∂z̄ .                      (J.3)

The super-derivatives obey the following basic relations,

                              Dθ2 = ∂z ,   Dθ̄2 = ∂¯z̄ ,   {Dθ , Dθ̄ } = 0.                     (J.4)

After expanding the integrand of (J.2) in the component fields X µ , ψ µ , ψeµ , F µ , and integrat-
ing out the Grassmann-odd variables (θ, θ̄), (J.2) reduces to (6.5) plus a quadratic term in
the auxiliary fields that does not affect the dynamics.
   The action (J.2) exhibits manifest 2D (1, 1) super-Poincaré symmetry. The supersym-
metry variation of the fields can be summarized as

                                       δϵ X = (ϵQθ + ϵ̄Qθ̄ ) X,                                 (J.5)

where ϵ and ϵ̄ are Grassmann-odd parameters, Qθ and Qθ̄ are defined as

                                 Qθ = ∂θ − θ∂z ,       Qθ̄ = ∂θ̄ − θ̄∂z̄ .                      (J.6)

It is easy to see that Qθ , Qθ̄ anti-commute with Dθ , Dθ̄ . Consequently, under (J.5), the
variation of the action (J.2) vanishes as it is the superspace integral of a total derivative.




                                                  744
J.2    N = 1 superconformal algebra

The holomorphic N = 1 superconformal symmetry is generated by a stress-energy tensor
T (z) that obeys Virasoro algebra of central charge c, together with a fermionic current G(z)
that is a weight 23 primary with respect to the Virasoro algebra. The OPE of G(z) with itself
takes the form
                                                2c     2
                                   G(z)G(0) ∼ 3 + T (0).                                 (J.7)
                                                3z     z
One of the coefficients on the RHS is fixed by the normalization convention for G, while
the other coefficient can be fixed by applying conformal Ward identities to the correlation
function ⟨G(z1 )G(z2 )T (z3 )⟩. Acting on any operator O(0) at the origin, we can perform the
Laurent expansion of G(z)
                                               X Gr

generated by Te(z̄) and e

    Similarly to how 2D conformal symmetries obey the same group relations as holomorphic
coordinate transformations z 7→ z ′ (z), the N = 1 superconformal symmetry generated by
T (z) and G(z) can be organized according to transformations of superspace coordinates

covariantly, namely

                                   z ′ (z, θ) = f (z) + θζ(z),

                 Dθ = (Dθ θ′ )∂θ′ + (Dθ z ′ )∂z′ = (h + θ∂g)∂θ′ + (ζ + θ∂f )∂z′ .       (J.12)

sign or branch of the square root is important. We will see in section 7.2 that this is related
to the spin structure on a super Riemann surface.

J.4     N = 2 superconformal algebra

primaries with respect to the Virasoro algebra. G± carry charge ±1 with respect to the

symmetry of the underlying CFT.
   If the spectral flows by integer η are symmetries of the CFT, then the spectral flow
together with the N = 2 SCA generate the extended N = 2 superconformal algebra. In
particular, the η = ±1 spectral flow maps the identity operator to a superconformal primary

K.1     Landau-Ginzburg models

We begin with the theory of a 2D noncompact free massless scalar field ϕ, and consider the
deformation of the Euclidean action by a scalar potential term
                                          Z
                                    ∆S = d2 z V (ϕ).                                (K.1)

A regularization scheme is required to define this deformation precisely. A convenient scheme
for perturbative computations is dimensional regularization as adopted in section I.1. A dif-
ferent scheme that is natural from the perspective of conformal perturbation theory is to treat
V (ϕ) as a normal-ordered operator in the free boson CFT, and represent the deformation
by (K.1) as inserting
                             ∞
                               (−)n
                             X      Z
              exp(−∆S) =                  d2 z1 · · · d2 zn V (ϕ)(z1 , z̄1 ) · · · V (ϕ)(zn , z̄n )   (K.2)
                             n=0
                                   n!

into correlation functions, namely ⟨· · · ⟩new = ⟨e−∆S · · · ⟩old . A priori, one needs to regularize
the overlapping integrals in (K.2), e.g. by restricting the integration to |zi − zj | > ϵ for
i ̸= j, and take ϵ → 0 in the end after including the appropriate counter terms. For
V (ϕ) a polynomial, however, there are only logarithmic singularities in the integrand on
the RHS of (K.2), and the integral over zi is manifestly convergent without the need for
regularization. Note that the different schemes are generally related by a redefinition of
V (ϕ). For V (ϕ) = ℓ≤K ℓ!1 gℓ ϕℓ a degree K polynomial, the redefinition relating different
                     P

schemes can modify the coefficients gℓ but does not change the degree K.
    For even positive integer K = 2m − 2 (m ≥ 2), as V (ϕ) is bounded from below, the
deformation (K.1) is expected to define a unitary QFT. If we further assume the Z2 symmetry
ϕ → −ϕ, i.e. V (ϕ) is an even function, there are m − 1 independent dimensionful coupling
constants g2 , g4 , · · · , g2m−2 , giving rise to a (m − 2)-parameter family of theories that are
inequivalent under scaling transformation. While a generic theory in this family is massive,
for special choice of coupling coefficients the theory flows to a nontrivial CFT in the infrared.
    The equation of motion amounts to an operator equation of the form
                                          1 ¯
                                             ∂ ∂ϕ = V ′ (ϕ).                                          (K.3)
                                         πα′
In fact, (K.3) is exact in the scheme defined by (K.2), where V (ϕ) and V ′ (ϕ) are understood
as normal-ordered operators, as the RHS of (K.3) arises from the contact term in the product
of ∂ ¯
     ∂ϕ with one of the V (ϕ) insertions. At the IR fixed point, V ′ (ϕ) is dominated by the

                                                 753
term of lowest power in ϕ. For instance, with the choice V (ϕ) = ϕ2m−2 , it follows that
the operator On = ϕn is a primary with respect to the Virasoro algebra of the IR CFT for
0 ≤ n ≤ 2m − 4, whereas ϕ2m−3 is a descendant proportional to L−1 L     e−1 ϕ. In this case, the
IR CFT is none other than the m-th minimal model, with central charge (E.63) and Virasoro
primaries O0 , · · · , O2m−4 , whose OPE close within the space of Virasoro descendants of On .
The scalar field theory that flows to the minimal model CFT is also known as the Landau-
Ginzburg model.
    A particularly useful generalization is the N = 2 Landau-Ginzburg model, based on a
chiral superfield X(z, z̄, θ± , θ̄± ) of the (2, 2) superspace (section J.3) and the action
                   Z                  Z              Z               Z            
                        2          1        4             2               2    ∗
               S= dz −                    d θ XX + d θ W (X) + d θ̄ W (X) ,                 (K.4)
                                 4πα′
where the superpotential W (X) is a degree k polynomial in X. Our convention for the 2D
superspace measure is such that d4 θ ≡ dθ+ dθ− dθ̄+ dθ̄− , d2 θ ≡ dθ+ dθ− , and dθ̄2 = dθ̄+ dθ̄− .
We will focus on the case W (X) = X k , where the action (K.4) admits U (1) × U (1) R-

                               i
                      X 7→ e k (φ+ +φ− ) X,     θ± 7→ eiφ± θ± ,    θ̄± 7→ e−iφ± θ̄± .                (K.5)

In a supersymmetric Wilsonian scheme (see section M.3 for further discussions), the effec-
tive superpotential does not receive quantum corrections.445 The U (1) × U (1) R-symmetry
becomes part of the (2, 2) superconformal symmetry at the IR fixed point. The SCFT that
arises in the IR limit is in fact none other than the N = 2 minimal model considered in sec-
tion 19.4.1 with central charge (19.50). In particular, the operator On = X n for 0 ≤ n ≤ k−2
is a chiral primary with respect to the holomorphic and anti-holomorphic superconformal
                                                                                  n
algebra, whose conformal weight is determined by its R-charge to be h = e   h = 2k  .


K.2      Gauged linear sigma models

The N = 2 or (2, 2) gauged linear sigma models (GLSM) are renormalizable 2D super-
symmetric gauge theories consisting of vector and chiral matter superfields, with minimally
coupled kinetic terms and suitable gauge-invariant superpotentials. The path integral for-
mulation of the GLSM will serve as useful tools for analyzing the SCFTs that arise at the
IR fixed points.
 445
    This can be seen by considering the theory with superpotential W = gX k , where the coupling g is
replaced with a chiral superfield whose kinetic term has infinite coefficient. In a supersymmetric Wilsonian
scheme, the effective superpotential Weff must be a holomorphic function in g and X. The U (1) global
symmetry g 7→ e−ikα , X 7→ eiα X restricts Weff to be a holomorphic function of gX k , and the R-symmetry
further restricts Weff = gX k . In this sense, the superpotential is not renormalized.

L.1     Spinor representations from the Clifford algebra

The spinor representations of so(1, d − 1) can be constructed starting from a representation
of the Clifford algebra,
                                      {Γν , Γν } = 2η µν .                             (L.1)
We will begin with the case of even d, in which case the Γµ ’s can be grouped in pairs,
                  1                         1                                  d
             Γ0± ≡ (±Γ0 + Γ1 ),        Γa± ≡ (Γ2a ± iΓ2a+1 ), a = 1, 2, · · · , − 1.      (L.2)
                  2                         2                                  2
The Γa± now behave like fermion creation and annihilation operators,

                      {Γa+ , Γb− } = δ ab ,       {Γa+ , Γb+ } = {Γa− , Γb− } = 0,        (L.3)
                                              d
for a, b ranging from 0 to d2 − 1. A 2 2 -dimensional complex spinor representation of the
Clifford algebra can be built by acting Γa± on a state vector ζ that obeys
                                                                       d
                                 Γa− ζ = 0,         ∀ a = 0, · · · ,     − 1.             (L.4)
                                                                       2
In other words, the spinor representation is spanned by the basis vectors ζs , for s =
(s0 , s1 , · · · , s d −1 ), where sa = ± 21 , defined as
             2

Any representation of the Clifford algebra also gives a representation of the Lorentz algebra,
by identifying the Lorentz generators as
                                                     i

where Γµν ≡ 21 [Γµ , Γν ], so that Σµν obeys

                         [Σµν , Σρσ ] = −i (η νρ Σµσ + η µσ Σνρ − (µ ↔ ν)) .              (L.7)

The spinor representation of the Clifford algebra is not an irreducible representation of the
Lorentz algebra. Irreducible spinor representations of so(1, d−1) can be obtained by imposing
suitable chirality and/or reality conditions. To understand the latter, we shall make use of
the explicit form of the Gamma matrices in the ζs basis. Starting with the d = 2 case, in

L.2    Majorana condition and conjugation

Depending on the spacetime dimension d, the complex chiral or anti-chiral spinor represen-
tations of so(1, d − 1) may or may not be irreducible as real representations. The possibility
of a reality condition or Majorana condition on a spinor representation begins with the ob-
servation that Γµ∗ and −Γµ∗ also obey the Clifford algebra, and can be related to Γµ by a
change of basis,
                                      d
                                  (−) 2 −1 Γµ∗ = B1 Γµ B1−1 ,
                                      d                                                (L.12)
                                  (−) 2 Γµ∗ = B2 Γµ B2−1 ,
where B1 = Γ3 Γ5 · · · Γd−1 , and B2 = ΓB1 . It follows that

                                Bi Σµν Bi−1 = −Σµν∗ ,           i = 1, 2.               (L.13)

Thus, the spinor ζ and Bi−1 ζ ∗ transform in the same way under the Lorentz transformation
generated by Σµν . A reality condition of the form

                                                 ζ ∗ = Bζ                               (L.14)

for B = B1 or B2 would be compatible with Lorentz transformations. However, such a
Majorana condition can be consistent only if B ∗ B is the identity matrix. In fact, we have
B1∗ B1 = 1 for d ≡ 0 or 2 mod 8, and B2∗ B2 = 1 for d ≡ 2 or 4 mod 8. Thus, a Majorana
condition is possible in even dimension d unless d ≡ 6 mod 8.


                                                      764
    Further, a Majorana condition of the form (L.14) can be imposed simultaneously with a
chirality condition if and only if BΓB −1 = Γ∗ . For even d, this holds if d ≡ 2 mod 8. In
particular, this means that Majorana-Weyl spinors of so(1, d − 1) exists for d = 2 or 10.
   The matrices −(Γµ )T also obey the Clifford algebra, and are related to Γµ by the charge
conjugation matrix C via
                                   CΓµ C −1 = −(Γµ )T .                              (L.15)
One may adopt C = B1 Γ0 for d ≡ 2 mod 4, and C = B2 Γ0 for d ≡ 0 mod 4.
    The case of odd d can be analyzed similarly, by identifying Γ as an extra Gamma matrix
                                                              d−1
to form a d+1 dimensional Clifford algebra. This leads to a 2 2 dimensional complex spinor
representation of the Lorentz algebra. It turns out that for odd d, a Majorana condition can
be further imposed if d ≡ 1 or 3 mod 8.
   Given any complex spinor ζ, we define
                                               ζ ≡ ζ † iΓ0 ,                                 (L.16)
                                                         i     µν              i        µν
so that under Lorentz transformation ζ 7→ e− 2 ωµν Σ ζ, ζ 7→ ζe 2 ωµν Σ . A Lorentz invariant
contraction between a pair of spinors ζ, η can thus be constructed as ζη.


L.3     so(1, 9) spinor conventions

Since we make extensive use of 10D Majorana-Weyl spinors in superstring perturbation
theory, it is useful to introduce a set of spinor conventions adapted to this case. We denote
the components of a chiral spinor ζ as ζα , and those of an anti-chiral spinor ζe as ζeα̇ . The
components of the Gamma matrix are written as (Γµ )α β̇ and (Γµ )α̇ β . The Majorana condition
can be written as
                                       ζ ≡ ζ † iΓ0 = iζ T C,                             (L.17)
where C = B1 Γ0 is the charge conjugation matrix. The components of C can be written as
C αβ̇ and C β̇α . Note that C is anti-symmetric, and so C αβ̇ = −C β̇α .
    We will use C to raise the index, e.g. ζeα ≡ C αβ̇ ζe , and use C −1 to lower the index, e.g.
                                                                 β̇
ζβ ≡ ζ α̇ (C −1 )α̇β . This allows for trading lower (upper) dotted anti-chiral spinor indices with
upper (lower) undotted chiral spinor indices, thereby eliminating all dotted indices. We can
also lower or raise both indices of the Gamma matrix. The resulting matrices

In the Euclidean signature, the d-dimensional Gamma matrices can be constructed starting

M       Super-Poincaré symmetry

M.1       1-particle representations of supersymmetry

The d-dimensional N -extended super-Poincaré symmetry is generated by the Lorentz trans-
formation Mµν , translation generator or energy-momentum vector Pµ , and supercharges QA  α
(A = 1, · · · , N ) that transform in minimal spinor representations of the Lorentz algebra
so(1, d − 1). QA α commute with Pµ , and obey the anti-commutation relation

                             {QA
                               α, Q
                                   Bβ
                                      } = −2δ AB (Γµ )α β Pµ − 2iZ AB δαβ ,                           (M.1)

where QB ≡ (QB )† Γ0 , and Z AB is a central charge that commutes with all super-Poincaré
generators.
    Let us inspect the representation of the super-Poincaré algebra on massless 1-particle
states. Without loss of generality, we can consider a Lorentz frame in which the energy-
momentum vector P µ of the massless particle obeys P 0 = P 1 and P i = 0 for i = 2, · · · , d−1.
In the absence of central charge, (M.1) can be written as
                                           B †

Representing the Γµ matrices as (L.9), we may write Γ01 = 2s0 and Γ2a,2a+1 = 2sa , a =
1, 2, · · · , and trace the spinor index α with s = (s0 , s1 , · · · ). (M.2) can be equivalently
expressed as
                                         B †

exists only if N K ≤ 32. The types of minimal spinor representations: Majorana-Weyl (MW),
Majorana (M), Weyl (W), Dirac (D), their dimensions, and the maximal admissible values

    In the presence of nonzero central charge Z AB , a unitary representation of the supersym-
metry algebra (M.1) satisfies the Bogomol’nyi-Prasad-Sommerfield (BPS) bound of the form
M ≥ |Z|, where M is the invariant mass (M 2 = −Pµ P µ ), and |Z| is the smallest absolute
value of the eigenvalues of the matrix Z AB . Moreover, a state that saturates the BPS bound
is necessarily annihilated by a set of linear combinations of the supercharges.

                                              773
M.3         (Non-)renormalization in 4D N = 1 gauge theories

It is useful to characterize the quantum dynamics of an N = 1 gauge theory, a priori defined
by the path integral based on the bare action (M.30), through a Wilsonian effective action
Sµ defined by integrating out the modes of the fields in the Euclidean path integral with
momentum above the “floating cutoff” scale |p| > µ. In order to maintain manifest super-
symmetry of the Wilsonian effective action, the gauge-fixing procedure and the momentum
cutoff scheme must be defined so as to preserve supersymmetry. This requires working in
the Batalin-Vilkovisky formalism (section 5.4), and integrate out momentum modes of the
fields and anti-fields in pairs (section C.2). For applications of the BV formalism to the
renormalization of perturbative Yang-Mills theory, see Weinberg, The Quantum Theory of
Fields [184], chapter 17, and Costello, Renormalization and Effective Field Theory [250]. We
will not attempt to construct a supersymmetric Wilsonian scheme explicitly here, but simply
assume its existence and explore the consequences.
    The Wilsonian effective action Sµ is expected to admit a derivative expansion whose
lowest order terms, as constrained by supersymmetry and gauge invariance, are analogous
to those appearing in (M.30),
       Z            Z                      Z                                          
           4    1          2            α            4
                                                       X
                                                             −1             a
  Sµ = d x        Im     d θ τ (µ) tr(W Wα ) + d θ        Zi (µ)Qi exp(Va tRi )Qi + · · · ,
               4π                                       i
                                                                                     (M.31)
where each chiral superfield Qi is assumed to be in an irreducible representation Ri of the
gauge group. τ (µ) and Zi (µ) are the renormalized complexified gauge coupling and the field
renormalization factors. As one varies the cutoff µ → µ′ by integrating out modes in the
momentum shell µ′ < |p| < µ, the evolution of τ (µ), Zi (µ), as well as the coefficients of
the higher dimensional operators in the omitted terms of (M.31), are characterized by the
Wilson-Polchinski RG equations.451
    A key constraint that follows from the N = 1 supersymmetry (and the assumption of
a manifestly supersymmetric cutoff scheme) is that ∂µ τ (µ) does not depend on the other
couplings coefficients appearing in (M.31). For instance, a coupling coefficient appearing
                                  R
in the full superspace integrand d4 θ · · · can be promoted to (the expectation value of) a
                                                                         R
real superfield, which cannot appear in the chiral superspace integral d2 θ · · · . Similarly,
coupling coefficients appearing in the chiral superspace integral can be promoted to chiral
superfields, which can only appear in the chiral superspace integrand holomorphically. It
follows that the beta function µ∂µ τ (µ) ≡ β can only be a holomorphic function of τ (µ).
The latter is further constrained by the invariance under 2π shifts of the theta angle, which
 451
       Polchinski, Nucl. Phys. B 231, 269 (1984) [251].

where an are constants. In particular, a0 represents a 1-loop contribution to the beta function,
whereas an≥1 would come from instanton effects. In fact, for typical chiral matter content,
there is an anomalous U (1)R symmetry that relates the theories at different theta angles. As
such, the beta function cannot depend on τ1 , leaving only the 1-loop contribution β(τ ) = a0 .
    One should be cautious that there are other commonly adopted renormalization schemes,
in which the vector superfields and the matter chiral superfields are normalized differently.

M.4         4D N = 2 gauge theories

The Lagrangian formulation of a 4D N = 2 gauge theory involves an N = 2 vector or
gauge multiplet associated with the gauge algebra g, and hypermultiplets that transform in
a representation R with respect to g. In the N = 1 superspace formulation, the N = 2 gauge
multiplet is described by an N = 1 vector superfield V and an chiral superfield Φ ≡ Φa ta in
the adjoint representation of g, whereas the N = 2 hypermultiplet is described by a pair of
N = 1 chiral superfields Q and Q  e that transform in the representation R and its complex
conjugate R∗ of the gauge algebra.
   The action of 4D N = 2 QCD is given by the N = 1 action (M.30) with chiral matter

N.1     Spinor fields in curved space

The d-dimensional spacetime metric gµν can be expressed in terms of the local frame field
ei µ as
                            gµν = ηij ei µ ej ν , ei µ ej µ = δij .                (N.1)
The (coordinate-dependent) matrices Γµ are related to Dirac gamma matrices Γ̂i by

                                              Γµ = ei µ Γ̂i ,                              (N.2)

and obey {Γµ , Γν } = 2g µν .
   A spinor field ψ has components ψα with respect to the local frame, where α is a spinor
index. The spin connection ∇spin
                            µ    is defined as
                                                1 ij
                                   ∇spin
                                    µ ψ ≡ ∂µ ψ + ωµ Γ̂ij ψ,                                (N.3)
                                                4
where ωµ ij is defined by the property that the spin covariant derivative of the frame field ei µ
is zero, namely
                                     ∇µ ei ν + ωµ i j ej ν = 0,                           (N.4)
where ∇µ is the Levi-Civita connection, ∇µ ei ν = ∂µ ei ν − Γρµν ei ρ .


N.2     11-dimensional supergravity

The N = 1 supersymmetry algebra in 11 spacetime dimensions is generated by a Majorana
spinor supercharge Qα with 32 real components. The only massless supermultiplet that
contains particles of spin (or helicity) no greater than 2 is the supergraviton multiplet,
which consists of 256 states that fall into three irreducible representations of the spin(9)
little group, namely the symmetric traceless tensor (44), the rank-3 anti-symmetric tensor
(84), and the Rarita-Schwinger spinor (128). The corresponding off-shell fields are the
metric gµν or the frame field eµ a , a 3-form gauge field Cµνρ , and the gravitino field ψµα .

N.5         4D N = 2 supergravity

The construction of the general 4D N = 2 supergravity effective action at the 2-derivative
order458 was an important milestone. For a derivation of the full action and the relevant
supersymmetry transformations, the reader should consult the excellent book Supergravity
by Freedman and van Proeyen [249]. Here we summarize some of the essential features.
     A 4D N = 2 supergravity theory contains a graviton multiplet, nV vector multiplets, and
nH hypermultiplets. The bosonic fields consist of the metric gµν , nV + 1 vector potentials
AIµ (I = 0, · · · , nV ) which include a vector boson in the N = 2 graviton multiplet known
as the graviphoton and the rest from the vector multiplets, nV complex scalars ϕi (i =
1, · · · , nV ) from the vector multiplets, and 4nH real scalars q a (a = 1, · · · , 4nH ) from the nH
hypermultiplets. The bosonic part of the action reads

N.5.1    Special Kähler geometry

The manifold MV admits a special set of projective complex coordinates X I , I = 0, · · · , nV ,
and a homogeneous degree 2 holomorphic function F (X) known as the (local) prepotential,
that determines the Kähler potential K(ϕ, ϕ∗ ) as

                           K = −κ−2 log iκ2 X I FI − X I F I ,
                                                            
                                                                                       (N.29)

where FI ≡ ∂F∂X(X)
                 I is homogeneous in the X J ’s of degree 1, and we use the notation X I ≡
(X I )∗ . Under any holomorphic rescaling of X I , K shifts by a harmonic function, and so
the Kähler metric Gij̄ related by (M.16) is well-defined. The functions NIJ appearing in the
gauge kinetic terms are determined in terms of the prepotential via
                                      NIK X K NKL X L

also be characterized through the following property of the Riemann tensor,
                                                                   2
                      Rij̄kℓ̄ = κ2 (Gij̄ Gkℓ̄ + Gkj̄ Giℓ̄ ) − e2κ K Cikm C j̄ ℓ̄n̄ Gmn̄ ,   (N.31)

where Cijk ≡ ∂i ∂j ∂k F (X 0 = 1, X i = ϕi ), and C īj̄ k̄ ≡ (Cijk )∗ . The relation (N.31) can

derivative order 4-point amplitude of vector multiplets in terms of its factorization into (on-
shell) 3-point amplitudes with the exchange of either a supergraviton or a vector multiplet.

When the gauge group is non-Abelian, i.e. the structure constants fIJ K nonzero, the prepo-
tential is further constrained to satisfy

                                   X J fJK I FI = −CK,IJ X I X J ,                          (N.38)

for some real constants CK,IJ . This gives rise to anomalous gauge transformations that are
canceled by those of the Chern-Simons term appearing in the last line of (N.26).
   The vector fields LI i appearing in (N.27) are constrained to obey

                          LJ i (∂i + κ2 ∂i K)X I = X K fKJ I − iκ2 X I PJ0 ,                (N.39)

where PI0 is a real function (moment map) given by
                                              2

Note that (∂i +κ2 ∂i K)X I transforms homogeneously with degree 1 under holomorphic rescal-

   The vector fields MI a appearing in (N.28) are constrained to obey

              −2nH κ2 P⃗I = J⃗a b ∇b MI a ,   MI a J⃗ab MJ b = fIJ K P⃗K − κ2 P⃗I × P⃗J ,   (N.41)

where P⃗I are a triplet of moment maps.

N.6     4D N = 1 supergravity

A 4D N = 1 supergravity theory contains a graviton multiplet, nV vector multiplets, and
nC chiral multiplets. The bosonic fields consist of the metric gµν , vector potentials AA   µ
(A = 1, · · · , nV ), and complex scalars ϕi (i = 1, · · · , nC ) whose target manifold M is
equipped with a Kähler metric Gij̄ (ϕ, ϕ∗ ) that can expressed locally in terms of a Kähler
potential K(ϕ, ϕ∗ ) via (M.16).
    The gauge charges of the chiral multiplets are specified by holomorphic Killing vector
fields LA i (ϕ) on M, which are governed by a set of real-valued functions (moment maps)
PA (ϕ, ϕ∗ ) via
                             LA i = −iGij̄ ∂j̄ PA , ∇i ∂j PA = 0.                   (N.43)

                                                  787
Here ∂i and ∂j̄ stand for derivative with respect to ϕi and ϕj∗ , and ∇i is the covariant
derivative with respect to the Levi-Civita connection. Additionally, they must satisfy

                                   Gij̄ (LA i LB j̄ − LB i LA j̄ ) = ifAB C PC ,        (N.44)

where LA ī ≡ (LA i )∗ , and fAB C are the structure constants of the gauge algebra. The
superpotential W (ϕ) is a holomorphic function that obeys

                                  LA i ∂i W + κ2 (LA i ∂i K + iPA )W = 0,               (N.45)

where κ is the gravitational coupling constant.
    The gauge kinetic terms are governed by holomorphic functions τAB (ϕ) that are symmet-
ric in its indices (AB) and obey

                       LC i (ϕ)∂i τAB (ϕ) = fCA D τBD (ϕ) + fCB D τAD (ϕ) + CAB,C .     (N.46)

Here CAB,C are real constants that amount to shifts in the theta angle, and would lead to
anomalous gauge transformation that must be canceled either by including Chern-Simons
terms or against quantum gauge anomalies.460 Assuming CAB,C = 0, the bosonic part of the
4D N = 1 supergravity action is of the form
                      √

O.3     Gravitational anomaly

In d = 4k + 2 dimensions, where k is a non-negative integer, the Weyl spinor representation
is self-conjugate, and a massless Weyl fermion field coupled to gravity is a priori subject to
quantum anomaly in the diffeomorphism symmetry, also known as gravitational anomaly.

P     Boundary conformal field theory

P.1    Conformal boundary conditions

We begin by considering a two-dimensional CFT of central charge (c, ce) on half of the Eu-
clidean plane, parameterized by complex coordinate z with Im(z) ≥ 0, subject to a suitable
boundary condition along Im(z) = 0. Locally, a conformal transformation generated by the
conformal Killing vector (CKV) field v(z)∂z + ve(z̄)∂z̄ preserves the boundary geometry if the
CKV is tangent to the boundary, namely

                                  [v(z) − ve(z̄)]|Im(z)=0 = 0.                          (P.1)

The boundary condition is conformally invariant if the corresponding Noether charge
                               I                                   
                                    dz              dz̄
                        Q=−
                        b              v(z)T (z) −      ve(z̄)T (z̄)
                                                              e                     (P.2)
                                C 2πi               2πi

is conserved i.e. invariant under deformation of the contour C in the UHP with end points on
the boundary Im(z) = 0. Consequently, correlation functions of local operators on the upper
plane obey conformal Ward identities. The independence of (P.2) on the end points of C
requires (12.3) holds as an operator equation on the boundary. Note that the compatibility
of the condition (12.3) with the holomorphic and anti-holomorphic Virasoro algebra requires
c = ce.
    Under the conformal transformation (12.6), a local boundary operator ψ inserted at z =
0 is identified with a state |ψ⟩ in the Hilbert space of the CFT the strip. In fact, one
may consider the strip equipped with different boundary conditions on the two sides, e.g.
boundary condition B along Re(w) = 0 and B ′ along Re(w) = π, with the corresponding
CFT Hilbert space denoted HBB ′ . The conformal transformation identifies a state |ψ⟩ ∈
HBB ′ with an operator ψ(0) inserted at the interface between the boundary condition B
along z ∈ R− and B ′ along z ∈ R+ of the UHP.
   Let C be a contour in the UHP that begins on R+ and ends on R− . The conformal

                                    HB1 ⊕B2 ,B ′ = HB1 B ′ ⊕ HB2 B ′                       (P.15)
